limitations: Unchecked gf_list_add return values: robustness only, requires allocator failure.
Early GF_OUT_OF_MEM returns leave partially built lists to be freed by the caller's box-deletion path; reachable only on allocation failure (broken environment).
Degenerate extent loop with offset_size = length_size = index_size = 0 and extent_count = 65535 allows a bounded number of fixed-size allocations (memory pressure, no overflow).
'iloc' versions > 2 are not rejected here, but no uninitialized value is consumed on that path; FullBox version validation may exist in the framework.

Concrete security impact (crash vs. silent truncation) depends on the gf_bs_read_int implementation; on common compilers the out-of-range shift yields garbage-but-masked values, so severity is assessed as medium.

verdict.summary: diST_box_read trusts the attacker-controlled declared box size (s->size) without validating it against the bytes actually available in the input bitstream and discards the return value of gf_bs_read_data. On a crafted file whose declared box size exceeds the remaining payload, the read is short and bytes [read_count..s->size-1] of the freshly allocated buffer stay uninitialized, then line 8 null-terminates at index s->size, producing a valid string that exposes uninitialized heap contents (CWE-908). Additionally, the allocation size arithmetic sizeof(char)*(s->size+1) has no overflow/truncation guard, so on size_t-narrowing (e.g. 32-bit) builds a declared s->size of 0xFFFFFFFF truncates the allocation to 0 while the read/terminator still use the unwrapped value, yielding a heap overflow / OOB write (CWE-190).

evidence.reason: The copy-length sink gf_bs_read_data is called with the unvalidated attacker-declared s->size, and its return value (bytes actually read) is discarded; there is no check that the bitstream holds s->size bytes. Trigger: a crafted MP4/DIMS file declaring a diST box size N with only M < N payload bytes remaining — the read fills M bytes, bytes M..N-1 remain uninitialized heap, and the terminator at index s->size certifies the whole range as string content, leaking heap memory. The same unvalidated s->size feeds the unchecked s->size+1 allocation arithmetic (line 5), which wraps/truncates for extreme sizes and desynchronizes allocation size from read length and terminator index.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_data reads at most the bytes remaining in the stream (short read at exhaustion) rather than failing outright, as in GPAC's bitstream implementation; this is what leaves the buffer tail uninitialized.
s->size is the box size parsed from the attacker-supplied file and can be any value the container parser accepts, including values larger than the actual remaining data.

The heap-overflow variant of the size+1 wrap (CWE-190) is reliably reachable only where the allocator's size_t is narrower than the 64-bit box size (e.g. 32-bit builds with declared size 0xFFFFFFFF) or where a declared SIZE_MAX box size reaches this function unclamped by the generic box parser, which is not shown in this snippet.
limitations: No gf_free of a pre-existing p->content_script_types before reassignment was observed; this is only a bounded memory leak and would require the box-read to run twice on the same box instance, which this code path does not permit — not a vulnerability here.

On mainstream 64-bit builds with a box parser that clamps declared size to the remaining file bytes, the C1 info-leak requires the parser to pass a declared size larger than the actual payload; the missing intake validation is nonetheless in this function.

gf_bs_read_data's u32 length parameter truncating a u64 s->size only makes the read smaller than the allocation on 64-bit and is benign in that direction; it merges into the 32-bit overflow case already noted.

verdict.summary: xml_parse_node() recurses once per attacker-controlled XML construct: once per nested element (sub-nodes loop), and once per processing-instruction or comment construct, with no recursion depth limit anywhere in the function. PJ_CHECK_STACK() is a debug diagnostic, not a limiter. A small XML document (tens of KB) containing deeply nested elements such as repeated '<a>' — or repeated '<?x?>' / '<!--x-->' constructs — crossing a trust boundary (e.g., a network XML body parsed by this parser) drives unbounded stack growth and stack exhaustion, crashing the process (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Uncontrolled recursion sink: the sub-nodes while-loop calls xml_parse_node once per nested element with no depth limit. Trigger: an XML document of N repeated '<a>' opens; each iteration adds a stack frame, so depth grows linearly with attacker input until the stack is exhausted (CWE-674).

Second instance of the same unbounded-recursion root cause: after consuming a PI construct, the function tail-recurses per construct (same pattern at line 40 for comments) with no depth accounting; N repeated '<?x?>' constructs accumulate N stack frames, exhausting the stack (CWE-674).

assumptions: pj_scanner functions (pj_scan_get_char, pj_scan_get_until_chr, pj_scan_get_until_ch, pj_scan_get_quotes, pj_scan_strcmp) throw a syntax-error exception at EOF and the scanned buffer is NUL-terminated, per the pjlib scanner contract; under that contract the *(curptr+1) dereferences (lines 12, 80-81, 93) stay in buffer.
on_syntax_error throws a scanner exception (does not return), so the fall-through after the initial '<' check is unreachable.
alloc_node/alloc_attr internals are not shown; their initialization behavior is outside this code.
PJ_CHECK_STACK is a no-op in default builds (PJ_OS_HAS_CHECK_STACK=0), so no runtime depth protection exists.
limitations: attr->value is never assigned when an attribute has no '=' (e.g., input '<a b c>'); if alloc_attr does not zero the pool allocation, this yields an uninitialized pj_str_t later consumed by XML users (possible CWE-457). Not confirmed because alloc_attr is outside this snippet.
Mixed content (element after text, e.g., 'text') and a comment placed between the last child and the closing tag cause a thrown syntax error — parser limitations with no security impact.
A top-level '<![CDATA[' is consumed by the comment branch; this causes only parsing confusion, not memory unsafety.
Integer arithmetic on node->content.slen (line 102) was checked: curptr only advances after content.ptr is fixed, so the pointer difference cannot go negative.

verdict.summary: The Quantize kernel consumes the attacker-controlled 'axis' op attribute and the runtime shapes of the input and min/max-range tensors without any bounds or consistency validation. If axis_ >= input.dims(), input.dim_size(axis_) performs an out-of-bounds read producing an unvalidated num_slices that then drives out-of-bounds reads/writes on the output tensor. Independently, num_slices (from the input tensor's shape) is never checked against minmax_shape.num_elements() (the shape of input_min_range/input_max_range, which also sizes the allocated min/max outputs), so the slice loop indexes min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) and takes addresses of output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i)/output_max_tensor->flat<float>()(i) beyond those allocations, yielding attacker-controlled heap out-of-bounds reads and writes. Both trigger inputs (model op attributes and tensor shapes) cross a trust boundary that this code is responsible for validating at intake.

evidence.reason: axis_ is an attacker-influenced op attribute (from a serialized model) that is only checked against -1, never against input.dims(). input.dim_size(axis_) requires 0 <= axis_ < input.dims(); TensorShape::dim_size only DCHECKs this bound, so for axis_ >= input.dims() (e.g., axis=4 with a [2,2,2] input) a release build performs an out-of-bounds read of dim_sizes_, yielding an arbitrary num_slices that later drives out-of-bounds chip<1>(i) reads and writes on the output tensor via bit_casted_shaped({pre_dim, num_slices, post_dim}). Root cause: missing bounds validation of attacker-controlled axis at the trust boundary (CWE-787 via CWE-20).

num_slices is derived from input.dim_size(axis_) while output_min_tensor/output_max_tensor are allocated with minmax_shape (the shape of input_min_range, line 31-34) and min_ranges/max_ranges are the input min/max-range tensors. The code never checks minmax_shape.num_elements() == num_slices. Minimal trigger: axis=1, input shape [4,4] (num_slices=4), min/max-range tensors of shape [1]; iterations i=1..3 perform out-of-bounds reads min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) and pass out-of-bounds addresses &output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i)/&output_max_tensor->flat<float>()(i) to QuantizeSlice, which writes to them — an attacker-controlled heap buffer overflow. Root cause: missing consistency/bounds validation between two independently attacker-controlled shapes (CWE-787 via CWE-20).

assumptions: axis_ is a member populated from the op's 'axis' attribute and mode_ from the 'mode' attribute; nothing in the presented code validates axis_ against the input rank, so the code is judged as written.

Release (NDEBUG) builds are assumed for the dim_size path, where TensorShape::dim_size's bound check is a DCHECK; in debug builds that path fails fast with an assertion, but the minmax-shape mismatch (evidence 2) is exploitable in both debug and release builds.

Input tensors of non-float dtype reaching flat<float>()/flat_inner_outer_dims<float,3> cause a CHECK failure (controlled abort) rather than memory corruption; this is treated as robustness, not a vulnerability.
limitations: Candidate: dtype mismatch on 'input' (e.g., int32 tensor with flat<float>()) causes a CHECK-failure crash — denial of service by abort only, no memory-safety or authz impact, so not counted as a vulnerability.
Candidate: mode_ == QUANTIZE_MODE_MIN_FIRST with axis != -1 is handled fail-closed by OP_REQUIRES with errors::Unimplemented, so no vulnerability there.

QuantizeTensor/QuantizeSlice internals are not shown; the OOB addresses passed to QuantizeSlice are counted as the sink because their derivation and the missing precondition are fully visible in this code.
Numerical robustness of min/max range contents (e.g., NaN or inverted ranges) affects quantization quality only, with no memory-safety sink in this function.

verdict.summary: njs_module_path indexes dir->start[dir->length - 1] without verifying dir->length >= 1. The only length guard inside the dir != NULL branch tests the combined length (dir->length + info->name.length) against zero, so a non-NULL, zero-length search-path entry combined with any non-empty module name reaches an out-of-bounds read one byte before the dir buffer; the byte read also controls whether a '/' is appended to the constructed path.

evidence.reason: The expression dereferences dir->start at index dir->length - 1 without any check that dir->length != 0. The preceding guard 'if (length == 0) return NJS_DECLINED;' only rejects the case where dir->length + info->name.length == 0, so with dir != NULL, dir->length == 0 and a non-empty module name (e.g., require("x") resolved against an empty configured search-path entry), length != 0 and the code reads dir->start[-1], an out-of-bounds byte before the dir string buffer (CWE-125); the read value also determines the 'trail' flag and thus a subsequent one-byte write into src.

assumptions: info->path is declared in njs_module_info_t as char path[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1] with NJS_MAX_PATH derived from PATH_MAX, so realpath()'s output contract fits the destination buffer; this sizing is outside the shown snippet.
dir is a search-path entry from the VM's configured module paths and info->name derives from the script's require() argument; both cross trust boundaries validated by this function.
limitations: realpath() followed by open() (lines 42-47) is a symlink-swap TOCTOU window (CWE-367 pattern), but exploitation requires an attacker who can race filesystem modifications between the two calls in the operator's own module directories; recorded as an environmental race, not an intake-validation defect in this code.
If dir == NULL and info->name.length == 0, an empty string is passed to realpath(), which returns NULL and yields NJS_DECLINED; robust but with no security impact.
size_t overflow of 'length' would require multi-exabyte strings and is unreachable.

verdict.summary: SVDF Prepare reads tensor dimension arrays (input->dims->data[0], weights_feature->dims->data[0], and later weights_time->dims->data[1], input->dims->data[1], bias->dims->data[0]) without ever validating that those tensors have the required dimensionality, and validates only rank != 0 rather than rank > 0. A malicious .tflite model (attacker-controlled tensor metadata crossing the trust boundary at model load) can declare an input/weights tensor with fewer dimensions, causing an out-of-bounds heap read of the TfLiteIntArray flexible-array member, and can supply a negative rank/num_filters that flows unvalidated into output and scratch tensor sizing.

evidence.snippet:
const int batch_size = input->dims->data[0];
  const int num_filters = weights_feature->dims->data[0];
evidence.reason: The dims (TfLiteIntArray) contents come directly from the parsed model file, but no NumDimensions/dims->size check is performed before indexing data[0]. GetInputSafe only guarantees the tensor index exists, not its shape. A crafted model with a rank-0/1-D input or 0-length weights_feature dims makes this read past the end of the heap-allocated TfLiteIntArray (same unvalidated pattern repeats at lines 30-33 and 37 for weights_time->dims->data[1], input->dims->data[1], and bias->dims->data[0]; by contrast, state IS checked with NumDimensions(state)==2 at line 47, confirming the missing guard is the defect).

params->rank is attacker-controlled model metadata validated only as 'not zero', so a negative rank passes; num_filters is likewise never checked positive. With e.g. rank=-2 and num_filters=-2 the modulo check passes and a negative/ill-defined num_units is propagated into output tensor sizing (output_size_array->data[1] = num_units) and scratch sizing — a missing input-validation defect (CWE-20) at the model-load trust boundary, for which this Prepare function is the intake validation point.

assumptions: The .tflite model file is treated as attacker-controlled input, which is the standard threat model for TFLite ops (Prepare must validate model-supplied tensor metadata).

GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe guarantee the tensor index exists in the node but do not validate dims->size; TfLiteIntArray data is a flexible-array member, so indexing beyond size is a heap out-of-bounds read.
limitations: Line 49-50 performs an unchecked signed multiplication memory_size * num_filters with two attacker-chosen dims; an overflow is reachable from a crafted model, but its security impact materializes in downstream Eval/allocation behavior outside this snippet, so it is recorded as a secondary hardening concern (CWE-190) rather than a primary confirmed finding.

quantization.params is reinterpret_cast to TfLiteAffineQuantization* and scale->data[0] is read with only a type check (lines ~152-170); a NULL params/scale would crash, but the flatbuffer schema normally guarantees a non-null union value for the checked quantization type, so this is treated as a robustness edge case, not a confirmed vulnerability in this code.
num_filters == 0 passes all consistency checks and yields zero-sized output/scratch tensors; no memory-unsafe path was demonstrated for that case, so it is noted as a robustness issue only.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor indexes input(1) and input(2) with restore_index via flat<tstring>()(restore_index) without ever checking that those tensors contain at least restore_index+1 elements. While input(0) is explicitly validated to have exactly 1 element, no equivalent NumElements check exists for inputs 1 and 2. In release builds flat()'s operator() performs no bounds checking, so an attacker who supplies a tensor_names (or shape_and_slice) tensor with fewer elements than the number of restored tensors causes an out-of-bounds read of a tstring object past the tensor buffer, leading to a crash or disclosure of adjacent heap data.

evidence.snippet:
const Tensor& tensor_name_t = context->input(1);
  const string& tensor_name = tensor_name_t.flat<tstring>()(restore_index);
evidence.reason: Input(1)'s element count is never validated (contrast with input(0), which is checked for NumElements()==1 at lines 6-11), yet it is indexed with restore_index at line 16. If the caller restores N tensors and input(1) holds fewer than N strings — a state this code accepts, since the tensor's size crosses the op-input trust boundary unchecked — flat<tstring>()(restore_index) reads a tstring object out of bounds (release builds have only a DCHECK), giving an OOB read (CWE-125) used to build the tensor name passed to HasTensor/CopySliceData.

Same missing intake validation on input(2): when restore_slice is true, the shape_and_slice tensor is indexed at restore_index with no check that its NumElements exceeds restore_index. An attacker-supplied undersized input(2) yields an out-of-bounds read of a tstring, after which the garbage string is parsed by ParseShapeAndSlice and used to size the restore operation.

assumptions: restore_index is an internal caller-supplied control value (the calling Restore kernel's loop index), but the indexed tensors' sizes are attacker-controlled op inputs; the mismatch between the two is accepted at intake by this function with no check.
flat<tstring>()'s operator() bounds-checks only via DCHECK, which compiles out in release builds; the OOB read therefore occurs in production configurations.

The containment of slice_to_load within saved_shape is delegated to checkpoint::ParseShapeAndSlice and TensorSliceReader::CopySliceData, whose implementations are not shown; the in-code check parsed_shape.IsSameSize(saved_shape) constrains the shape portion of the spec, so no additional defect is claimed there.
limitations: Line 44 uses context->expected_output_dtype(0) instead of expected_output_dtype(restore_index) inside the type-mismatch error message: misleading diagnostics only, no security impact.
CHECK_NOTNULL(reader) at line 32 cannot fail because the preceding branches always assign reader; robustness-only, not a vulnerability.
Exploitability of the OOB tstring read beyond crashing depends on heap layout of adjacent allocations; the defective read path itself is fully reachable as written.

verdict.summary: The historical stack-buffer-overflow in ReadPCLImage's token-accumulation loop is patched: the write '*p++=(char) c' is followed by a verified bounds condition '(size_t)(p-command) < (MaxTextExtent-1)' that guarantees data writes stay below index MaxTextExtent-2 and the NUL terminator at worst occupies index MaxTextExtent-1, then resets p. Delegate command construction substitutes only numerically formatted values and generated unique temp filenames into a trusted config template, so no command or format injection exists. The one reachable defect is a validation gap on attacker-controlled CropBox/MediaBox coordinates (negative deltas wrap via the (size_t) cast of CastDoubleToLong's negative result to ~SIZE_MAX page dimensions), but within this function those values reach only length-bounded numeric formatting, the delegate command line as a numeric -g argument, and image->page metadata; they never size an allocation, index memory, or form a string sink, so the impact in this code is robustness/DoS-level and is recorded in limitations.

assumptions: CastDoubleToLong is ImageMagick's standard helper that clamps to [LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX] and returns 0 for NaN, so the floor(...) result cannot produce an invalid long conversion.

delegates.xml / GetDelegateCommands is trusted local configuration, not data crossing a trust boundary; MaxTextExtent == MagickPathExtent == 4096 and AcquireString allocates MagickPathExtent extra bytes, so the density/options FormatLocaleString calls are in-bounds.

image_info options (page, density-derived resolutions, ping, number_scenes) are caller API configuration treated as trusted under the ImageMagick coder threat model; the attacker-controlled surface is the decoded PCL blob.
limitations: Improper input validation of parsed file geometry (potential CWE-20): a PCL file containing a token such as 'CropBox [1 1 0 0' yields a negative x2-x1 delta; CastDoubleToLong returns -1 and the (size_t) cast wraps it to ~SIZE_MAX, so page.width/page.height become enormous. Within this function the value only feeds bounded numeric FormatLocaleString calls, the '-g%.20gx%.20g' delegate option (numeric, no injection), and image->page metadata; any memory-safety or exhaustion consequence would occur in the external GhostPCL delegate or in downstream consumers of image->page, not in this code. Reaching an out-of-range double-to-size_t conversion at the page.width recomputation additionally requires resolution > 72.

The return value of ExternalDelegateCommand is stored in 'status' and never checked, but the subsequent ReadImage on the delegate's output fails closed via the NULL check, so this is not a fail-open path.
When read_info->number_scenes != 0, FormatLocaleString overwrites 'options', silently dropping the '-g' geometry option — a functional bug, not security-relevant.
On the delegate_info == NULL early return, the input_filename temporary file is not relinquished — a bounded one-file-per-call resource leak with no exhaustion path inside this function.
The 'geometry' buffer is formatted but never used (dead store), and the stale count==4 flag merely recomputes identical geometry on later delimiter tokens — both harmless.

verdict.summary: MakeDataset validates only the shapes (matrix/vector) of the attacker-supplied 'indices', 'values', and 'dense_shape' tensors, never their dtypes or column counts, then accesses indices and dense_shape as int64 via indices->matrix<int64_t>()(i, 0) and dense_shape->vec<int64_t>(). A caller of this op can supply indices of a non-int64 dtype (e.g., DT_INT32), causing an incompatible-type read of the tensor buffer (fatal CHECK failure or misinterpreted/OOB read depending on build). Independently, indices with shape [n, 0] together with values of shape [0] satisfies every check in this function (IsMatrix([n,0]) is true and the empty-consistency branch sees 0 == 0), after which the loop reads element (i, 0) out of a zero-element buffer for i = 0..n-1 — an out-of-bounds read. dense_shape's dtype and element validity are likewise unchecked before vec<int64_t>() and TensorShape construction. All triggers are reachable purely from untrusted op inputs this code itself accepts.

evidence.reason: Typed int64 access into the attacker-controlled 'indices' tensor without any validation that indices->dtype() == DT_INT64 and without any check that indices->dim_size(1) >= 1; only matrix-ness (dims()==2) was verified. Concrete triggers: (a) indices supplied as an int32 or float matrix [k,k'] makes matrix<int64_t>() reinterpret a non-int64 buffer (accessor CHECK-abort, or type-confused/OOB read in builds without the release check); (b) indices = int64 tensor of shape [5,0] with values = shape [0] passes IsMatrix and the 0==0 empty-consistency branch, then the loop reads (i,0) from a zero-element, 5x0 buffer — an out-of-bounds read for i = 0..4 (Eigen index assertions are compiled out in release).

The attacker-controlled 'dense_shape' tensor is read via vec<int64_t>() and its raw elements are used to construct a TensorShape, with no check anywhere in this function that dense_shape->dtype() == DT_INT64 or that its elements form a valid (non-negative) shape. Supplying dense_shape as a float or int32 vector reaches this sink through every preceding check (which test only shapes), producing an incompatible-type read of the buffer and a TensorShape built from garbage, before SparseTensor::Create can perform any validation.

assumptions: Row-count consistency between indices->dim_size(0) and values->NumElements() when both are nonzero, and order-permutation consistency of std_order, are delegated to sparse::SparseTensor::Create; this analysis assumes Create performs those checks on the path shown, so they are not treated as gaps of this snippet.

Exact runtime consequence of the missing dtype checks depends on the TensorFlow build: if Tensor::matrix<T>()/vec<T>() enforce a release-mode dtype CHECK the result is a reachable fatal CHECK failure (denial of service); if not, the result is a type-confused or out-of-bounds read. The [n,0]-indices out-of-bounds read at line 43 holds even with a correct int64 dtype and thus does not depend on this assumption.

The op's inputs are untrusted: any client able to invoke the op (e.g., via tf.data.Dataset or raw op execution on untrusted models/saved graphs) controls the dtypes, shapes, and contents of indices, values, and dense_shape.
limitations: The ordering check next_batch_index >= previous_batch_index permits a first batch index of -1 (previous_batch_index is initialized to -1) and permits duplicate batch indices; within this snippet those values only feed the monotonicity gate and are passed downstream, so no memory-unsafe sink was demonstrable in this code alone.

The empty-vs-empty consistency check (lines 18-25) only fires when one of the tensors has zero elements; a nonzero row-count mismatch between indices and values is not caught here and is relied upon to be caught by SparseTensor::Create.

If a hosting environment never exposes this op to untrusted input, the triggers would require a trusted-caller contract violation; judged on the code as written (a user-invokable TensorFlow op), the missing intake validation is the vulnerability.

verdict.summary: DecodeChunk validates chunk/tile offsets from the EXR file's offset table with overflow-prone arithmetic: 'offsets[i] + sizeof(int)*5 > size' (tiled) and 'offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int)*2 > size' (scanline). offsets entries are attacker-controlled 64-bit file values; a value near UINT64_MAX (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0) wraps the addition modulo 2^64 to a small number, so the guard passes, and 'head + offsets[i]' plus the subsequent memcpy reads (tile coordinates / line_no / data_len) dereference memory outside the 'size'-byte chunk buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read reachable from a malicious EXR file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the bounds check on the attacker-supplied 64-bit tile offset (read from the file's offset table) is performed with wraparound-prone unsigned arithmetic. With offsets[tile_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0 and size >= 20, the sum wraps to 4, the check passes, and head + offsets[tile_idx] (used by the memcpy of tile_coordinates at line 106) reads out of bounds.

Same root cause on the scanline path: with offsets[y_idx] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF9 and size >= 8, the sum wraps to 1, the insufficient-data guard passes, and head + offsets[y_idx] feeds memcpy(&line_no, ...) and memcpy(&data_len, ...) which read bytes before the chunk buffer.

assumptions: offsets entries are chunk offsets taken from the EXR file's offset table and reach DecodeChunk without 64-bit range pre-sanitization (any upstream clamping is outside this snippet); as written, the values used in the checks are arbitrary attacker-supplied file data.

64-bit platform (sizeof(void*) == 8), where head + offsets[i] with an offset near UINT64_MAX wraps to a pointer before/around the buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read; on any width the arithmetic is still unchecked and the guard is bypassable.
limitations: Signed overflow UB in 'line_no + num_scanline_blocks' (scanline path) is reachable with line_no near INT_MAX, but every resulting state is rejected by the num_lines <= 0, int64 range, and line_no < 0 guards, so no defective value reaches a sink; recorded as UB/robustness note, not a vulnerability.

Results of calloc and AllocateImage are not NULL-checked; a huge attacker-supplied tile_size_x/y can drive allocation failure and a later NULL dereference in DecodeTiledPixelData — crash/DoS robustness only, needs a failing allocator.
tile_coordinates[0..1] are passed to DecodeTiledPixelData without range validation; the sink is outside this code and could not be verified here.
Benign data race on the 'invalid_data' flag under OpenMP (error flag only, no security impact).

verdict.summary: This is the patched Flatpak setup_seccomp: the TIOCSTI ioctl block (CVE-2017-5226) and the clone3/new mount-API blocks (GHSA-67h7-w3jq-vh4q) are present, and the socket-family allowlist gap arithmetic is correct for all run_flags combinations. All attacker-influenceable inputs (arch string, run_flags, allowed_personality) reach only string comparisons and bit tests against static tables; no tainted value reaches a memory, length, path, format, or authorization sink. Remaining error-handling weaknesses (non-EFAULT rule-add errors and seccomp_rule_add_exact/socket results ignored, unchecked lseek) are fail-open only under environment failure (e.g., ENOMEM) or documented libseccomp limitations, and are recorded as limitations rather than reachable vulnerabilities.

assumptions: libseccomp's default BADARCH behavior kills syscalls issued under architectures not added to the filter, so syscalls from non-native ABIs (e.g., x32) cannot bypass the blocklist when the matching arch token was not added.
SCMP_SYS(x) resolves to compile-time kernel syscall numbers; unknown-to-the-kernel syscalls cannot be invoked by the guest even when a rule for them fails to be added.

run_flags and the arch string originate from app/runtime metadata and install/system configuration (app packer or local admin influence) but are consumed only via strcmp and bit tests against compile-time constants.
limitations: Fail-open error handling at the seccomp_rule_add result checks: the condition 'r < 0 && r == -EFAULT' returns an error only for -EFAULT, so other rule-add failures (e.g., -ENOMEM under host memory pressure) are silently ignored, leaving that syscall permitted under the SCMP_ACT_ALLOW default. Not judged a vulnerability because no attacker-controlled input can produce the failure; it requires a broken/pressured host environment.

Return values of seccomp_rule_add_exact in the socket-family loop are deliberately ignored (per the in-code comment referencing seccomp/libseccomp issue #8): on 32-bit/multiarch sandboxes the socket-family blocklist may not be enforced. Exploitation would additionally require capabilities (e.g., CAP_NET_RAW for AF_PACKET/AF_BLUETOOTH) that sandboxed processes do not hold in the host network namespace, so this is treated as a documented defense-in-depth limitation.
lseek(seccomp_tmpf.fd, 0, SEEK_SET) return value is unchecked; failure requires a pathological /tmp/tmpfs and would result in a malformed seccomp program that fails closed in bubblewrap.
The filter uses a default-allow posture (SCMP_ACT_ALLOW with a blocklist) rather than default-deny; this is the upstream design and not a defect introduced by this code.
In --devel mode the ptrace/perf_event_open/personality restrictions are intentionally omitted; this is documented developer-mode behavior.

verdict.summary: No reachable security defect in this code. Every crypto sink (X509_digest, EVP_DigestUpdate) has its return value asserted (fail-closed) and every buffer/length precondition is enforced before use: hash_buffer is EVP_MAX_MD_SIZE (64 bytes) while X509_digest with EVP_sha256 writes exactly 32 bytes, and hash_length is pinned to SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH by an assert before it is read. The config-derived allow lists flow only as opaque bytes into the hash and never reach indexing, allocation sizing, format strings, or path sinks. The only substantive weakness found — the digest folds verify_certificate_hash_list_ and verify_certificate_spki_list_ bytes without domain separation — requires an administrator to configure the identical 32-byte SHA-256 value into two mutually exclusive, semantically different fields on listeners sharing resumption state; no attacker-controlled input can create that state, so it is a hardening note, not a vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: verify_certificate_hash_list_ and verify_certificate_spki_list_ are std::vector-like containers of uint8_t (so sizeof(value_type)==1 and the size arithmetic is an identity), populated from admin-controlled configuration, with entries validated as SHA-256 digests at config load (Envoy's documented contract).

Session-id digest is finalized by the caller via EVP_DigestFinal_ex, which returns the final length; therefore hash_length being passed by value (so the caller's copy is not updated by X509_digest) has no effect on the caller.
The member vectors are not mutated concurrently with this function (config contexts are swapped wholesale, not edited in place).
limitations: hash_length is passed by value but handed to X509_digest as an out-parameter (&hash_length); the caller's variable is never updated. Benign here: the value is written by X509_digest, asserted to equal SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH, and only then read — but the signature is misleading and should use a reference or the value should be ignored.

No domain separation in the digest between hash-list and SPKI-list entries (no labels or lengths are mixed in). Two validators sharing session-resumption state, one configured with verify_certificate_hash_list_=[X] and the other with verify_certificate_spki_list_=[X] (same 32-byte X), produce identical digest contributions, so a session fully validated under one acceptance semantics could be resumed under the other. Dismissed as a vulnerability because this requires an administrator misconfiguration (the same hash placed in two mutually exclusive fields), not any attacker-reachable input; recorded as a hardening recommendation (mix a mode tag/list lengths into the digest).
RELEASE_ASSERT on any crypto failure aborts the process — an availability (crash) behavior, but fail-closed and intentional, not a security vulnerability.

If ca_cert_ is null and both allow lists are empty, the function adds nothing to the digest; all such validators share the same digest contribution, which is semantically correct since their acceptance behavior is also identical.
Potential integer overflow in hash.size() * sizeof(value_type) is unreachable (size_t arithmetic over fixed-size SHA-256 entries).

verdict.summary: BD_DecMFFieldVec decodes an attacker-controlled element count (nbFields, up to 2^31-1 via NbBits read from the BIFS bitstream) and passes it unvalidated as the allocation size to gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc and as the loop/index bound for gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item. A crafted bitstream (NbBits=31, nbFields=0x7FFFFFFF) can overflow the allocation-size arithmetic, causing an undersized heap allocation followed by out-of-bounds writes over nbFields loop iterations, or at minimum force a multi-GB allocation from ~36 bits of input (memory exhaustion).

evidence.reason: The BIFS bitstream is a trust boundary, and nbFields (attacker-controlled, range 0..2^31-1 when NbBits=31) is decoded here with no cardinality/bounds validation. This is the intake point where the check is missing; the unvalidated value flows directly into allocation sizing and loop bounds.

Sink: the unvalidated attacker count nbFields is used as the allocation element count (gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc) and as the loop bound whose per-iteration gf_sg_vrml_mf_get_item indexes/writes item i. Trigger: encode NbBits=31 and nbFields=0x7FFFFFFF in the stream; element sizes >=4 bytes overflow the byte-size computation, yielding a small allocation while the loop writes 2^31-1 items, producing a heap out-of-bounds write. Even without wrap, the same input forces an enormous allocation (DoS).

assumptions: gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc computes the byte size from the element count (e.g., count * per-element size with fixed-width arithmetic); a wrapped product yields a successful small allocation, after which the loop's per-item writes are out of bounds.
gf_bs_read_int returns zeros (not an error that halts decoding) when reading past the end of the bitstream, so the nbFields-iteration loop runs to completion.
BIFS command streams are attacker-supplied content (e.g., MP4 file or streamed scene), so bs is untrusted input this decoder is responsible for validating at intake.
limitations: Memory leaks on early error returns in the MFNODE branch (registered child nodes are not unregistered when gf_node_register or gf_node_list_add_child_last fail mid-loop) — robustness defect with no demonstrated exhaustion path.

gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length stores the unvalidated nbFields into decoder state used by later QP14 decoding; any defective use of that state occurs outside this snippet (same root cause, no separate sink here).
Commented-out assignments (qp_local = 1; qp_local = 0;) are dead code/style issues only.
The QP handling path (gf_bifs_dec_qp_set / gf_bifs_dec_qp_remove with local/global flags) relies on decode-time behavior not visible in this snippet; no concrete defect established within this code.

verdict.summary: The Gather kernel validates only that indices are non-negative but never checks them against the size of the input's gathered dimension. A model-supplied positions tensor with all-nonnegative values greater than or equal to the axis dimension size passes the TF_LITE_ENSURE gate and is used by optimized_ops::Gather to read input tensor data out of bounds, enabling information disclosure (leaked values flow into the output tensor) or a crash.

evidence.reason: This is the only validation applied to the attacker-controlled positions/indices tensor, and it enforces only the lower bound (index >= 0). There is no check that each index is less than the size of the input tensor's gathered dimension before optimized_ops::Gather (line 18) uses these indices to address input data. Trigger: a model supplies an all-nonnegative indices tensor, e.g., a single int32 index 0x7FFFFFFF against an input of shape [2, ...]; the ensure passes and Gather reads far past the input buffer, an out-of-bounds read whose result is written to the output tensor and is observable downstream.

assumptions: positions, input, and params originate from a model file or runtime op outputs, which are treated as attacker-influenced (trust boundary).
PositionsT (int32/int64) matches the positions tensor type selected by the kernel dispatch; the negative-value scan and the Gather kernel read the same buffer with the same element width.

The generic optimized_ops::Gather implementation does not independently bounds-check indices against the input dimension; the validation obligation falls on this wrapper, which is where the check is missing.
Exploitation as an info leak assumes the output tensor (which receives the out-of-bounds-read values) is observable through subsequent graph operations or returned tensors, which is the normal case.
limitations: No TOCTOU issue: within this single-threaded kernel invocation, positions data cannot change between the validation loop and the Gather call.
positions->bytes not being a multiple of sizeof(PositionsT) only truncates num_indices in the scan; no out-of-bounds access results within this code.
Potential type confusion between PositionsT and the actual tensor dtype requires the op resolver to violate kernel registration contracts, which this code cannot itself produce.
axis/batch_dims from params are forwarded to the framework Gather kernel; framework-level axis validation is outside this code's scope and no defect is produced here.

verdict.summary: check_attestation_fido_u2f builds the U2F signature payload into a fixed 200-byte stack buffer (data_signed[200]) using memcpy calls whose lengths (credential_id_len, cert_x_len, cert_y_len, and rpid_hash_len) come from the attacker-controlled WebAuthn/FIDO registration response and are never bounds-checked in this code. A registration with a credential id longer than 70 bytes (or oversized COSE key coordinates) overflows the stack buffer with attacker-controlled bytes, enabling memory corruption and potential code execution.

evidence.reason: Unbounded memcpy into the fixed 200-byte stack buffer data_signed: credential_id and credential_id_len are attacker-controlled registration data crossing the trust boundary, and this function performs no check that data_signed_offset + credential_id_len <= sizeof(data_signed). Trigger: a registration response with a credential id of 300 bytes reaches this line after all preceding checks pass, copying 300 bytes into ~135 bytes of remaining buffer space and then writing 0x04 out of bounds at line 111 — stack memory corruption with attacker-controlled content.

Second unbounded memcpy into the same fixed stack buffer: cert_x_len and cert_y_len come from the attacker-supplied COSE key in the registration response and are never asserted to be 32 (the U2F protocol requirement) or bounds-checked against data_signed_offset before copying. Trigger: a registration whose COSE key carries x/y byte strings of arbitrary length overflows data_signed[200] even with a short credential id; identical defect at lines 114-115 for cert_x.

assumptions: credential_id/cert_x/cert_y and their lengths are derived from the client-supplied WebAuthn registration response (attStmt/authData/COSE key), as in the upstream Glewlwyd caller; under any reading, this function itself documents and enforces no length constraints on them.

rpid_hash_len is expected to be 32 by protocol contract but is likewise not verified inside this function (line 102 copies rpid_hash_len bytes unchecked); a caller passing a non-32 value would also overflow.
limitations: Map-key matching uses o_strncmp with MIN(strlen("x5c"), key_len), so a CBOR key of "x5" or "si" is misdispatched as "x5c"/"sig"; both values are still strictly type- and size-checked downstream, so this is a logic quirk with no demonstrated security impact.

cbor_bytestring_handle(att_cert) is taken at line 53 without verifying att_cert is a bytestring; the value only feeds gnutls_x509_crt_import, a validating parser with a handled error path, so this is robustness only.
The 'break' statements inside the for-loop (lines 39/45) exit only the loop, not the do-while, but the subsequent x5c == NULL check at line 48 still reports the error, so control flow remains safe.

verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi computes rpsi_len from the attacker-controlled RTCP 16-bit length field without validating it is >= 2, causing an unsigned wrap; the subsequent guard 'length < rpsi_len + 12' itself wraps and fails open. Additionally, the payload byte 'padlen' is subtracted without any bound, underflowing rpsi_bit_len. The wrapped length reaches pj_strset, which sets rpsi->rpsi to point at up to ~8KB beyond the actual packet buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read on remotely supplied RTCP PSFB RPSI packets.

evidence.reason: The RTCP length field is attacker-controlled but never validated to be >= 2. With length field = 0, (0-2)*4 = -8 wraps to a huge pj_size_t, and the guard's own addition 'rpsi_len + 12' wraps to 4, so the check 'length < 4' always passes for any length >= 8. The missing lower-bound validation is the root cause; the wrapped guard fails open and lets the poisoned length flow to the pj_strset sink.

padlen is an attacker-controlled payload byte never validated against the available payload bits. Trigger: a 16-byte packet with hdr->length = 3 (rpsi_len = 4) and padlen = 0xFF makes '32 - 16 - 255' underflow to a huge value; pj_strset then sets rpsi->rpsi to a ~8KB length against a 16-byte buffer, reading far out of bounds (CWE-125 via CWE-190). The same sink is also reached via the rpsi_len underflow of lines 18-19.

assumptions: 'length' is assumed to be the actual size of the buffer 'buf', per the documented contract; both triggers use consistent length values, so the vulnerabilities hold under this contract.
rpsi->rpsi_bit_len is presumed to be a 16-bit field per the pjmedia RTCP-FB API; if it were wider, the out-of-bounds read would be even larger, so the finding stands either way.
limitations: The unvalidated read of padlen/pt at buffer offsets 8-9 when length == 8 (guard only enforces length >= 8, and the wrapped check reduces to length >= 4) is a 1-2 byte out-of-bounds read subsumed by the same missing length-field validation at line 18.
The code performs no semantic validation of the RPSI payload contents (e.g., that the payload type byte is meaningful), which is a robustness issue, not a memory-safety vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The Gather op forwards attacker-influenced data (index values from the positions tensor, and the model-supplied axis/batch_dims parameters) straight into optimized_ops::Gather without validating that indices are within the gathered input dimension or that axis/batch_dims are consistent with the input and positions shapes. A malicious or corrupted model can supply out-of-range position values or an invalid axis, causing an out-of-bounds read of the input tensor's memory inside the gather loop.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing intake validation at the op trust boundary. The model-controlled 'params.axis' and 'params.batch_dims' are assigned verbatim (lines 4-5) and the attacker-influenced positions index values (GetTensorData<PositionsT>(positions), line 8) are passed straight into the gather sink (lines 6-9) with no check that each index lies within the gathered dimension of 'input' and no check that axis/batch_dims are consistent with the tensor shapes. Trigger: a model whose positions tensor contains an index >= the size of the gathered axis (e.g., input shape [2,3], axis=0, positions=[100000]) reaches the memory-indexing loop in optimized_ops::Gather and reads out of bounds (CWE-125 / CWE-20).

assumptions: Tensor data (including positions values) and the axis/batch_dims parameters originate from the serialized model and runtime tensor inputs, which cross a trust boundary and are treated as untrusted.

optimized_ops::Gather performs the actual indexing with only the shapes/data passed to it; since this wrapper provides no validated guarantee, the callee's index and axis preconditions are unenforced.
limitations: A potential output-buffer overflow (CWE-787-style write) was considered but depends on the runtime's tensor allocation, which happens outside this function; it is a downstream consequence of the same missing validation, not a separate defect in this code.

Integer overflow in the callee's size/offset arithmetic and the unconditional kTfLiteOk return (no error path exists at this layer) were considered and judged to be consequences of the same missing-check root cause rather than independent vulnerabilities in this code.

Analysis is based solely on the given snippet; if the enclosing TFLite framework performs equivalent validation before invoking this wrapper, exploitability would be reduced, but no such check is visible in this code.

verdict.summary: TensorSliceReader::CopySliceData passes data parsed from a checkpoint-file record (sts.data().data(), i.e. raw TensorProto tensor_content bytes) directly into CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice without validating that the buffer's length matches the element count implied by the stored slice 'slice_s' within tss->shape(), nor that its dtype matches T. A crafted or untrusted checkpoint shard file can supply an undersized (or wrong-dtype) tensor_content; after ParseProtoUnlimited succeeds, the copy reads prod(intersection of slice_s and slice) elements of type T from the undersized heap buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read that leaks memory into the returned slice. Only proto parse success is checked (line 35); no size or dtype check exists between the parse and the copy sink.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unvalidated trust-boundary data used at a bulk-copy sink. 'value' (raw record bytes from the checkpoint sstable) is parsed into SavedTensorSlices 'sts' at line 35 with only a parse-success check; the tensor_content buffer 'sts.data().data()' is then reinterpreted as elements of type T and used as the copy source with no check that its byte length equals prod(slice_s extents within tss->shape()) * sizeof(T) and no dtype check. Trigger: a checkpoint file whose record for key EncodeTensorNameSlice(name, slice_s) is a well-formed proto with an undersized data().tensor_content(); FindTensorSlice succeeds, sss_[idx]->Get returns the record, ParseProtoUnlimited succeeds, and the copy reads past the end of the heap buffer holding the content — heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) via missing input validation at the file-intake boundary (CWE-20).

assumptions: The caller allocates 'data' large enough for the requested 'slice' (standard contract of this function); the destination-side write geometry is bounded because FindTensorSlice only matches query slices within tss->shape(), enforced here by the null check at lines 14-17.
TensorProtoData<T>(proto) exposes the raw tensor_content buffer reinterpreted as T, so the buffer's actual length is the length of the attacker-supplied content string.

The checkpoint/sstable files being read are a trust boundary this reader validates at intake; loading an attacker-supplied or corrupted checkpoint is the realistic threat model (as with the equivalent upstream TensorFlow fix).
limitations: CHECK_GE(idx, 0) at line 25 aborts the process if the loaded metadata references a filename absent from fname_to_index_; this requires an internally inconsistent state not producible by the normal load path and is at worst a controlled crash (availability), so it is not counted as a vulnerability.

'tss' is used after the mutex scope closes, but it points into the member tensor_slice_set_ map which is not mutated on this path after the lookup (LoadAllShards is only called earlier under the same lock); no use-after-free path exists in this code.

No arithmetic on attacker-controlled integers is performed in this function itself; geometry computation resides in CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice (outside the given code) and was analyzed only through its source-buffer precondition.

verdict.summary: iloc_box_read reads the 4-bit offset_size, length_size, base_offset_size and index_size fields directly from the attacker-controlled MP4 file and never validates them against their spec limits (0/4 for offset, length and index; 0/4/8 for base_offset). These unvalidated nibbles are multiplied by 8 and passed to gf_bs_read_int, a u32-returning bit reader that can legally consume at most 32 bits, so a crafted iloc box (e.g., base_offset_size=15) makes it request up to 120 bits, violating the callee's contract, producing truncated/garbage offsets or a reachable assertion abort, while spec-legal values like base_offset_size=8 (64 bits) already exceed the 32-bit reader. All box-size accounting via ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is internally consistent, so the root defect is the missing trust-boundary validation of these parsed size fields.

evidence.reason: base_offset_size is an unvalidated 4-bit value read from the file (line 9) that this code lets range 0-15 (spec allows only 0/4/8). The multiplier 8*base_offset_size can therefore reach 120 bits, which is passed to gf_bs_read_int, a u32-returning reader limited to 32 bits; trigger: a crafted iloc box with base_offset_size=15 (or the spec-legal 8) reaches this sink after the matching ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, 2+base_offset_size) passes, causing an out-of-contract read (assertion abort / truncated base_offset). Root cause: missing validation of attacker-controlled parsed metadata at the trust boundary.

offset_size and length_size are unvalidated 4-bit file-supplied fields (line 7-8); the same crafted-box trigger (e.g., offset_size=15 or length_size=15) drives gf_bs_read_int with up to 120 bits, again exceeding the 32-bit capacity of the u32-returning reader. The ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, offset_size+length_size) accounting matches the byte count, so the defect is the missing input validation, not the size accounting.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE is the standard GPAC macro that returns GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE when the remaining box size is smaller than the requested byte count and otherwise subtracts it; no wraparound is possible with the byte counts used here (max 30).

gf_bs_read_int returns u32 and, by signature and GPAC contract, is intended for at most 32-bit reads (GPAC provides gf_bs_read_long_int for wider fields); the exact behavior on nBits>32 (assertion abort vs. silent truncation) is in the callee, outside the given code.
The box's declared size (ptr->size) is assumed pre-validated against the real file length by the upstream box parser, so reads covered by ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE stay within the file.
limitations: A secondary resource-exhaustion issue exists: with offset_size=length_size=0, each extent-iteration consumes zero box bytes while still performing GF_SAFEALLOC + gf_list_add, so a crafted box (extent_count=0xFFFF per item, many items) amplifies a small file into up to ~65k heap allocations per item (CWE-400-style memory/CPU exhaustion DoS). It is reachable but is an availability/robustness issue, not memory corruption.

Early returns on GF_OUT_OF_MEM leave already-added entries in ptr->location_entries / extent_entries lists; these are owned by the box and freed by the standard GPAC box destructor on parse failure, so this is not a leak.
The item_count and extent_count loops are correctly bounded by the ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE accounting (each item iteration consumes at least 2-4 bytes), so no unbounded-loop finding survives.

verdict.summary: DecodeChunk validates attacker-controlled 64-bit chunk offsets from the EXR file with a wraparound-prone unsigned addition (`offsets[i] + sizeof(int)*N > size`). An offset near 2^64 (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC tiled, 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 scanline) wraps the sum to a small value, bypassing the guard, after which `head + offsets[i]` produces a wildly out-of-bounds pointer that is read by memcpy (tile coordinates / line_no / data_len) and fed to the pixel decoders, causing out-of-bounds reads in both the tiled and scanline paths.

evidence.reason: Root cause (tiled path): the only intake bounds check for the attacker-controlled uint64 offset is the unsigned addition `offsets[tile_idx] + 20`, which wraps modulo 2^64. Trigger: tiled EXR with offsets[0] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEC makes the sum 0 <= size, the guard passes, then line 103 computes data_ptr = head + (2^64 - 20) and line 106 memcpy(tile_coordinates, data_ptr, 16) reads out of bounds (line 121 reads at data_ptr+16; data_size at line 101 also underflows to `size`, letting attacker data_len pass line 125 and driving an OOB decompression read at data_ptr+20).

Root cause (scanline path): same wraparound defect — `offsets[y_idx] + 8` is computed in 64-bit unsigned arithmetic. Trigger: scanline EXR with offsets[0] = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8 wraps the sum to 0, the guard passes, line 192 computes data_ptr = head - 8, and the 4-byte memcpys at lines 195 and 197 read 8 bytes before the input buffer; with data_size underflowing to `size` at line 190, a small valid data_len then reaches DecodePixelData which decodes from the unvalidated out-of-bounds pointer.

assumptions: `offsets`, `exr_header` fields, and `head`/`size` all originate from an attacker-supplied EXR file and cross a trust boundary at this function; no documented caller contract pre-validates offsets, and this code's own checks are the enforcement point.

Bodies of DecodeTiledPixelData, DecodePixelData, AllocateImage, and ComputeChannelLayout are not shown; tile_coordinates[0]/[1] are passed unvalidated to DecodeTiledPixelData and the row bounds handed to DecodePixelData are verified here, so callee-internal defects cannot be confirmed from this code alone.
limitations: Unchecked calloc result for exr_image->tiles (lines 82-83) followed by the write at line 87: NULL-pointer dereference crash, but only reachable under memory-allocation failure with an enormous attacker-chosen tile count (OOM DoS, environment-dependent) — not counted as a vulnerability.

Data race on the shared bool invalid_data under `#pragma omp parallel for` (acknowledged by the in-code TODO): writes are monotonic false->true of an aggregate flag with no memory-safety consequence — not a vulnerability.
Early returns inside the tiled loop (lines 98, 114, 117, 129) leak exr_image->tiles and already-allocated tile images (resource leak with no exhaustion path within a single call).

On 32-bit builds the overflow heuristic `total_data_len_overflown` is hardcoded false and size_t(data_width)*size_t(data_height)*size_t(num_channels) can wrap, fail-opening the oversized-image guard; the subsequent allocation occurs in the unseen AllocateImage so no OOB is confirmable in this code.

exr_image->num_tiles is left unset when num_tiles == 0 or on early error return, and static_cast<int>(num_tiles) would truncate for > INT_MAX offsets (impractical memory-wise) — state-hygiene issues only.

verdict.summary: In IsConstantFoldable, the loop over the shape_map entry for a node uses the attacker-influenced length of the shape list as its bound and indexes n->output_type(i) without ever checking i < n->num_outputs(). A crafted GraphDef/SavedModel can attach more shape entries than the node has outputs, causing an out-of-bounds read at n->output_type(i). Additionally, the oversized-constant guard 'num_elements() * DataTypeSize(...) > max_constant_size_in_bytes' can overflow/wrap for large fully-defined shapes, fail-open bypassing the size limit and enabling oversized constant folding (DoS).

evidence.reason: The loop bound is the size of the shape list stored in shape_map, which derives from attacker-controlled serialized graph attributes, and it is never validated against the node's actual output count before the index i is used in the sink n->output_type(i). A crafted model with more shape entries than declared outputs (e.g., a 1-output op with a 5-entry shape list) reaches n->output_type(i) for i >= num_outputs, an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The same expression also multiplies num_elements() (attacker-influenced, up to ~2^63) by DataTypeSize (up to 16) in 64-bit arithmetic that can wrap, so the guard comparing to max_constant_size_in_bytes is bypassed and oversized nodes are constant-folded (fail-open size check, CWE-190).

assumptions: Graphs passed to constant folding originate from serialized GraphDef/SavedModel data, so node attributes, the shape_map entries, and their list lengths are attacker-influenced.

Node::output_type(i) is a per-node output-type lookup with no internal bounds validation performed by this function; the only bounds enforcement available to this code is a check against n->num_outputs(), which is absent.
limitations: MaybeReplaceShapeOp is not shown, so its behavior cannot be audited here.
Null dereference of n is not treated as a vulnerability: callers (the graph-rewriting driver) guarantee non-null nodes per documented contract.
Shapes that are not fully defined skip the size guard by design (size unknown); this alone is not judged a defect, though it slightly widens the fail-open surface.

verdict.summary: Array.prototype.splice() captures the receiver's length before running re-entrant ToInteger coercions (valueOf) on attacker-supplied start/deleteCount arguments, which can execute arbitrary guest JavaScript and shrink the fast array. The code never re-validates the live array->length afterwards, so delete is clamped only against the stale length. When the live length is smaller than delete - items, the unchecked update array->length += delta (line 115) wraps the unsigned length field to a huge value while the backing allocation stays small, turning every subsequent fast-array element access into a heap out-of-bounds read/write.

evidence.reason: Unchecked update of the live array length using delta computed from a stale length captured before re-entrant attacker JavaScript ran. Trigger: a = [0..99]; a.splice(0, {valueOf(){ a.length = 0; return 100; }}, 'x'); — valueOf at line 37 shrinks the fast array to length 0, but delete is clamped to 100 against the stale length (line 42), so delta = -99 and array->length (unsigned) wraps to ~4.29e9 while the allocation holds 100 elements; subsequent element accesses (bounds-checked only against array->length) become heap OOB reads/writes. The line 47 check only guards the upper bound against the stale length, never the lower bound against the live length.

assumptions: njs_value_to_integer() on the start/deleteCount arguments can invoke attacker-defined valueOf/toString, executing arbitrary guest JavaScript between the length read (line 16) and its uses (standard ECMAScript coercion semantics implemented by njs).
njs_array_t.length is an unsigned field, and fast-array element access in njs bounds-checks only index < array->length before indexing array->start[].
Setting .length to a smaller value on a fast array truncates it (sets array->length) without releasing the backing allocation, and the array remains a fast array.
limitations: Under the same trigger, njs_array_copy_within (lines 109-110) receives a negative count (array->length - (start + delete) = -100); whether that causes memory unsafety depends on the helper's implementation, which is not shown — if it loops on a signed counter it is a silent no-op.

Under the same trigger, the deleted-copy loop (line 62) reads slots beyond the truncated length; if truncation retains the allocation this is only a stale-data exposure, and it is OOB only if njs reallocated on shrink (could not be verified from this code).

splice()/splice(x) with fewer than two arguments deletes all elements because delete = length - start with start clamped to 0 from undefined — an ECMAScript spec deviation, but with no security impact.
The memcpy at line 121 is safe under the shown trigger only because truncation is assumed to retain capacity; it does not constitute an independent finding.

verdict.summary: BM_ParseGlobalQuantizer inverts the reference-counting protocol: the comment requires the node to be registered twice (once for the command's new_node field, once for scenegraph->global_qp), but the code calls gf_node_unregister(node, NULL) twice instead. For an attacker-chosen USE node with num_instances == 1, the first unregister drops the count to zero and frees the node while codec->ActiveQP, codec->scenegraph->global_qp, inf->new_node and the scene graph still reference it; the second unregister immediately operates on freed memory (use-after-free/double free), and later command/scenegraph destruction unregisters the dangling pointers again. For freshly created nodes the unsigned num_instances underflows, corrupting the count so later releases free a still-referenced node. Trigger is fully attacker-controlled via the BIFS bitstream (GlobalQuantizer command referencing a QuantizationParameter node).

evidence.reason: Reference-count inversion / double release. The code must acquire two references for the two holders it just stored the pointer into (inf->new_node at line 37 and scenegraph->global_qp at line 29, plus codec->ActiveQP at line 27); instead it releases two references. Trigger: attacker-supplied BIFS stream with a GlobalQuantizer command resolving to a USE QuantizationParameter node having num_instances == 1 — the first gf_node_unregister frees the node (premature free, CWE-416), the second unregisters freed memory (double free, CWE-415), and subsequent scenegraph/command teardown unregisters the dangling global_qp / new_node pointers, yielding use-after-free. Root cause is the missing register (replaced by unregister) at this exact site.

assumptions: GPAC gf_node_unregister decrements node->sgprivate->num_instances and deletes the node when it reaches zero; num_instances is the unsigned reference counter, consistent with the in-code comment that freshly parsed nodes have num_instances == 0 and USE nodes have >= 1.

Command destruction (gf_sg_command_del) and scenegraph reset release the references stored in inf->new_node and scenegraph->global_qp via gf_node_unregister, as the code's own 'register TWICE' comment documents.
The BIFS bitstream and the serialized node table are attacker-controlled input (untrusted media/scene file), which is the trust boundary this parser must validate.
limitations: The error path (lines 19-21) manually forces num_instances = 1 before unregistering a freshly created node; this is fragile internal-invariant manipulation but is self-consistent and has no independent security impact.

Return values of gf_sg_command_new / gf_sg_command_field_new / gf_list_add are unchecked allocation results; failure would need a broken allocation environment and causes at most a crash-like robustness issue, not a controllable vulnerability.

In the freshly-created-node variant of the double unregister, the immediate effect is an unsigned refcount underflow (leak); the security-relevant free occurs later via the holders' teardown paths, but the USE-node path already confirms memory unsafety.

verdict.summary: The kernel computes a flat output index from attacker-controlled sparse indices and shape without any bounds validation, then writes to the output tensor at that index. Input indices are never checked against input_shape (ValidateInputs is called only with shape and reduction_axes), so a coordinate exceeding the declared shape produces idx beyond the output tensor allocated from reduced_shape, causing a heap out-of-bounds write at out_flat(idx).

evidence.snippet:
const int64_t idx = CoordinatesToFlatIndex(g.group(), output_strides);
      out_flat(idx) = reduced_val();
evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787, root cause missing input validation CWE-20). g.group() yields coordinates taken from attacker-supplied input_indices, which this code never validates against input_shape (line 8 validates only shape_t and reduction_axes_t). output_strides and the out_values allocation (line 24) are derived from input_shape via reduced_shape. Trigger: invoke the op with input_shape=[2] and input_indices containing a row such as [100]; CoordinatesToFlatIndex returns idx=100 while out_flat has 2 elements, and out_flat(idx) writes past the end of the heap-allocated output tensor. No bounds check exists between idx computation and the write.

assumptions: SparseTensor::Create's internal index-vs-shape validation is not visible in the given code; this analysis relies only on the shown code, which itself enforces no range guarantee on g.group() coordinates and no bounds check before out_flat(idx).
Op inputs (input_indices, input_values, input_shape) are treated as crossing a trust boundary, as is standard for TensorFlow op kernels whose inputs are model-supplied data.
limitations: CHECK_EQ(coords.size(), strides.size()) inside CoordinatesToFlatIndex can abort the process if helper invariants break, but that is a robustness CHECK failure, not a memory-safety vulnerability.
The DeepCopy workaround for Reorder()'s in-place mutation (lines 16-18) correctly avoids aliasing state issues and is not a finding.
Potential int64 overflow in idx += coords[i]*strides[i] is treated as a secondary mechanism of the same unguarded sink, not a separate finding.

verdict.summary: The constant-folding size guard computes out_shape.num_elements() * DataTypeSize(n->output_type(i)) in 64-bit arithmetic with no overflow check. An attacker-supplied model can define a fully-known output shape whose element count times the per-element type size wraps around 2^64 (e.g., a single dimension of 2^62 elements with a 4-byte DT_FLOAT output yields a product of 0), so the comparison against max_constant_size_in_bytes fails open and the oversized node is reported constant-foldable, authorizing downstream materialization of a gigantic tensor (memory exhaustion / DoS).

evidence.reason: Unchecked integer overflow at the enforcement point of the constant-size limit. num_elements() is derived from attacker-controlled shape dimensions in the model (any non-negative int64 dim is accepted), and DataTypeSize comes from the attacker-chosen output type. For a fully-defined shape [4611686018427387904] with output type DT_FLOAT, the product 2^62 * 4 wraps to 0 in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic, so '0 > max_constant_size_in_bytes' is false, the oversized-output guard on line 31 is never taken, and the function reaches 'return true', declaring the node foldable; downstream constant folding then attempts an enormous allocation. Root cause: missing overflow check (CWE-190) causing a fail-open bounds/size bypass.

assumptions: 64-bit platform where int64 * size_t promotes to 64-bit unsigned and wraps mod 2^64; on such platforms PartialTensorShape dims up to 2^62 are valid non-negative int64 values.
The shape_map entries are produced by shape inference over the attacker-supplied graph, so dimension magnitudes are attacker-influenced.
Constant folding subsequently allocates/copies tensors for nodes this function reports foldable, so bypassing the size cap leads to oversized allocation attempts (OOM/DoS).
limitations: n->output_type(i) is indexed with a bound taken from the shape_map vector length and is not checked against n->num_outputs() in this code (lines 26-29). Dismissed because producing a vector longer than the node's output count requires the caller's shape inference to violate its documented one-shape-per-output contract, not merely attacker model data.

The size check only runs when shape_map != nullptr, the node appears in the map, and the shape is fully defined; shapes that are not fully defined skip the check by design ('skip the node if an output is known to be oversized'), which is a documented design gap rather than a defect reachable with a deterministically oversized value.
No null check on n or on members accessed via helpers; these are internal caller contracts and not attacker-reachable preconditions.

verdict.summary: This is the guarded version of the SparseTensor reduce kernel: the attacker-influenced flat write index (derived from input_indices coordinates, input_shape strides, and reduction_axes) is range-checked immediately before the out_flat(idx) write, and the group-size condition that protects the CHECK_EQ in CoordinatesToFlatIndex is verified by an OP_REQUIRES before the lambda call. No reachable memory-safety, crash, or fail-open path exists in the code as written.

assumptions: ValidateInputs (not shown) performs the intended validation of input_shape and reduction_axes contents; this code hard-fails via OP_REQUIRES_OK if it returns an error before any consumption of those tensors.
SparseTensor::Create and tensor::DeepCopy uphold their documented contracts (dimension/type consistency), as they are internal library code, not attacker-supplied data paths.
The op registration constrains input_values to type attribute T, preventing dtype mismatch at g.template values<T>().
limitations: Integer overflow in the stride/coordinate accumulation inside CoordinatesToFlatIndex is possible with extreme shape values, but every resulting out-of-range index is rejected by the explicit bounds check before the write; in-bounds overflow results are correctly sized writes, so this is robustness-only with no security impact.
The VLOG(2) diagnostics and Internal (rather than InvalidArgument) error codes are stylistic; they fail closed.

If ValidateInputs (external to this snippet) were itself deficient, unvalidated shape/axes data could reach the stride computation, but the final write is still bounds-checked, so no OOB write would result; this is outside the code shown.

verdict.summary: mrb_ary_shift_m validates its only trust-boundary input (the guest-supplied shift count n) before every memory sink: it rejects n<0 via mrb_raise, clamps n>len to len, and early-returns on len==0 or n==0 before any dereference. Consequently mrb_ary_new_from_values reads at most len elements, the L_SHIFT pointer advance (ptr+=n, len-=n) stays inside the underlying buffer with len remaining non-negative, and the shift-left copy loop touches only indices [0,len). No reachable path uses an uninitialized, negative, or oversized n, and the shared/embedded array invariants of the surrounding runtime prevent type confusion at the L_SHIFT label. No vulnerability found in this code as written.

assumptions: The code runs inside the mruby interpreter of the matching version, whose core maintains RArray invariants: ARY_LEN >= 0, the buffer holds at least ARY_LEN elements at ARY_PTR(a), shared arrays are never embedded, and the embed capacity is far smaller than ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN (10), so the len > ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN gate before ary_make_shared/L_SHIFT guarantees heap-backed storage.

mrb_get_args with format "|i" returns 0 exactly when no argument was given (early return path) and returns 1 only after writing the integer argument into &n; type errors raise (longjmp) rather than returning a nonzero count without initialization.
For shared arrays, the core maintains heap.ptr + heap.len <= shared->ptr + shared->len, and the L_SHIFT mutation (ptr+=n, len-=n) preserves this invariant since 0 < n <= len.
limitations: Candidate dismissed (unreachable): use of uninitialized n would require passing mrb_get_args without supplying the argument, but the ==0 check returns early in that case.

Candidates dismissed (guarded in-code): n<0 reaching pointer arithmetic/length decrement and n>len causing out-of-bounds ptr+=n, negative heap.len, and OOB reads in mrb_ary_new_from_values are both prevented by the explicit raise and clamp at the 'if (n < 0)' and 'if (n > len) n = len;' lines.

Candidate dismissed (invariant-based): type confusion where an embedded array reaches a->as.heap.ptr+=n would require an embedded array that is either flagged shared or has len > ARY_SHIFT_SHARED_MIN; both contradict the runtime's structural invariants.

Candidate dismissed (semantic, not fail-open): ary_modify_check does not detach shared arrays before the in-place ptr/len adjustment, but this only moves this array's view within bounds of the shared buffer and does not expose unvalidated data or an authorization decision.

Robustness note: the function relies on mrb_get_args raising on non-Integer arguments; in mruby versions where 'i' coerces Floats, a large float could yield an arbitrary mrb_int, but the negative check and >len clamp in this function would still contain it.

verdict.summary: ReadPCLImage parses attacker-controlled 'CropBox[...]'/'MediaBox[...]' tokens from the input file with sscanf %lf and converts the coordinate deltas to size_t via width=(size_t) floor(bounds.x2-bounds.x1+0.5) without validating sign, finiteness, or range. A crafted PCL file such as 'MediaBox[0 0 -640 -480' makes the negative delta wrap to ~SIZE_MAX, and the wrapped page dimensions propagate into image->page (allocation-relevant metadata consumed for canvas sizing) and into the GhostPCL delegate command line ('-g%.20gx%.20g'), causing integer wraparound/undefined conversions and denial of service. The byte-copy loop into command[] is bounds-safe in this version, so the wraparound at the MediaBox/CropBox conversion is the surviving root-cause defect.

evidence.reason: bounds.x1..y2 are filled exclusively by sscanf("%lf") from file-supplied CropBox/MediaBox tokens, with no sign, finite (NaN/Inf accepted by %lf), or magnitude validation. For a file containing 'MediaBox[0 0 -640 -480\n', bounds.x2-bounds.x1 is negative, floor() yields a negative double, and the cast to size_t wraps to ~SIZE_MAX; the wrapped value always passes the following 'if (width > page.width)' check, flows through a second unchecked double->size_t cast (page.width=(size_t) floor(page.width*resolution.x/delta.x+0.5)) into the GhostPCL '-g<W>x<H>' delegate option and into image->page for every returned image. This is an attacker-triggerable integer wraparound (CWE-190) caused by missing range validation of external file data at the parse boundary (CWE-20).

assumptions: FormatLocaleString is vsnprintf-bounded to MagickPathExtent, so command/density/options formatting cannot overflow their buffers; AcquireString("") allocates MagickPathExtent bytes, matching the sizes passed to FormatLocaleString.
MagickPathExtent equals sizeof(command), so the token-copy loop guard is measured against the actual buffer.
GetDelegateCommands(delegate_info) returns admin-owned delegates.xml content, treated as trusted configuration; its use as a format string is not attacker-reachable in this code.
image->resolution.x/y and other image_info-derived options are operator-set, not file-derived, so the ping-path 'columns *= resolution.x/2.0' conversion is not file-triggerable.

The wrapped page dimensions reach allocation-relevant metadata (image->page) and the external delegate; downstream ImageMagick resource limits may downgrade memory-corruption potential to denial of service, but the defective wrapped values themselves are produced entirely within this function.
limitations: Candidate rejected: stack buffer overflow in the token-copy loop. The write '*p++=(char) c' precedes the guard, but the continue-path requires post-increment (p-command) <= MagickPathExtent-2, so every byte write lands at index <= MagickPathExtent-2 and the terminating '*p="\0"' at index <= MagickPathExtent-1; the guard is airtight in this version, so no out-of-bounds write is reachable.

Candidate rejected: unchecked return of AcquireUniqueFilename(read_info->filename) — on failure read_info->filename would retain the original input path, but reaching that state requires unique-file creation to fail (broken environment), not attacker input.

Candidate rejected: unchecked ExternalDelegateCommand return value — on delegate failure the subsequent ReadImage returns NULL and ThrowReaderException(DelegateError) fires, so the path is fail-closed with no security impact.

'geometry' is formatted but never used (dead code); the sscanf'd token buffer is always NUL-terminated and length-bounded before LocaleNCompare/sscanf, so no over-read; options/density/read_info and unique temp files are released on all paths.

verdict.summary: The ISOBMFF top-level box parser dereferences attacker-controlled parsed-file structure pointers without validation: (1) in the MOOV case, each track's trak->Media->information->sampleTable chain is dereferenced without checking that the attacker-supplied moov actually contains mdia/minf/stbl for every trak, and (2) in the MOOF case under GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS, mov->moof->mfhd is dereferenced without checking that the moof contains an mfhd box. A crafted file with an incomplete trak or a mfhd-less moof crosses the trust boundary this function is responsible for validating and crashes the parser (NULL pointer dereference, denial of service).

evidence.reason: NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): the code validates mov->moov->mvhd but never validates that each trak in the attacker-supplied moov has a Media (mdia), an information (minf), or a sampleTable (stbl) box before dereferencing the chain trak->Media->information->sampleTable. Minimal trigger: a file whose moov contains mvhd plus a trak lacking mdia (or mdia lacking minf/stbl); box parsing succeeds, the non-debug track loop reaches this line and dereferences NULL, crashing the parser.

NULL pointer dereference (CWE-476): in the GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS branch of the MOOF case, mov->moof->mfhd is dereferenced with no check that the parsed moof box actually contained an mfhd child. Minimal trigger: a file opened with openMode == GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS containing a moof without an mfhd box; the path reaches this line with mfhd == NULL and crashes, while sibling code in the same case demonstrates such checks are needed (traf->tfhd, traf->trex are checked).
