Robustness/cosmetic (no security impact): OP_ASET asserts mrb_array_p(regs[a]) while the actual array operated on is regs[b]; assert-only guard with no release-build effect.
Unchecked failure of internal helpers (e.g., mrb_stack_extend) would require a broken allocation environment; no exhaustion path attributable to attacker input exists in this function.

verdict.summary: In stl_remove_degenerate, when a degenerate facet has no neighbor on an edge, the code passes the OTHER edge's neighbor value to stl_update_connects_remove_1 without validating it is not the -1 'no neighbor' sentinel. A crafted STL file containing an isolated facet with two identical vertices sets neighbor1 == neighbor2 == -1, so both calls at lines 49 and 52 pass -1, which the callee uses as an index into stl->neighbors_start, producing an out-of-bounds write (num_neighbors decrement) at neighbors_start[-1], i.e., heap memory before the array.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the -1 sentinel ('no neighbor') is passed unchecked as a facet index to stl_update_connects_remove_1. Trigger: a crafted STL file supplies a degenerate facet (two equal vertices, so the line-26 branch is taken) whose degenerate edges match no other facet, so neighbors_start[facet].neighbor[edge1] and .neighbor[edge2] are both -1. Line 48's condition is true and line 49 executes stl_update_connects_remove_1(stl, -1); line 51's condition is also true and line 52 repeats it. The callee indexes stl->neighbors_start[-1] and decrements it, an out-of-bounds write before the allocated neighbors array (CWE-129 invalid array index, CWE-787 OOB write).

assumptions: stl_update_connects_remove_1(stl, n) uses n as an index into stl->neighbors_start (decrementing num_neighbors) and performs no validation of its own, which is the standard definition of this admesh helper.

The neighbor and which_vertex_not tables are populated by the library's facet-matching phase from STL file contents; a facet can legitimately have all neighbors == -1 (unmatched edges), and degenerate facets are exactly what this function is called to process.
facet and neighbor indices other than the -1 sentinel are internally constrained to [0, number_of_facets) by the library's matching/iteration code.
limitations: The `facet` parameter is used to index stl->facet_start and stl->neighbors_start without a bounds check in this function; this was dismissed because the index is supplied by the library's own in-range iteration, not by data crossing a trust boundary.

The `(vnot + 1) % 3` index arithmetic is unchecked for negative vnot values; dismissed because vnot is computed (not raw file data), valid vnot values are paired with valid neighbors, and the neighbor != -1 guards skip the writes when vnot is unset.

The neighbor-link rewiring performed before stl_remove_facet may leave logically stale links if the swap in stl_remove_facet relocates a referenced facet; this is a correctness/robustness issue, not a memory-safety vulnerability in this code as written.

verdict.summary: njs_function_frame_save copies the active VM frame into a caller-provided buffer using counts (value_count, lambda->temp, args_offset, args_count) all derived from the same active frame it reads, so every write is self-consistent with the source frame's geometry. The candidate memory-safety issues (unbounded copy into destination, u.lambda union access, args_offset-1 underflow, local-pointer-slot overrun) each require a precondition that the surrounding njs VM prevents: the destination spare-space contract computed from the same frame, lambda-only active frames at save sites, and args_offset >= 1 enforced at function construction. No trigger reachable from guest-JS-influenced inputs within this code's own contracts was found.

assumptions: njs frame-construction code (njs_function_frame/njs_function_frame_alloc and the vmcode call sites) allocates every frame with value slots for `this`, bound arguments, all declared parameters, actual arguments and compiler temporaries, and computes the saved-frame spare space from the same active-frame data this function reads.
njs_function_frame_save is only invoked while a lambda frame is active, so active->function->u.lambda is a valid lambda (no native-function type confusion).
function->args_offset >= 1 always (it counts the `this` slot), so `args_offset - 1` cannot underflow.

value_count = njs_function_frame_value_count(active) and njs_function_frame_args_count(active) are derived from active->size, i.e., from values the VM itself computed at frame allocation, not raw guest numbers.
limitations: C1 (heap overflow if the destination buffer is smaller than NJS_FRAME_SIZE + (value_count+temp)*sizeof(njs_value_t *) + value_count*sizeof(njs_value_t)): this function takes no size parameter and structurally cannot bounds-check its destination; any caller that miscomputes the spare space would overflow here. With only this code given, the mismatch cannot be triggered by data this code accepts, so it is recorded as a caller-contract dependency (CWE-129/CWE-787 would apply to such a caller).

C4: when a function has more declared parameters than compiler temporaries and is called with many actual arguments, the local pointer slots written by the final for-loop can extend past the saved frame's pointer area and alias bytes inside its own value area; worst case is in-buffer corruption (correctness), not an out-of-bounds write, based on the layout invariants assumed above.

The code performs no validation of function->u.lambda being non-NULL or of active->function being a lambda; this is safe only under the VM's lambda-frame invariant at all call sites — a hardening opportunity, not a reachable defect.

verdict.summary: esp_output_head validates all attacker-shaped skb geometry before each sink: pskb_put is guarded by the tailen<=skb_tailroom branch or by skb_cow_data's sizing; the page-frag path is guarded by nr_frags<MAX_SKB_FRAGS, skb_page_frag_refill allocation of allocsize>=tailen, and locked offset advancement; and the historically dangerous stale esp->esph across skb_cow_data is preempted by the esph_offset save/restore. All error paths unlock x->lock and propagate negative returns. No reachable memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, integer, or fail-open defect exists in this code as written.

assumptions: esp->tailen/plen/tfclen are computed by in-tree callers from skb length, MTU and xfrm state, so tailen is structurally bounded far below any ALIGN overflow threshold; no in-tree caller can supply a tailen near INT_MAX.
skb_page_frag_refill honors its documented postcondition: on success, the frag page has at least fragsz bytes of space at pfrag->offset.
An skb undergoing XFRM output is single-owner (no concurrent frag-list mutation), so re-reading nr_frags under x->lock cannot exceed the previously checked bound.
skb_cow_data returns a trailer skb with at least tailen bytes of tailroom on success (negative return signals failure).
limitations: Candidate: integer overflow in ALIGN(tailen, L1_CACHE_BYTES) and tailen-based length additions — rejected; tailen derives from packet length (bounded ~64K even with GSO) plus small padding, so the trigger state cannot be produced by this code or its in-tree callers.

Candidate: out-of-bounds fragment index in __skb_fill_page_desc(skb, nfrags, ...) — rejected; entry is guarded by skb_shinfo(skb)->nr_frags < MAX_SKB_FRAGS with no intervening frag insertion and a single-owner skb.

Candidate: stale esp->esph pointer after skb_cow_data reallocates/copies the skb — rejected as not present; the code computes esph_offset before the cow and reconstitutes esp->esph from the new transport header afterwards.
Candidate: trailer write past the page-frag region — rejected; skb_page_frag_refill guarantees allocsize>=tailen bytes at pfrag->offset and pfrag->offset advances by allocsize under x->lock.

Candidate: pskb_put(skb, trailer, tailen) exceeding tailroom — rejected; the skip_cow entry requires tailen <= skb_tailroom(skb), and the cow path relies on skb_cow_data's sizing contract which is enforced before use.
Candidate: TOCTOU between the outer nr_frags check and the locked re-read — rejected; output-path skbs are not concurrently modified.

Candidate: unlocked/fail-open behavior on the skb_page_frag_refill failure goto cow — rejected; spin_unlock_bh(&x->lock) precedes the jump and the cow path fully re-writes and appends the trailer, returning negative on skb_cow_data failure.
Candidate: uninitialized nfrags return — rejected; every control path assigns nfrags before reaching out.

verdict.summary: QPaintEngineEx::stroke consumes the QVectorPath element-type array and point buffer without validating them: (1) the default case of the point-consumption switch advances neither 'points' nor 'types', so any element type outside {MoveToElement, LineToElement, CurveToElement} (e.g. CurveToDataElement=3) in attacker-influenced path data makes 'while (points < lastPoint)' an infinite loop (CPU denial of service); (2) the CurveToElement case reads six qreals (points[0..5]) while the loop only guarantees two remain, so a CurveToElement near the end of the types array with fewer than 6 qreals left reads out of bounds past the points buffer. Both defects stem from missing validation of path element data at the intake trust boundary.

evidence.reason: The default case of the point-consumption loop (guarded only by 'while (points < lastPoint)', line 111) advances neither the 'points' nor the 'types' pointer. If the attacker-influenced element-type array contains any value other than MoveToElement, LineToElement or CurveToElement (e.g. CurveToDataElement = 3, reachable from parsed/deserialized vector path data that this code does not validate at intake), the loop condition never changes and the function spins forever, hanging the render/paint thread (CWE-835).

evidence.snippet:
case QPainterPath::CurveToElement:
                    d->activeStroker->cubicTo(points[0], points[1],
                                              points[2], points[3],
                                              points[4], points[5]);
evidence.reason: The CurveToElement case reads six qreals from the points buffer, but the loop guard 'points < lastPoint' only guarantees at least two qreals remain before 'lastPoint = points + pointCount*2'. There is no check that a curve element has 3 points (6 qreals) available, so a types array containing CurveToElement with fewer than 6 remaining qreals (e.g. pointCount=1 with types={CurveToElement}, permitted because this code never validates the types/point-count correspondence) reads 4 qreals (32 bytes) past the end of the points buffer (CWE-125).

assumptions: Path data (points, element types, element count) can cross a trust boundary: vector paths are routinely built from parsed file formats, deserialized model/saved-state data, or replayed drawing records; this code performs no validation of that data at intake.
The identical defective patterns exist in the cosmetic-pen branch of the same function: the unchecked 6-qreal curve read at lines 184-186 and the non-advancing 'default: break;' at lines 193-194.
limitations: Integer overflow of 'path.elementCount()+4' (line 13) and 'pointCount<<1' (line 88) requires an element count near 2^31 (point data far exceeding 16 GB), so it is not a practically reachable vulnerability; noted as theoretical (CWE-190 style).
Under QT_DEBUG_DRAW, line 4 ('qDebug() << ... << pen') references the undefined identifier 'pen' (the parameter is 'inPen'); this is a debug-build compile-time defect with no runtime security impact.

A QVectorPath constructed with a null points pointer and a positive element count would cause a null dereference at lines 139/203, but this violates the documented QVectorPath constructor contract (valid points for count>0) and is a caller contract issue, not enforced/validatable here.
The '(const QPointF *) points' casts rely on QPointF being layout-compatible with two qreals; this is a language-purity concern, not a memory-safety defect.

Dash-pattern arithmetic (lines 36-42) is clamped (qMin to 32) and the 'extent / patternLength' division is guarded by qFuzzyIsNull(patternLength), so no divide-by-zero or unbounded loop exists on that path.

verdict.summary: SQClass::NewSlot is the guarded variant: every attacker-influenced input (script-supplied key, val, bstatic) flows only to sinks whose preconditions this code enforces before use. Field/method index writes (_defaultvalues[...], _methods[...]) use indices created in lockstep with the corresponding push_back in this same function and never shrink; the metamethod write is guarded by an explicit != -1 check and the shared-state metamethod index table; and all container-growth paths are preceded by the CountUsed() >= MEMBER_MAX_COUNT cap, preventing index-packing overflow and unbounded growth. No reachable memory-safety, bounds, or input-validation defect exists in this code as written.

assumptions: SQClass::Create/Copy clone _members together with _defaultvalues/_methods so inherited/copied member indices remain consistent (upstream Squirrel invariant).

SQTable::NewSlot overwrites an existing key in place without growing, so the overwrite paths (method replaced by field via non-static val) orphan a vector entry but never desynchronize CountUsed from vector sizes.
ss->GetMetaMethodIdxByName returns indices bounded by the metamethod enum, matching the fixed-size _metamethods array.
SQVM::IsEqual unconditionally assigns its result parameter on all paths.
limitations: Robustness only: if SQClosure::Clone() returns NULL under allocation failure, _closure(theval)->_base would dereference NULL; Squirrel's allocator treats OOM as fatal, so no attacker-reachable path exists.

Stale-entry: a key existing as a method, when re-assigned with a non-closure, non-static value, overwrites the _members mapping to a field while leaving an orphaned entry in _methods — wasted memory only, no out-of-bounds access.

Design choice, not a defect: a locked class (with live instances) still accepts static-table additions (bstatic or closure values), per the code's own comment; this monkey-patching is intended Squirrel semantics.

A NULL key passed through the raw embedding API would reach SQTable::NewSlot's assert in this function's callee; this function does not validate key non-nullness itself, but the VM and sq_newslot API layer reject null keys before reaching this code.

verdict.summary: __bpf_ringbuf_reserve truncates the 64-bit result of round_up(size + BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ, 8) into the u32 variable len. For any size in [0xFFFFFFF1, 0xFFFFFFF7] (all permitted by the RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ check), size+8 rounds up to 0x100000000, which truncates to len = 0. This defeats both the record-vs-ring-size check (len > rb->mask + 1) and the free-space check (new_prod_pos - cons_pos > rb->mask, since new_prod_pos == prod_pos), so the reservation succeeds, producer_pos is not advanced, yet hdr->len records the full ~4GB size and the returned pointer is verifier-treated as a size-byte writable region — enabling a massive out-of-bounds write into and past the ringbuf mapping by the calling BPF program.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the round_up expression is evaluated in u64 (size is u64, up to RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ = 0xFFFFFFF7) but its result 0x100000000 is truncated to u32 len = 0. The subsequent length check is therefore bypassed: for a caller-supplied size such as 0xFFFFFFF7, len == 0 passes the ring-size check, new_prod_pos == prod_pos passes the space check, and the function returns a pointer that the BPF verifier tracks as a 0xFFFFFFF7-byte writable region over a mapping of at most rb->mask + 1 bytes, while hdr->len is also set to the un-truncated size — an out-of-bounds write of up to ~4GB reachable purely with inputs this code permits.

assumptions: RINGBUF_MAX_RECORD_SZ is UINT_MAX - BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ (0xFFFFFFF7) and BPF_RINGBUF_HDR_SZ is 8, matching the upstream kernel definitions, so sizes in [0xFFFFFFF1, 0xFFFFFFF7] reach the truncation.

The caller is the BPF helper bpf_ringbuf_reserve, which records the requested size as the length of the returned PTR_TO_MEM, permitting the calling BPF program to write up to size bytes — size being a constant in a user-loaded (attacker-influenced) BPF program.

rb->mask + 1 equals the ringbuf data-area size (power-of-two, at most a few hundred MB), so the returned ~4GB region extends far beyond the mapping; the double-mapped pages only make in-range wrapping safe, not this overflow.
limitations: The consumer_pos read at line 14 happens before the lock is taken, but consumer positions only advance, making the space check conservative rather than under-restrictive; no security impact.
The in_nmi() trylock failure path and all other error paths fail closed (return NULL); no fail-open behavior found.
hdr->pg_off computation and producer_pos release/store pairing are consistent with the double-mapped ringbuf design; no separate defect found there.

verdict.summary: get_visual_text() computes the selected-text length from raw Visual-selection columns (VIsual.col / w_cursor.col) without ever validating them against the length of the line it just fetched from the buffer. The only intake guard, `**pp == NUL` (line 31), checks just the first byte of the selection, so when the selection-end column is stale or otherwise greater than the current line length (e.g., the line was shortened after the Visual anchor was recorded, by :s, an operator, an autocommand/plugin, or via gv restoring an old position), *lenp extends past the line's terminating NUL. The function then reads out of bounds at `(*pp)[*lenp - 1]` (line 39) and at `(*mb_ptr2len)(*pp + (*lenp - 1))` (line 38), and returns the over-long (pointer, length) pair to callers (Visual-mode */n search assembly, gn), causing further out-of-bounds reads of heap memory. Trigger: line '0123456789', v0 (VIsual.col=9, cursor.col=0), shorten line to 3 bytes, re-select the same line and run a command that calls get_visual_text() — lenp becomes 10 for a 3-byte line and pp[9] is read past the buffer content.

evidence.reason: Missing bounds check: *lenp is computed purely from the raw selection columns. VIsual.col is attacker-influenced state (buffer content plus editing operations can leave the Visual anchor beyond the current end of line, e.g. after the line is shortened while the stored selection remains, or via gv restoring a stale position) and is never compared to the length of the line returned by ml_get_pos(). The subsequent `**pp == NUL` guard (line 31) only validates the first byte, so a non-NUL start byte with an out-of-range end column yields *lenp larger than the bytes actually available from *pp.

Out-of-bounds read sink: both statements dereference *pp at offset *lenp - 1, which is past the line's terminating NUL whenever the selection end column exceeds the line length (precondition `*lenp <= line bytes from *pp` is enforced nowhere before this point). mb_ptr2len can additionally read up to four bytes at/after the out-of-range offset. The unvalidated (pp, lenp) pair is also returned to the caller for string assembly, extending the over-read.

assumptions: VIsual/w_cursor are global editor positions whose columns are assumed-but-not-verified by this function to lie within the fetched line; Vim's stored Visual selection is not revalidated by this code and can become stale relative to a modified buffer (the code re-reads the line fresh via ml_get_curline/ml_get_pos but never re-clamps the columns).
ml_get_pos() adds pos->col to the line pointer without clamping, so column validity must be established by the caller — this code does not do so.
Callers such as nv_ident()/normal_search() consume (*pp, *lenp) directly to build search strings, propagating an over-long length.
limitations: In the multibyte branch (line 38) a trailing NUL is not excluded from *lenp the way the non-mbyte branch (line 39) does; a selection ending on the end-of-line position (possible with 'virtualedit') yields a length counting the NUL byte. This is a correctness/robustness issue without memory-safety impact and is not counted as a vulnerability.

unadjust_for_sel() (line 7) mutates w_cursor.col before it is used at lines 21-29; its implementation is outside the shown code, so only its effect as another writer of unvalidated column state was considered.

A signedness/underflow issue in the column arithmetic was rejected: the LT_POS/else branch structure guarantees end-column >= start-column on each path, so a wrapped negative *lenp is not reachable in this code.
Only out-of-bounds reads (crash / limited information exposure into search patterns) are demonstrated; no write sink exists in this function.

verdict.summary: gen_hash compiles attacker-sized hash literals (AST pair lists) but enforces an internal per-segment register/pair bound: the loop-tail check 'if (val && cursp() >= slimit)' flushes with OP_HASH/OP_HASHADD and resets len on every path, slimit is tightened to INT16_MAX when cursp() is already >= GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX, and all push/pop accounting (pop_n(len*2), pop_n(len*2+1), the extra pop() under update) is balanced on every reachable path. This is the upstream fixed version; no memory-safety, bounds, integer, or fail-open defect is reachable from the code as written.

assumptions: GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX, GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX and INT16_MAX are defined upstream consistently with the 16-bit operand/register capacity of genop_2; the snippet itself does not define them, so the slimit=GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX path is judged on that assumption.
codegen(s, node, val) honors its internal contract: when val is true it leaves exactly one value pushed on the compiler stack; hash-pair AST nodes are well formed per the parser grammar.
Callers of gen_hash handle the documented -1 'variable length' return without using it as a pop count.
limitations: The 'limit' parameter is completely unused (dead parameter). If a caller passed a tighter bound expecting enforcement it is silently ignored; however, the internal slimit check enforces an equivalent bound at the same sinks, so no missing-validation defect exists in this code.
In a degenerate kw-rest-only literal at high cursp(), the loop-tail flush can emit a semantically neutral OP_HASHADD with a pair count of 0; register accounting stays balanced, no security impact.

A complex key/value subexpression could transiently push temporaries beyond slimit within a single iteration before the tail check fires; the overshoot is bounded by the codegen one-value contract and no concrete unbounded path is demonstrable here.

When val == 0 and the literal contains NODE_KW_REST_ARGS, update is still set and -1 is returned; harmless because no register accounting occurs on val==0 passes and callers ignore the return value there.

verdict.summary: issuerAndThisUpdateCheck fails to verify that the closing double-quote of the issuer or thisUpdate string was found before advancing x past it. When the string runs to the end of the input (the mandatory trailing '}'), the scan loop exits with is->bv_len == x.bv_len (or tu->bv_len == x.bv_len), and the subsequent unsigned subtraction x.bv_len -= len + 1 underflows to SIZE_MAX while x.bv_val is moved one byte past the end of the input buffer. The trailing space-eating loop, the comma check, and strncasecmp then read out of bounds (and can walk arbitrarily far into the heap if the bytes past the buffer are spaces), enabling remote crash/DoS and heap-content-dependent behavior from a malformed attribute value.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the preceding scan loop can exit without ever finding the closing '"' (tu->bv_len == x.bv_len); this code then advances x.bv_val one byte past the input buffer and subtracts tu->bv_len + 1 from the unsigned x.bv_len, wrapping it to SIZE_MAX. Trigger: an attacker-supplied value such as '{issuer rdnSequence:"",thisUpdate "YYMMDDhhmmssZ}' (passes the length and brace checks) leaves the thisUpdate string unterminated at the '}', so the subsequent space-eating loop dereferences x.bv_val[0] out of bounds, walking the heap under a SIZE_MAX length if the following bytes are spaces.

Identical unchecked advance for the issuer string: if the scan loop at lines 65-77 exits because no terminating '"' exists in the region (string extends to the '}'), is->bv_len equals x.bv_len, and this subtraction underflows x.bv_len to SIZE_MAX while x.bv_val moves one byte past the buffer end. Trigger: a value like '{thisUpdate "YYMMDDhhmmssZ",issuer rdnSequence:"aaaa}' causes out-of-bounds reads in the subsequent space-eating/comma/strncasecmp code.

assumptions: in (and thus x) is a caller-supplied struct berval whose bv_val is not guaranteed to be NUL-terminated, so reads past bv_len but within the allocation are still reads of adjacent heap memory, and reads past the '}'' go past the buffer.
ber_len_t is an unsigned type (as in OpenLDAP), so x.bv_len -= len + 1 wraps rather than going negative.
limitations: ber_dupbv_x( &ni, is, ctx ) and slap_sl_malloc() return values are not checked; on allocation failure *is would be left BER_BVNULL (bv_val NULL) for the caller. This requires a broken/allocation-failing environment and is a robustness gap, not an attacker-triggerable memory-safety defect in this code.

The space-eating loops evaluate x.bv_val[0] before testing x.bv_len, and strncasecmp may read a few bytes past the logical region; while the x-invariant (x.bv_val + x.bv_len points at the final '}') holds these reads stay inside the buffer, so they are manifestations of the confirmed underflow, not independent vulnerabilities.
The is->bv_val[is->bv_len+1] read (double-dquote check) can reach at most the '}' byte, which is in-bounds.

verdict.summary: The FTPWHO bookkeeping code computes the memcpy source index as sl - sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename) - 1U; when the client-supplied filename length equals sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename), the guard 'sl < sizeof ...' fails, the else branch runs, and the index underflows to (size_t)-1, so memcpy reads one byte before the filename buffer (out-of-bounds read copied into shared memory visible to pure-ftpwho). The same else branch also never NUL-terminates the filename field. Additionally, under QUOTAS the per-transfer size cap is dead logic (max_filesize is initialized to -1 and the conjunct 'max_filesize >= 0' is always false, so the cap is never computed and ul_init receives -1 = unlimited), a fail-open quota enforcement gap reachable by any uploading user.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one in the source index of a length-controlled memcpy. sl = strlen(name) is attacker-controlled via the STOR command argument. The branch guard at line 150 only accepts the safe case (sl < N); the else branch admits sl == N, where sl - N - 1U underflows to (size_t)-1, making the source pointer one byte before name's allocation, so sizeof shm_data_cur->filename bytes are read starting at name[-1] — an out-of-bounds read whose result is copied into the shared-memory record read by pure-ftpwho. The else branch also fills the field completely without writing a NUL terminator. Trigger: FTP client sends STOR with a syntactically valid filename whose length is exactly sizeof shm_data_cur->filename, on an FTPWHO build with shm_data_cur != NULL.

Fail-open quota cap via always-false condition. max_filesize is initialized to (off_t) -1 (line 13) and is assigned nowhere else before this conjunct, so 'max_filesize >= (off_t) 0' is always false and the assignment computing the remaining-quota cap never executes. max_filesize therefore remains -1 (unlimited) when passed to ul_init, so a user whose quota is exhausted can still complete a single arbitrarily large upload; the cap is only reported after the fact. Trigger: any authenticated user uploads a file on a QUOTAS build — no precondition in this code prevents reaching this path.

assumptions: The filename argument 'name' is the remote client's STOR/APPE parameter, only filtered by checknamesanity (syntax), so lengths up to sizeof shm_data_cur->filename are attainable; the FTPWHO code is compiled in and shm_data_cur is mapped for the session.

If ul_init() can return failure without initializing ulhandler.total_uploaded, then 'uploaded += ulhandler.total_uploaded' and displayrate() on the failure path (ul_init != 0) read uninitialized stack memory; this cannot be confirmed from the given code and depends on ul_init's internals.
The QUOTAS finding requires a build with QUOTAS defined; the FTPWHO off-by-one requires a build with FTPWHO defined.
limitations: FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) at line 180 uses descriptor f after (void) close(f) at line 174 — a use-after-close, but no descriptor is allocated in between, so it fails with EBADF and only suppresses an informational disk-space reply; robustness, no security impact.

unlink(atomic_file) on early error paths (e.g., quota rejection at line 122 after the original file was renamed to the atomic name at line 46) destroys the original file's content on a failed command; this is a data-integrity issue but the attacker already had write permission over that file, so no privilege boundary is crossed.

no_truncate is set to 1 when autorename != 0 and never restored, polluting global state so subsequent non-autorename uploads take the atomic (rename-based) path; behavioral change only, no demonstrated security impact.
checknamesanity followed by open/rename leaves a theoretical filesystem TOCTOU window, partially mitigated by O_NOFOLLOW; not remotely exploitable within this single-threaded session model.

verdict.summary: dynamicGetbuf computes remain = logicalSize - pos and copies rlen bytes via memcpy without validating that remain (or the len parameter) is non-negative. If dp->pos exceeds dp->logicalSize (or len is negative), rlen is negative and sign-extends to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t at the memcpy sink, causing a massive out-of-bounds read from dp->data and write into buf.

evidence.reason: No non-negativity check on remain (dp->logicalSize - dp->pos) or on len before rlen is used as the memcpy length. Trigger: context state with dp->pos > dp->logicalSize (e.g., after a seek past the logical size) and a call dynamicGetbuf(ctx, buf, 1): remain < 0 fails 'remain >= len', is not 0, so rlen = remain (negative); memcpy's size_t parameter sign-extends to ~SIZE_MAX, producing a huge out-of-bounds read from dp->data and write into buf. The same sink is reached with a negative len parameter, which the function also never validates.

assumptions: dp->pos can exceed dp->logicalSize through other operations on the same dynamic IO context (seek/put logic in the surrounding module), which is attacker-influenced parsed state; even if that invariant were guaranteed elsewhere, this function relies on it without verifying it before a raw memcpy.
len is propagated from the gd IO layer, where read sizes can derive from externally parsed image data, so a negative len is within this function's accepted int domain.
limitations: The destination buffer size (buf) is trusted per the caller contract; overwriting it only occurs as a consequence of the negative-rlen defect, not as an independent missing check.
dp->pos += rlen with a negative rlen corrupts context state, but this is a secondary effect of the confirmed memcpy defect, not a separate vulnerability.

verdict.summary: QPaintEngineEx::stroke consumes the attacker-influenced QVectorPath element-type and coordinate arrays without validating their pairing. The stroking loops only guarantee that 2 qreals remain (points < lastPoint) before each iteration, but the CurveToElement case unconditionally consumes 6 qreals (points[0..5]) and 3 type entries, so a path whose type sequence ends with a CurveToElement (or whose types desynchronize from the point count, e.g., a deserialized/untrusted QPainterPath) reads up to 32 bytes past the points buffer (CWE-125) at both the non-cosmetic and cosmetic sinks. Additionally, the default: case advances neither pointer, so any unexpected element-type value leaves points < lastPoint forever, causing an infinite loop/hang (CWE-835). The same structural non-validation applies in both branches.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). The enclosing loop guard 'while (points < lastPoint)' only guarantees 2 qreals remain, but the CurveToElement case reads points[0..5] (6 qreals) and advances points by 6 without checking that 6 points/3 types remain. Minimal trigger: a stroked path whose type sequence is [MoveToElement, CurveToElement] with elementCount==2 (4 qreals); the first MoveTo leaves 2 qreals, the loop re-enters, and cubicTo reads 4 qreals (32 bytes) past the points buffer, then points += 6 overshoots lastPoint. This code performs no intake validation of the types/points pairing, so any untrusted or deserialized path data crossing the rendering trust boundary reaches the sink.

Same root cause in the cosmetic-pen branch (CWE-125): the loop guard 'points < lastPoint' ensures only 2 qreals remain, but the CurveToElement case dereferences three QPointF values (6 qreals) at ((const QPointF*)points)[0..2] with no remaining-length check, reading past the coordinate buffer for a path ending in a CurveToElement or with desynchronized types.

Infinite loop (CWE-835). If *types holds an unexpected value (any element-type not equal to MoveTo/LineTo/CurveTo, e.g., a stray CurveToDataElement or a garbage value from attacker-influenced path data), the default case neither advances points nor types, so the loop condition 'points < lastPoint' stays true forever and the application hangs in a tight loop; no validation of element-type values is performed at this intake.

assumptions: The QVectorPath element-type and coordinate arrays are treated as attacker-influenced because they ultimately derive from data crossing a trust boundary (parsed vector/SVG documents, QDataStream-serialized QPainterPath state, or drawing commands from untrusted sources); paths built exclusively through QPainterPath's public API currently maintain the 3-elements-per-curve invariant, so exploitation of the OOB requires a path that bypasses those invariants (e.g., deserialized or engine-constructed paths).
The out-of-bounds reads are of up to 32 bytes past a heap allocation, so practical impact is primarily a crash/DoS with limited information-disclosure potential.
limitations: The cosmetic branch omits the empty-handler check ('if (!d->strokeHandler->types.size()) return;') that the non-cosmetic branch has before constructing and filling strokePath; reachable but benign (filling an empty path), not a vulnerability.
'path.elementCount()+4' can theoretically overflow int, but requires ~2^31 elements, which cannot be allocated; dismissed as unreachable.
NaN/Inf path coordinates are not sanitized and propagate into the dasher/stroker; any defective behavior (e.g., hangs) would reside in QDashStroker/QStroker, outside the statements analyzed here.
Negative pen widths pass the 'penWidth == 0' check straight to setStrokeWidth; no memory-safety effect within this code.

verdict.summary: ReadCINImage assigns the attacker-controlled CIN header byte cin.image.channel[0].bits_per_pixel directly to image->depth with no domain validation (and raw pixels_per_line/lines_per_image to image->columns/rows). The unvalidated depth flows into GetBytesPerRow, which sizes the per-row read length, and into ImportQuantumPixels, which decodes quantum_info->depth bits per channel per pixel from that length-sized stream buffer. For depths the row-size computation treats as 8-bit but the generic importer decodes at full bit width (e.g. 9-15, 255), ImportQuantumPixels consumes more bytes than were read, reading past the end of the blob-stream/quantum buffer - a heap out-of-bounds read reachable from a crafted .cin file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the raw, attacker-controlled header fields are assigned to image->depth/columns/rows with no validation of the depth domain. image->depth (a full 0-255 byte) then controls both the row read length (GetBytesPerRow, line 379/383) and the ImportQuantumPixels consumption (line 398); a crafted file with bits_per_pixel=9 (or any depth outside the handled set) makes the importer decode more bytes per pixel than GetBytesPerRow accounted for, reading past the length-sized buffer.

Sink: the stream buffer is guaranteed to hold only `length` bytes (the count==length check bounds what was read, not what the importer consumes), yet ImportQuantumPixels decodes according to the unvalidated quantum_info->depth set from the header byte. With bits_per_pixel=9, columns=64, rows=1, number_channels!=1, the row length is sized as ~3*64 bytes while the importer consumes 3*9/8*64=216 bytes, over-reading the heap buffer by 24 bytes.

assumptions: GetBytesPerRow and ImportQuantumPixels are the standard ImageMagick implementations: GetBytesPerRow sizes unhandled depths via its case 8/default branch (8-bit-equivalent row length) while ImportQuantumPixels' generic path consumes quantum_info->depth bits per channel per pixel, so depths such as 9-15 or 255 cause the importer to read past the length-sized row buffer.
MagickSizeType is 64-bit, so the columns*image->rows product at line 348 cannot wrap; columns and rows are each at most 2^32-1.
limitations: The columns*rows/8 vs GetBlobSize heuristic at line 348 is far too weak for depth>8 (a depth-8 RGB row needs 3x more data than checked), but the per-row count!=length break turns this into a graceful early exit, not memory unsafety.

On 32-bit builds columns*rows could wrap and bypass the file-size heuristic, but SetImageExtent and pixel-cache resource limits reject the resulting oversized allocation, so impact is a handled error/DoS.

`offset` is advanced by the requested read size even when ReadBlob returns short, so offset can overestimate the true blob position and pixel data may be read from a misaligned offset - robustness/cosmetic only.
depth==0 or depths where the importer consumes less than the row length merely produce garbage/blank image content with no memory-safety impact.
`(void) extent;` at line 378 is a dead computation (GetQuantumExtent result unused); style issue.

verdict.summary: The function dereferences its RBinFile pointer (`bf->rbin`) before performing its own NULL check (`r_return_val_if_fail (bf, -1)`), so the guard can never protect that access; a NULL bf — a state this function's own guard declares it must handle — causes a NULL-pointer dereference (crash/DoS) before validation.

evidence.reason: Root cause: use-before-NULL-check (CWE-476). `bf` is read at line 3 to initialize `bin`, but the NULL guard `r_return_val_if_fail (bf, -1)` only executes later (line 10), so the intended validation is dead with respect to this access. Trigger: any call with bf == NULL — a state the function's own guard asserts it handles — dereferences NULL at `bf->rbin` and crashes before the check runs.

assumptions: The decoder/charset helpers (r_utf8_decode, r_utf16le_decode, r_utf32le_decode, r_utf8_encode, r_charset_encode_str, r_utf_block_list) honor their length/size parameters as their signatures indicate; all buffer accesses in the scan loop were verified in-bounds under that contract.
`bf == NULL` is treated as a permitted input state because the function's own `r_return_val_if_fail (bf, -1)` exists precisely to handle it.
limitations: `int outlen = len * 4` (line 47) is a signed integer overflow (CWE-190) for scan ranges > 512 MB when RABIN2_CHARSET is set, but the wrapped bound is only passed to r_charset_encode_str, and the output buffer is correctly sized via calloc(len, 4); with a bound-respecting callee the result is truncation or no encoding, not memory corruption, and it additionally requires an operator-supplied environment variable — recorded as robustness-only.

The return value of `r_buf_read_at(bf->buf, from, buf, len)` (line 42) is unchecked; on short/failed reads the calloc'ed buffer remains zero-filled, so all subsequent parsing stays in bounds — robustness only.

The section cache (`s`, `vdelta`, `pdelta`) is computed once and reused for subsequent strings (reset only when from==0 && to==bf->size), yielding incorrect vaddr values — correctness issue without memory-safety impact.
The escape-sequence lookup table maps r==92 ('\\') into a blank run, so a literal backslash is rendered as a space — cosmetic defect; the r<93 index check keeps the access in bounds.

Despite the 'may oobread' comment on the scan loop, all `buf` accesses are bounded by `to - from`, which never exceeds the allocated buffer size (len, or 4*len after charset conversion), so no out-of-bounds read actually occurs.

verdict.summary: Two confirmed defects: (1) In the FTPWHO block, when strlen(name) == sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename), the unsigned source index 'sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U' underflows to (size_t)-1, making memcpy read one byte before the attacker-controlled filename buffer (and the branch never NUL-terminates the destination). (2) The anonymous-overwrite denial path (guest != 0) is reached AFTER the client-forced rename(name, atomic_file) has moved the pre-existing original file onto the atomic name; the deny branch jumps to 'end:' where unlink(atomic_file) deletes that original, so a guest who is explicitly denied overwrite permission can destroy an existing non-empty file via 'REST n' + 'STOR'.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read via unsigned underflow: 'name' is the attacker-controlled upload filename and sl = strlen(name). The else branch is taken when sl >= sizeof shm_data_cur->filename (N). When sl == N, the size_t expression sl - N - 1U equals (size_t)-1, so &name[(size_t)-1] is name - 1 and memcpy reads one byte before 'name' and copies N bytes with no NUL terminator written (the if-branch terminates, this branch does not). Trigger: STOR with a filename of length exactly N in an FTPWHO build; the code performs no length check enforcing sl > N before the sink.

Authorization path fails to preserve protected data: with attacker-controlled restartat > 0 (REST n), lines 45-46 rename the pre-existing original file onto atomic_file before this guest overwrite-authorization check runs. On denial the branch jumps to 'end:' (line 255-256) where unlink(atomic_file) deletes the original file. Trigger: anonymous session with anonymous uploads enabled (anon_noupload == 0), default build without ANON_CAN_RESUME, binary type; client sends 'REST 1' then 'STOR <existing non-empty file>' and the file the guest is not permitted to overwrite is destroyed.

assumptions: Finding 1 requires the FTPWHO compile-time option to be enabled (shm_data_cur != NULL) and that an upload filename of length exactly sizeof(shm_data_cur->filename) can reach dostor (no length cap is visible in this code).
Finding 2 assumes the default build (ANON_CAN_RESUME not defined) and a configuration where anonymous uploads are permitted (anon_noupload == 0), so the guest passes the top-level check at line 24.
checknamesanity, get_atomic_file, and quota helpers behave as their names imply; their implementations are not shown.
limitations: FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) at line 179 (SHOW_REAL_DISK_SPACE) uses fd 'f' after close(f) at line 173; no fd-reallocating call occurs between them in this code, so the call simply fails with EBADF - robustness only, not a vulnerability.

The end-cleanup unlink also destroys the pre-rename original on non-guest failure paths after the line 45-46 rename (quota denial at line 121, failed data connection at line 125) - an availability defect for authorized users sharing the same missing-rollback root cause as finding 2.

On aborted transfers (ret != 0), the atomic rename at line 224 still commits partial data over the original; plausibly intended 'keep what was uploaded' semantics, so not counted as a separate vulnerability.

The else branch of the FTPWHO copy writes exactly sizeof shm_data_cur->filename non-terminated bytes into a char array read by the separate ftpwho process; if that field is not over-allocated, the consumer performs an OOB read (CWE-170-style), but the struct definition is not shown.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse() contains a remotely triggerable infinite loop: when a peer has PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY set, receipt of an MP (CAPABILITY_CODE_MP) capability causes `continue` to skip the `pnt += cap.length + 3` advance, so the `while (pnt < end)` loop never terminates and bgpd spins forever (remote DoS). Additionally, `memcpy(&cap, pnt + 1, sizeof(struct capability))` is performed before the capability length check, reading up to sizeof(struct capability)-3 bytes past the end of the message when fewer bytes than sizeof(struct capability) remain, an out-of-bounds read of network-supplied data.

evidence.reason: This `continue` (taken when cap.code == CAPABILITY_CODE_MP and PEER_FLAG_OVERRIDE_CAPABILITY is set) skips the loop-invariant advance `pnt += cap.length + 3` at the bottom of the while loop, so `pnt` never changes and `while (pnt < end)` loops forever. Any remote peer can trigger it by sending a Capability message containing an MP capability code, hanging the BGP daemon (CWE-835, remote DoS).

This memcpy copies sizeof(struct capability) bytes although the preceding check only guarantees 3 bytes remain (pnt + 3 <= end). When a truncated capability sits at the end of the message (3 to sizeof(struct capability)-1 bytes remaining), it reads attacker-positioned data past the end of the received message buffer (CWE-125 out-of-bounds read).

assumptions: sizeof(struct capability) is larger than 3 bytes (it contains code, length and an mpc afi/safi pair, typically 6+ bytes), which is what makes the memcpy over-read possible.

The C2 over-read crosses the actual allocation boundary only if the capability message ends at the end of the underlying stream buffer; with buffer slack it remains a read of data past the logical message. The C1 infinite loop requires no such assumption beyond the peer being configured with override-capability, a documented Quagga/FRR option.
limitations: The afi/safi array writes (peer->afc_recv[afi][safi] etc.) were examined and are safely guarded by the enumerated-value check (afi limited to AFI_IP/AFI_IP6, safi to SAFI_UNICAST/SAFI_MULTICAST/BGP_SAFI_VPNV4, all valid indexes), so no OOB write exists on that path.
cap.length + 3 cannot overflow (max 258), and the length check `pnt + (cap.length + 3) > end` correctly bounds the pointer advance on non-continue paths.

verdict.summary: adts_decode_extradata validates the parser return (off < 0), rejects out-of-range object type (unsigned comparison catches the -1 underflow case), escape sample-rate index, and illegal GASpecificConfig flags before enabling write_adts, and bounds the fixed-size PCE copy via init_put_bits with MAX_PCE_SIZE. Attacker-influenced extradata cannot reach a memory-unsafe or fail-open-to-invalid path within this function as written.

assumptions: init_get_bits/skip_bits_long/get_bits and init_put_bits/put_bits enforce their documented buffer and size contracts (out-of-range reads yield 0; put_bits respects the buffer end set by init_put_bits).

avpriv_mpeg4audio_get_config2 returns a bit offset within the consumed bits of buf (off >= 0 checked here), so skip_bits_long cannot advance beyond the initialized buffer by more than the bitreader tolerates safely.
MAX_PCE_SIZE is sized to hold a maximal valid AAC PCE, and ff_copy_pce_data reads element counts from the bitstream via the bounded GetBitContext.
limitations: size is not checked for <= 0 before init_get_bits(buf, size*8); a zero/negative size yields an invalid bitreader, but the path fails closed (get_config2 errors, off < 0 returns), so no security impact.

If extradata is truncated after the offset returned by the parser, the three get_bits(&gb,1) flag checks read 0 and silently pass, and ff_copy_pce_data may emit a degenerate (zero-filled) PCE — a robustness/validation-weakening issue producing malformed ADTS output, not memory unsafety or privilege impact.

adts->pce_size is derived from ff_copy_pce_data's return without an explicit comparison against MAX_PCE_SIZE; safety relies on the put-bit layer's buffer-end handling, which is internal and correct as used.

m4ac.object_type - 1 is stored before the range check; if the parser could yield 0 the stored value is -1, but the subsequent unsigned comparison (> 3U) rejects it before any use, so no defect materializes.

verdict.summary: ex_copy() is not vulnerable as written. The destination n is gated by u_save(n, n+1) failing on out-of-range values before any buffer mutation; within the copy loop, the index arithmetic provably maintains line1 <= line2 <= ml_line_count at every ml_get(line1) call (line2 grows at most 1 per iteration while the buffer grows exactly 1 per successful append, line1 is bounded by line2 at the loop condition, and the one-time 'line1 == n' reset keeps line1 >= 1), and cursor.lnum = n + k - 1 never exceeds the growing buffer. The only in-function defect is a fail-open desync when vim_strsave() returns NULL or ml_append() fails: the loop indices advance without the buffer growing, which could later drive ml_get() past the end of the buffer — but reaching it requires process memory exhaustion (a broken-environment condition), not attacker-controlled data.

assumptions: line1, line2 arrive within the buffer and with line1 <= line2, per the ex-command parser contract that normalizes and validates ranges before dispatching :copy.
u_save(n, n+1) returns FAIL for a destination outside 0..ml_line_count+1, which is the documented contract of u_save; this code correctly aborts on FAIL.
linenr_T is a long; line numbers are bounded by MAXLNUM and ml_line_count, so count = line2 - line1 + 1 and n + count cannot overflow in any parser-permitted state.
ml_append() appends after lnum for lnum <= ml_line_count (lnum 0 meaning before the first line), per memline contract; no reentrancy (autocommands) fires during this loop.
limitations: Fail-open error path: if vim_strsave() returns NULL (or ml_append() fails, its return value is ignored), the loop still increments line1, line2 and cursor.lnum without the buffer growing, breaking the line2 <= ml_line_count invariant; subsequent ml_get(line1) could then reference a line past the end. This is only reachable under allocator failure (memory exhaustion), i.e. a broken-environment condition, so it is recorded as robustness degradation rather than a vulnerability here.

curbuf->b_op_start.lnum / b_op_end.lnum are written before u_save validates n; if u_save fails the function returns with stale marks. Marks are inert integers and downstream mark consumers clamp to the buffer, so there is no memory-unsafe consequence.

Validation of line1/line2/n is delegated to the command parser and u_save rather than re-checked in this function; if either upstream guard were removed, the loop arithmetic would no longer be provably in-bounds. This reliance is a contract, not a defect in this code as written.

verdict.summary: In drill_parse_T_code(), the tool-change-stop-switch path executes tmps = get_line(fd++), whose post-increment advances the local fd pointer past the single heap-allocated gerb_file_t object; the immediately following gerbv_stats_printf argument fd->filename then reads the filename member out of bounds, and the garbage pointer value is subsequently dereferenced as a %s string, producing an attacker-triggerable heap out-of-bounds read (crash/information exposure) from any drill file containing a TCST sequence.

evidence.reason: Root cause: stray pointer increment `fd++` (line 26) moves the local fd to fd_orig + sizeof(gerb_file_t), i.e., past the end of the single allocated gerb_file_t object; the very next statement dereferences `fd->filename` (line 30) on that out-of-bounds pointer, and the garbage pointer read there is passed as a %s argument to gerbv_stats_printf, causing a second uncontrolled string read. Trigger: an untrusted drill file containing the byte sequence 'T','C','S','T' (e.g., a 'TCST' line) with at least two further bytes in the buffer takes the path temp=='C', (fd->ptr+2)<fd->datalen, next=='S', next=='T', reaching lines 26-30 directly from file content crossing the trust boundary; no check anywhere on this path restores or validates fd before the member read.

assumptions: TOOL_MAX used in the tool_num bounds check is assumed to be no larger than the capacity of image->aperture[], so the guarded index image->aperture[tool_num] stays in bounds (the check 'tool_num < TOOL_MIN || tool_num >= TOOL_MAX' precedes every indexing use).
fd references a single heap-allocated gerb_file_t (standard usage in the gerbv parser), so fd_orig + sizeof(gerb_file_t) lies outside the object and the member read at line 30 is out of bounds.
gerb_fgetc/get_line are assumed to respect fd->datalen, so the (fd->ptr + 2) < fd->datalen guard and the four bytes consumed since entry keep fd->ptr -= 4 non-negative.
limitations: The '\n'/'\r' restore inside the 'if (EOF == temp)' block (dead check, never fires) is a parsing-robustness blemish only; the loop still terminates via the default case and no memory-safety impact results.
gerb_fgetint may overflow on extremely long tool numbers (defect located in the helper, not this code); the wrapped value is still range-checked here before any array indexing.

Drill sizes rejected as unreasonable (<=0 or >=10000) are still passed to drill_stats_add_to_drill_list; this only affects reported statistics, with no allocation sizing or memory access keyed on the value.
g_new0 return is checked against NULL only in the 'C' case and the fallback block via GERB_FATAL_ERROR; g_new0 aborts on failure under GLib semantics, so no unchecked-allocation path exists.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced data (sourced file bytes via fgets, sourced buffer lines) reaches only guarded sinks: every ga_data write is preceded by an enforced ga_grow headroom guarantee, every buf[len-1]/buf[len-2] access is guarded by len>=1/len>=2 which hold on all reachable paths (fgets non-NULL implies at least one byte plus NUL; the buffer branch always appends a NUL so len>=1), and loop continues re-establish headroom via ga_grow before re-entry. The only reachable defect is a correctness quirk in the source_from_buf path (a buffer line that leaves exactly one free byte causes the next buffer line to be concatenated after an embedded NUL, silently skipping script lines), which has no security impact since the skipped content is the attacker's own script text already being executed on the user's behalf.
