A crafted spell file yields: heap out-of-bounds read at byts[n]/byts[arridx[depth]] (lines 37, 51-54), heap out-of-bounds write at idxs[arridx[depth]] (line 40), and stack out-of-bounds writes to arridx/curi/wordcount/tword once depth reaches MAXWLEN (lines 86-89). The only bounds check present (line 77, n+1 < sl_fbyts_len) is applied solely to the NUL-skip loop, not to the primary indexing sites.

evidence.reason: Heap out-of-bounds write: arridx[depth] is a raw index taken from the spell-file-supplied sl_fidxs array (set at line 87, arridx[depth] = idxs[n]) and is never checked against the size of idxs. A crafted .spl file containing an idxs value beyond the array length reaches this write once the node's children are exhausted, writing wordcount[depth] to an attacker-chosen offset.

Out-of-bounds heap read: n is computed from file-controlled arridx[depth] (via idxs[n]) plus curi[depth] and is dereferenced as byts[n] with no check that n < sl_fbyts_len (the same function only bounds-checks the NUL-skip loop at line 77). A crafted spell file with an out-of-range idxs entry triggers this read; the loop-bound read byts[arridx[depth]] at line 37 is similarly unchecked.

Stack out-of-bounds write via unbounded depth: depth is incremented per non-NUL byte with no check against MAXWLEN, yet tword, arridx, curi and wordcount are all fixed-size MAXWLEN stack arrays. A crafted spell file whose idxs chain produces MAXWLEN+1 consecutive non-NUL bytes makes depth reach MAXWLEN, so arridx[depth] = idxs[n] (and curi/wordcount stores) write past the end of these stack arrays, and the loop top at line 37 then also reads them out of bounds.

assumptions: slang->sl_fbyts, sl_fidxs and sl_fbyts_len are populated from a spell (.spl) file on disk (runtime/downloaded spell files), so their contents cross a trust boundary; this function consumes them without any re-validation of index values or tree depth.
Reasoning is based only on the given code; any validation performed by the (unseen) spell-file loader is not relied upon, and the defect stands on the unchecked dereferences present here.
limitations: words_done is split into MSB/LSB (words_done >> 16, words_done & 0xffff) when passed as flags/region to tree_add_word; for very large word counts this is a truncation-style logic concern, not a memory-safety defect in this code.
spell_soundfold() and tree_add_word() are external to this snippet; their internal handling of tsalword was not audited here.
Resetting spin->si_blocks_cnt to 0 each iteration is an intentional anti-compression measure, not a defect.

verdict.summary: thread_call forwards attacker-chosen argument objects and an argument count into sq_call on the target thread's VM, but every sink is guarded by the VM's own mechanisms: Push/sq_move grow the stack, sq_gettop bounds the copy loop, SQVM::Call re-validates the fetched callable's type, and push/pop counts are exactly balanced so the closure slot index can never go negative. The one real gap — no check that the target thread is in a pristine/idle state before pushing its roottable and arguments — is reachable from an untrusted script (suspend the thread, then call again), but the resulting wrong-slot object fetch and stack-slot residue are type-tagged and type-checked, producing at worst clean VM errors or invocation of a closure the script could already call directly; no memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, or authorization impact is demonstrable from this code as written.

assumptions: Squirrel 3.x semantics: sq_call's params count includes the implicit 'this' (the pushed roottable) with the closure at stackbase-1; ::newthread pre-pushes the thread's closure so the target thread's _top is at least 1 before any call.
SQVM::Push and sq_move grow the thread stack when full (no unchecked fixed-capacity write), and SQVM::Call raises a VM error for non-callable objects instead of dereferencing them.
All VM stack slots are tagged SQObjectPtr values, so no in-buffer or cross-slot overwrite path in this function can manufacture type confusion.
thread_call is invoked via the thread delegate registration (typemask guaranteeing a receiver), so stack_get(v,1) is never an empty-stack access under the embedding's documented contract.
limitations: No validation of the target thread's execution state: calling call() on a suspended or previously-run thread makes sq_call fetch the 'closure' from a live attacker-influenced frame register instead of the thread's stored closure; SQVM::Call type-checks it, so the outcome is a clean error or an invocation of a closure the script can already call — a robustness/state-integrity defect, not a security vulnerability.

Ignoring the failure mode of _thread(o)->Push / sq_move (allocation failure during stack growth) would let sq_call run with fewer pushed items than nparams claims, but reaching it requires an out-of-memory environment, and the affected slots are null-initialized tagged values.

The suspended-thread success path leaves the pushed roottable/argument slots resident on the thread's stack; repeated call/suspend/wakeup cycles can grow the thread's stack without bound, equivalent to the script's inherent ability to allocate unbounded memory — DoS-grade at most.

Calling call() on the thread that is currently executing makes the closure slot resolve to the last argument (self-thread case), invoking an attacker-supplied closure with pushed arguments; no privilege change results.
v->_lasterror = _thread(o)->_lasterror shares the error object by reference; harmless under Squirrel's refcounting but notable state sharing.

verdict.summary: jsP_dumpsyntax consumes only internal/trusted inputs: an AST node produced by the codebase's own parser (used solely for a type comparison and delegation to printers) and a formatting flag whose sole effect is an extra newline. No trust boundary is crossed here, no attacker-influenced data reaches a memory-safety, allocation, path, command, or authz sink within this function, and the sole dereference (prog->type) is contractually guaranteed non-NULL by the parser that produced it. The only candidate defects (missing NULL guard, ignored putchar return, mutable global) are caller-contract, environmental, or cosmetic robustness issues, not vulnerabilities in this code as written.

assumptions: jsP_dumpsyntax is invoked with the return value of the codebase's own parser, which always returns a valid, non-NULL js_Ast root on the success path (syntax errors are reported via the error handler, not by returning NULL).
The dump routine is a synchronous, single-threaded utility; the global 'minify' is not accessed concurrently.
Callees pstmlist, pstm, and nl are outside the provided snippet; the analysis of this function assumes their contracts, and any vulnerability inside them would be a separate finding in that code.
limitations: prog is dereferenced (prog->type) without a NULL check; if any future caller could pass NULL, this would be a NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476). With the code as written, no reachable path in this snippet or its documented contract produces that state.
The return value of putchar is ignored; failure (e.g., closed stdout) is silently tolerated. This is robustness degradation only, with no security impact.
'minify' is a mutable global set per call; in a hypothetical multi-threaded embedding this could race (CWE-362), but no concurrent invocation path exists in this code.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir computes the read cursor (bytes) and loop bound (size) from unvalidated inode fields of the filesystem image ((*i)->offset, (*i)->data, (*i)->start) and never checks them against the length of directory_table; attacker-controlled offsets and per-entry size advances drive out-of-bounds reads of directory_table at the header and entry memcpy sinks (including negative-index reads via signed overflow of bytes += (*i)->offset).

evidence.reason: bytes and size are derived from unvalidated inode fields read from the filesystem image and become the read offset and loop bound; no comparison against the directory_table size is ever performed, and bytes += (*i)->offset can wrap the int negative, so the subsequent while(bytes < size) loop permits reads outside the table.

Sink: the directory header is memcpy'd from directory_table + bytes with bytes fully attacker-controlled (inode offset plus attacker-advanced dire->size values) and never bounds-checked against the table length; a crafted image with a large inode data field and offset near the table end (or a wrapping offset) makes this read out of bounds (CWE-125).

Sink: each directory entry is read from directory_table + bytes, where bytes is advanced per iteration by attacker-controlled dire->size + 1 and bounded only by the attacker-controlled size computed at line 49; the missing check that bytes stays within directory_table allows an out-of-bounds read of attacker-chosen offset (CWE-125).

assumptions: directory_table and directory_table_hash are the directory table loaded from the squashfs image being unpacked; the image crosses a trust boundary and is not trusted to be well-formed.
struct dir_ent.name is sized SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 (standard unsquashfs definition), making the strcpy of a validated (< SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) name in-bounds.
read_inode, lookup_entry, and SQUASHFS swap macros are assumed to behave as in upstream unsquashfs 3.x; their internal checks do not bound bytes/size against the table size.
limitations: The corrupted: error path returns NULL after freeing allocations; how the caller handles a NULL dir is outside this function and no fail-open bypass was found within this code.

The comment-asserted invariants (dir_count <= SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, dire->size < SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN) are actually enforced by checks at lines 65-68 and 82-85, so those candidate overflows were dismissed as unreachable.

Possible signed overflow in size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3 (CWE-190) is folded into the primary OOB-read finding since it manifests as the same unbounded cursor; it does not independently constitute a distinct sink.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML converts attacker-controlled gopher-server response data (inbuf) into HTML without adequately validated bounds, NULL checks, or escaping. (1) The clamp at the 'Buffer overflow' guard permits gopherState->len + llen to equal TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, after which line[llen + 1] = '\0' writes one byte past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE buffer (CWE-787). (2) In the telnet/3270 branch, port may be NULL when the gopher line lacks a port field; '*port ? ":" : ""' dereferences NULL, crashing the worker (CWE-476). (3) The raw host and port fields are inserted unescaped into HREF attributes, while name and selector are escaped on the same lines, allowing a malicious gopher server to inject markup/script into the client-rendered page (CWE-79).

evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write. The guard 'if (gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE)' only clamps when the sum reaches TEMP_BUF_SIZE, so llen may be exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (either directly when gopherState->len==0, or after 'llen += gopherState->len' at line 91). The sink then writes the terminator at index llen+1 == TEMP_BUF_SIZE, one byte past the TEMP_BUF_SIZE-byte 'line' array. Trigger: a gopher server sends a single response line of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes ending in '\n' (or a partial-chunk continuation summing to exactly that length); the NUL byte is written past the buffer.

NULL pointer dereference and unescaped markup insertion. port = strchr(host, TAB) may be NULL when the gopher line has no port field; the 'if (port)' block at line 130 only guards the chopping logic, not these uses, so '*port ? ":" : ""' dereferences NULL and crashes the proxy worker. Additionally, the raw, unescaped port string (and host-derived content) is inserted directly into the HREF attribute: a malicious gopher server can supply a port/host containing '"' to break out of the attribute and inject markup, while name and selector are escaped on the same call. Trigger: line 'Tfoo\tselector\thost\n' (NULL deref), or a port field containing '" onmouseover="...' (attribute injection).

evidence.snippet: outbuf.appendf(" %s\n", icon_url, host, gtype, escaped_selector, html_quote(name));
evidence.reason: HTML/attribute injection: 'host' is the raw host field parsed from the attacker-controlled gopher response (delimited only by TABs, so it may contain '"', '<', '>') and is inserted into the HREF attribute without any HTML or URL escaping, unlike name (html_quote) and selector (escaped_selector) on the same line. Trigger: a gopher server sends a directory line whose host field is 'h" onmouseover="alert(1)' followed by a TAB, producing '<A HREF="gopher://h" onmouseover="alert(1)/...">' in the page rendered to the client.

assumptions: TEMP_BUF_SIZE is the fixed size (4096 in Squid) of the LOCAL_ARRAY 'line' and of gopherState->buf, as implied by the clamp arithmetic at line 75; if gopherState->buf were smaller than TEMP_BUF_SIZE, additional overflows would exist at line 83.
gtype constants (GOPHER_TELNET, GOPHER_DIRECTORY, etc.) map to single characters of the first byte of each attacker-controlled gopher line, as in standard gopher protocol and Squid's gopher.cc.

The gopher response data in inbuf originates from a remote gopher server (network trust boundary) and the converted HTML is rendered to the client, so markup-bound strings must be escaped by this function.
limitations: The OOB write is limited to a single NUL byte one position past a fixed-size array; practical impact depends on adjacent static data layout.

The NULL dereference (CWE-476) at lines 220-222/224-226 is a confirmed remotely triggerable denial of service but is a crash, not memory corruption; it is covered in evidence 2 and the summary though the CWE list is capped at two entries.

line[llen] is left stale between iterations because the terminator is written at llen+1 instead of llen; parsing can then operate on stale bytes from a previous line, but all reads remain in-bounds due to the in-bounds terminator — robustness/correctness issue only.
Return values of entry->append()/entry->flush() are unchecked; failure requires a broken environment and yields no security impact here.

A negative llen from the clamp would require gopherState->len >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE, a state this code cannot produce (len is only ever set to a value <= TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1), so it was rejected as unreachable.

verdict.summary: e1000_send_packet is a thin dispatch function: it routes a guest-generated packet to either the loopback receive handler or qemu_send_packet and updates TX statistics. The guest-influenced inputs (packet buffer, packet size, PHY_CTRL loopback bit) are used only as (a) a bit test on a constant-index register, (b) arguments passed to bounds-managed net subsystems, (c) a comparison-chain bucketed stats index in e1000x_increase_size_stats (always within PTCregs[0..5]), and (d) a fixed 6-byte broadcast/multicast address read from the device's embedded staging buffer. No memory access, copy length, allocation sizing, indexing, or authz decision in this function consumes attacker data without an enforced precondition, so no vulnerability exists in this code as written.

assumptions: buf points into the device's own fixed-size TX staging buffer inside E1000State and the caller (xmit_seg/process_tx_descriptors) keeps buf and size consistent, i.e., size bytes were actually written into that buffer; this function cannot be blamed for caller-side inconsistency.
nc->info->receive in loopback mode is the device's own receive function, which pads undersized frames and applies its own RX-ring bounds logic before writing guest memory.
qemu_get_queue(s->nic) returns a non-NULL NetClientState for an initialized device; realize failure is outside guest-reachable state.
e1000x_increase_size_stats selects the PTCregs index via an if/else comparison chain (thresholds 64/127/255/511/1000/1518), which keeps the index in [0,5] for any int size including negative values.
limitations: No explicit range validation of size is performed in this function before nc->info->receive / qemu_send_packet; this is safe only because the net subsystem (frame padding, MTU/queue handling) and the receive callback re-validate, and because the caller constructs a consistent pointer/length pair.

inc_tx_bcast_or_mcast_count reads 6 bytes of buf regardless of size; for size < 6 this reads bytes beyond the logical packet (though still inside the embedded fixed-size buffer), which is a robustness nuance, not memory unsafety.
nc is dereferenced without a NULL check; NULL would require device realize failure, not an attacker-reachable state.
The loopback path calls nc->info->receive directly, bypassing net-queue filtering; this is intended emulation behavior with no demonstrated security impact.

verdict.summary: xfrm_expand_policies() validates every externally-influenced pointer before dereferencing it: pols[0] is checked for NULL (line 7) and IS_ERR (line 12), and pols[1] — the result of xfrm_policy_lookup_bytype(), which can return ERR_PTR for unsupported families — is checked for NULL (line 27) and IS_ERR (line 28) before *num_pols is incremented (line 33) and its fields are read (line 34, 39). The final loop only touches pols[0] and pols[1], both of which are proven valid on every reachable path. Error paths release exactly the references they hold (xfrm_pols_put runs with *num_pols == 1 on the pols[1] error path). No sink in this code uses attacker-influenced data for memory access, allocation sizing, or copy length without an enforced precondition.

assumptions: Callers follow the kernel-internal contract: xfrm_lookup() passes a pols[XFRM_MAX_DEPTH]-sized array with *num_pols in {0, 1} as produced by xfrm_policy_lookup(), and checks the return code before consuming *num_xfrms. These are static, same-file kernel callers, not an external trust boundary.

Policy objects in the table (pols[i]->xfrm_nr, action, type, if_id) were validated at the netlink intake boundary (install-time checks bound xfrm_nr to XFRM_MAX_DEPTH), so field values consumed here are constrained to their defined ranges.

CONFIG_XFRM_SUB_POLICY code paths were analyzed as compiled-in; the analysis holds identically with the block compiled out (then num_pols stays <= 1 and only pols[0] is dereferenced after validation).
limitations: Stale *num_xfrms on the IS_ERR(pols[0]) exit (lines 13-14 reset only *num_pols): harmless because every caller gates on the negative return value before reading *num_xfrms; robustness note only.

Combined template count: line 34 can produce *num_xfrms = pols[0]->xfrm_nr + pols[1]->xfrm_nr, potentially exceeding XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (6) when a SUB policy with 6 templates coexists with a deep MAIN policy. Within this function the value is a plain int output used for no memory access, allocation, or copy; an out-of-bounds would have to be demonstrated in downstream bundle-resolve code (which independently re-derives per-policy depths from pols[]), so no sink violation could be proven from this snippet alone.
The write pols[1] = ... assumes the caller's array has at least 2 slots; safe for all current in-kernel callers (XFRM_MAX_DEPTH-sized arrays) but is an implicit contract not enforced locally.

verdict.summary: All sinks reachable from attacker-controlled terminal input (tp/typebuf) are guarded by explicit length checks before access: len<3 for GUI CSI, len<slen for termcode matches, len<=modslen and len<j for the xterm modifier path, and nr>=tp+len before each *nr deref in the DEC-mouse count loop. Remaining unbounded reads exist only in GUI-internal event decoding (scrollbar/tabline/menu branches), whose CSI/KS_* byte groups are generated solely by Vim's own GUI encoder and cannot be produced by terminal input; the KS_MENU pointer is validated via check_menu_pointer with a fail-closed KE_IGNORE path. No memory-safety, bounds, authz, or fail-open defect is reachable from data crossing a trust boundary.

assumptions: typebuf.tb_buf allocation (TYPEBUF_SIZE + 4*MAXMAPLEN + headroom) and the tb_len/tb_off invariants are maintained by ins_typebuf/alloc_typebuf as in upstream Vim; the getdigits post-call bound check relies on this headroom.
termcodes[] entries registered via set_termcode maintain modlen < len, so code[modslen] and code[slen-1] reads are in-bounds.

handle_csi, handle_osc, handle_dcs, check_termcode_mouse and put_string_in_typebuf bodies are not shown; the audit covers only this function's control flow, which passes correct len/buflen/slen arguments to them.
GUI builds in practice define USE_ON_FLY_SCROLL, compiling out the scrollbar loops entirely.
limitations: DEC-mouse count loop: getdigits(&nr) is bounded only by the check placed after the call, so the final digit scan may dereference tp[len] (one byte past valid data) when tp[2..len-1] are all digits; the read stays within the typebuf allocation and the function then returns -1 (fail-closed), so no security impact.

GUI scrollbar loops (KS_VER_SCROLLBAR/KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR) read tp[j], tp[j+1], tp[j+2] without comparing j to len and can set slen=j beyond len; reachable only in FEAT_GUI builds without USE_ON_FLY_SCROLL and only from byte groups Vim's own GUI encoder writes in fixed-size well-formed units — no attacker-reachable trigger.
KS_MENU casts four decoded input bytes to a vimmenu_T*, but check_menu_pointer validates it against root_menu (pointer comparison, no deref of the candidate) and falls back to KE_IGNORE on failure.

atoi() on attacker-supplied modifier digit runs can overflow a signed int (UB); the result only feeds decode_modifiers bitmask tests and bounded writes into the 43-byte string buffer — no memory-safety impact.
put_string_in_typebuf with slen from check_termcode_mouse/handle_csi cannot be audited (bodies not shown); this function passes correctly derived values.

verdict.summary: start_visual_mode only sets visual-mode state flags, conditionally normalizes the virtual column via validate_virtcol()/coladvance() (which internally clamps to the line), and marks redraw state. Attacker-influenced inputs (the key code parameter and one byte of buffer text read via gchar_cursor()) are used only in comparisons and flag assignments; no memory access, length, index, format, path, or authz sink consumes tainted data without an enforced precondition. No reachable defect exists in this function as written.

assumptions: The editor core maintains the invariant that curwin->w_cursor points inside the buffer when this function is reachable; this function contains no path that could invalidate it first.
coladvance() clamps the requested column to the actual line length per its contract, so passing w_virtcol after validate_virtcol() cannot move the cursor out of bounds.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: gchar_cursor() is called without an explicit in-function cursor bounds check; rejected because reaching this function presupposes a valid cursor maintained by the editor core, and the read result is only compared against TAB.
Candidate dismissed: coladvance(curwin->w_virtcol) could in principle take an out-of-range column; rejected because validate_virtcol() recomputes the value and coladvance() clamps internally.

Non-security observations: clip_star.vmode assignment and redraw-flag updates are benign state changes; no error paths are ignored and no resources are allocated, so no leak or fail-open behavior exists.

verdict.summary: In get_recurse_data_length (pcre2 JIT), the CASE_ITERATOR_TYPE_PRIVATE_DATA_2B handler advances the bytecode pointer by 'cc += 1 + IMM2_SIZE;', but the class-range repeat opcodes it covers (OP_CRRANGE/OP_CRMINRANGE/OP_CRPOSRANGE for {n,m} quantifiers on character classes) encode TWO 2-byte counts, so the correct stride is 1 + 2*IMM2_SIZE. A compiled pattern such as (?1)([ab]{2,3}) makes the walker land on the attacker-controlled second count byte, which is then dispatched as an opcode; subsequent operand-driven jumps (GET(cc,1) up to 65535, cc[1] lengths, OP_CLASS's 32-unit read, GET_EXTRALEN) read outside the compiled-pattern buffer while the only guards (SLJIT_ASSERT cc==ccend, cc!=NULL) are debug-only and the loop test 'cc < ccend' cannot detect overshoot. This yields an out-of-bounds read (crash/info leak) and a corrupted recursion stack-frame length during JIT compilation of an attacker-supplied regular expression.

evidence.reason: CASE_ITERATOR_TYPE_PRIVATE_DATA_2B covers the bounded class-repeat opcodes (OP_CRRANGE, OP_CRMINRANGE, OP_CRPOSRANGE), each of which stores two IMM2 counts (min and max of an {n,m} range), so the pointer must advance by 1 + 2*IMM2_SIZE (as the same JIT does elsewhere: min = GET2(cc,1), max = GET2(cc,1+IMM2_SIZE)). Advancing by only 1 + IMM2_SIZE leaves cc pointing at the attacker-controlled second count byte; the switch then interprets that byte as an opcode and the walk desynchronizes, allowing operand-driven skips and 32-unit class reads past ccend and beyond the compiled-pattern allocation (the SLJIT_ASSERT(cc == ccend) and next_opcode NULL checks are no-ops in release builds, and the 'cc < ccend' loop test cannot detect overshoot). Minimal trigger: a JIT-compiled pattern whose recursion target contains a class with a range quantifier, e.g. (?1)([ab]{2,3}).

assumptions: CASE_ITERATOR_TYPE_PRIVATE_DATA_2B expands to the class-range repeat opcodes OP_CRRANGE/OP_CRMINRANGE/OP_CRPOSRANGE, which encode two IMM2 counts; this is corroborated within the code itself by the sibling CASE_ITERATOR_TYPE_* handlers advancing single code units (class repeats have no character operand, hence no SUPPORT_UNICODE/HAS_EXTRALEN block), by the get_class_iterator_size usage for the preceding OP_CLASS, and by the same file's next_opcode stride of 1 + 2*IMM2_SIZE for these opcodes.
SLJIT_ASSERT compiles to nothing in release builds, so the SLJIT_ASSERT(cc == ccend) and SLJIT_ASSERT(cc != NULL) invariants are not enforced at runtime.
limitations: The release-only removal of SLJIT_ASSERT checks (cc != NULL after next_opcode, cc == ccend after the loop) is a hardening weakness, but it only becomes memory-unsafe via the confirmed stride bug on line 172; on well-formed bytecode the asserts hold.

common->optimized_cbracket[offset] (line 80) and the OP_COND read *alternative = cc + GET(cc,1) (line 106) are indexed/dereferenced without local bounds checks; on compiler-produced well-formed bytecode the capture number and LINK offsets are within their allocated tables/blocks, so no trigger was constructible and they are not counted as vulnerabilities here.

The desynchronized walk also miscounts 'length', the number of private-data words the recursion compile path pushes for the stack frame; an undercount could additionally make JIT-generated machine code access beyond the pushed frame, but confirming an out-of-bounds write requires analysis of compile_recurse beyond this function, so only the out-of-bounds read is asserted.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir parses attacker-controlled squashfs image data without validating that the byte cursor (bytes) and loop bound (size), both derived from inode fields (data, start, offset) in the image, stay within the allocated directory_table buffer. A crafted image makes while(bytes < size) walk SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_HEADER/SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_ENTRY/memcpy past the end of directory_table (heap out-of-bounds read). Additionally, size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3 truncates a long long into int, and dir_count = dirh.count + 1 can become negative, bypassing the dir_count > SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT check (signed comparison), enabling ~2^31 further out-of-bounds reads.

evidence.reason: size is computed from attacker-controlled inode fields ((*i)->data is an unvalidated unsigned int from the image, bytes already contains the unvalidated (*i)->offset) and is never checked against the actual directory_table allocation size; the long long sum is also truncated into int, allowing wrap. A crafted image with a large data field makes the subsequent while(bytes < size) loop read directory_table out of bounds.

Out-of-bounds read sink: bytes indexes the heap buffer directory_table using only the attacker-derived bound size, with no check that bytes (or bytes + sizeof(dirh)) is within the table. Once bytes exceeds the table size (driven by the inode's data/offset fields or by accumulated entry sizes), this swap reads past the end of the heap buffer. The same unvalidated index is used at SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_ENTRY and as the memcpy source.

The guard against excessive entry counts is a signed comparison on int dir_count, but dir_count = dirh.count + 1 wraps when the 32-bit attacker-controlled header count is >= 0x80000000, yielding a negative value that passes this check. while(dir_count--) then executes ~2^31 iterations, each reading directory_table + bytes out of bounds as bytes grows — a signedness bypass (CWE-190) enabling the CWE-125 overread.

assumptions: directory_table is a heap buffer of finite size (the image's directory table) allocated elsewhere in unsquashfs, and lookup_entry returns offsets within it; the inode and directory-table contents are untrusted data from the squashfs image file crossing a trust boundary.
struct dir_ent's name field is sized at least SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 bytes, so the strcpy of the (size-checked) name is in-bounds.

struct squashfs_dir_entry uses a zero/one-byte trailing name array so the aligned buffer of sizeof(struct squashfs_dir_entry) + SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1 exactly accommodates memcpy of dire->size + 1 bytes and the NUL at dire->name[dire->size + 1] for the maximum permitted dire->size = SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN - 1.
squashfs_dir_header.count is a 32-bit field as swapped by SQUASHFS_SWAP_DIR_HEADER, enabling the dir_count wrap.
limitations: malloc/realloc NULL-check paths are handled via EXIT_UNSQUASH; allocation failure requires a broken environment and has no security impact here.
dire->name[dire->size + 1] = '\0' and the memcpy into the aligned local buffer are in-bounds given the preceding dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN check; not a vulnerability.
The (*i)->data == 3 early-return path and the bytes == -1 lookup failure path are correctly handled; no fail-open issue there.

verdict.summary: squashfs_opendir reads directory entries from the global directory_table at offsets (bytes) and lengths (size) derived entirely from the untrusted squashfs image (inode start/offset/data, dir header count, entry size) without ever validating them against the directory table's allocated size, causing heap out-of-bounds reads at the header swap, entry swap, and memcpy sinks. The loop bound size = (*i)->data + bytes - 3 is also truncated into an int.

evidence.reason: bytes (attacker-influenced via inode start/offset and lookup_entry) and size (attacker-influenced via inode data, truncated from long long to int) are used as the sole guard before reading directory_table + bytes; no comparison against the directory table's allocated length exists anywhere, so a crafted image with a large directory-size inode field drives reads past the end of directory_table (heap OOB read, CWE-125; size truncation CWE-190).

Inside the inner loop, bytes is advanced by sizeof(dirh), sizeof(*dire), and dire->size+1 (attacker-controlled, up to 256 per entry) without any check that bytes remains within size or within the directory table's bounds, so the entry-swap read at directory_table + bytes goes out of bounds for entries near or past the table end.

The memcpy source directory_table + bytes with attacker-controlled length dire->size + 1 (up to 256 bytes) is read without verifying that bytes + dire->size + 1 stays inside the allocated directory table, producing an out-of-bounds heap read whose contents are then copied into the parsed directory entry name.

assumptions: directory_table is a heap buffer holding only the directory table read from the untrusted squashfs image, with a finite allocated size that this function never consults.

struct dir_ent.name is sized SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN + 1, and struct squashfs_dir_entry.name is a zero/variable-length field, so the destination-side of the dire->name memcpy and the strcpy at line 97 are within bounds given the line-71 check.

SQUASHFS_DIR_COUNT, SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN, DIR_ENT_SIZE are the standard squashfs constants (256, 256, 64-ish), making the existing dir_count and dire->size guards sufficient for those specific sub-checks.
limitations: The strcpy at line 97 was examined and dismissed: the line-71 check (dire->size >= SQUASHFS_NAME_LEN rejected) plus the line-78 NUL terminator guarantee the source string fits the destination buffer, so no destination overflow is reachable as written.

lookup_entry returning a value other than -1 that is nonetheless outside the table is a contract issue of the hash builder; the exploitable consequence here is entirely due to this function's missing length validation and is covered by the confirmed findings.
The OOB reads are read-only (information disclosure into parsed names/metadata and potential crash), not writes, which bounds impact at the high rather than critical level.

verdict.summary: start_visual_mode() only records editor state (mode character, cursor position, redraw flags) from locally trusted sources; the keystroke parameter and all window state it reads are constrained by Vim's command dispatcher and internal invariants, and no memory, length, format, path, or authorization sink receives an unvalidated value on any path in this function.

assumptions: The parameter c originates from Vim's normal-mode command dispatcher, which only invokes start_visual_mode for the legal visual-mode start characters; no external API or script bypasses that constraint in this code.
curwin->w_cursor is validated against the buffer by the normal_cmd loop before this function runs, per Vim's standard control flow.
limitations: VIsual_mode = c stores the caller's mode character without a range check, but the dispatcher guarantees it is one of the legal mode chars and it is consumed only via equality comparisons, not indexing.
The coladvance(curwin->w_virtcol) call relies on validate_virtcol() executed on the immediately preceding line; both are present, so the precondition is enforced in this code.
gchar_cursor() is called before any explicit cursor validation in this function, but it safely returns NUL at end-of-line and the cursor is validated upstream.
clip_star.vmode = NUL, the w_old_* assignments, and the conceal bookkeeping are pure state updates with no security-relevant sink.

parse_errors: no valid JSON verdict found in output

verdict.summary: In apprentice_load, the constructed per-entry magic-file path is formatted into the fixed-size stack buffer mfn[MAXPATHLEN] via snprintf, but only a negative return value is treated as an error. Truncation (mflen >= sizeof(mfn)) is not detected, so the truncated prefix path is stat'd and, if it names a regular file, passed to load_1 and parsed as a magic database file. Since both the directory path (caller/config-supplied) and directory entry names (filesystem contents) cross trust boundaries, the function fail-opens on a corrupted, unvalidated path instead of rejecting it. The downstream estrndup clamp prevents memory corruption, so the impact is parsing an unintended file as trusted magic rules, not a buffer overflow.

evidence.reason: The snprintf that builds the per-entry path into the fixed 1024-byte (MAXPATHLEN) buffer mfn checks only for a negative return; it omits the required truncation check (mflen >= sizeof(mfn)). Trigger: a near-MAXPATHLEN directory path fn plus an entry name d.d_name whose combined length exceeds sizeof(mfn) makes snprintf return a value >= sizeof(mfn) that is not negative; the code then stats the truncated prefix path and, if it is a regular file, passes it to load_1 to be parsed as a magic database. Both fn (caller/configuration-supplied path) and d.d_name (filesystem directory contents) cross trust boundaries, and this code is responsible for validating the combined path at intake; the missing truncation check lets a corrupted value flow into the file-open/parse sink (root cause: improper input validation, CWE-20).

assumptions: MAXPATHLEN is the conventional 1024 (or 4096) bytes; the trigger requires a magic-directory path within a few bytes of that limit plus an entry name that overflows the buffer.

Meaningful security impact requires the truncated prefix path to collide with an existing regular file different from the intended directory entry, enabling parsing of an unintended file as magic rules.
No memory-safety violation results from this defect: snprintf NUL-terminates mfn and the estrndup call clamps the copy length to sizeof(mfn)-1 when mflen exceeds the buffer.
limitations: qsort(filearr, files, ...) is called with filearr == NULL and files == 0 when the magic directory is empty; this is formally undefined behavior per C but a no-op in every real libc, with no security impact.

maxfiles = (maxfiles + 1) * 2 and mlen = maxfiles * sizeof(*filearr) can theoretically overflow size_t, but reaching it requires an astronomically large number of directory entries, which no real readdir loop can produce.
On erealloc failure the previous filearr pointer is lost (leak), but this is an out-of-memory robustness issue only, with no attacker-driven exhaustion path in this code.
The signed/unsigned comparison in (mflen > sizeof(mfn) - 1) is safe because mflen is guaranteed non-negative by the preceding < 0 check.
Behavior of php_stream_readdir regarding NUL-termination of d.d_name is external to this snippet and assumed to be guaranteed by the stream wrapper.

verdict.summary: In the erealloc failure path of apprentice_load's directory-loading branch, the code calls efree(mfn) where mfn is the stack buffer char mfn[MAXPATHLEN] declared in the same scope, not a heap pointer. If the array-growth allocation fails (a state this code explicitly permits and branches on) while processing attacker-influenced directory entries under the caller-supplied path fn, the stack address is passed to the heap deallocator, corrupting allocator state (free of memory not on the heap).

evidence.reason: mfn is the automatic (stack) array 'char mfn[MAXPATHLEN]' declared at the top of the directory branch; it was never obtained from an allocator, yet it is passed to efree on the erealloc failure path. Trigger: fn names a readable directory containing at least one regular file (forcing the files >= maxfiles growth), and the erealloc of filearr returns NULL — a state this code explicitly models and branches on — causing the heap deallocator to be invoked on a stack pointer, corrupting the allocator. Root cause: free of memory not on the heap (CWE-590/CWE-761).

assumptions: The erealloc failure state is treated as reachable because this code explicitly tests for a NULL return and handles it; in some PHP builds erealloc aborts on OOM instead of returning NULL, which would make the branch dead, but the code as written permits the NULL return.
fn and the contents of the directory it names are attacker-influenced (userland-supplied magic database path in the fileinfo extension), which is the data driving this loop.
limitations: snprintf truncation of the constructed path 'fn/d.d_name' is not rejected: a truncated path that happens to name an existing regular file is duplicated and loaded by load_1 (wrong-file load). No memory-safety violation occurs in this code because snprintf NUL-terminates and the estrndup length is clamped; recorded as a robustness/logic issue.
TOCTOU: the stat(mfn)/S_ISREG check is performed before load_1 later reopens the file, so the file can be swapped (e.g., symlink) in between; no memory-safety or authz consequence within this code.
Resource leaks on the erealloc failure path (previously estrndup'd filearr entries and filearr itself are never freed); no exhaustion path within a single invocation.
The earlier code did not check snprintf for truncation (only < 0); the clamped estrndup length expression is correct for all non-negative mflen values since the negative case already branched out.

verdict.summary: unix_expandpath copies attacker-influenced directory entry names (readdir) and the remaining path into a heap buffer sized STRLEN(path)+BASENAMELEN+5. Tracing every write shows a safe invariant: the copied prefix and the remaining suffix partition the original path (s_offset + rest_len <= STRLEN(path)), so the maximum written offset is STRLEN(path)+dname_len+4. With Vim's BASENAMELEN (500) exceeding any producible readdir name (NAME_MAX=255), no write exceeds the allocation on any reachable path. Multibyte handling delegates to mb_ptr2len, whose contract prevents walking past the NUL. Remaining defects (misaligned fnamencmp offset after backslash removal, unbounded multi-component recursion depth, empty-component EW_NOTWILD match) are logic/robustness issues with no memory-safety or authorization impact.

assumptions: BASENAMELEN is Vim's constant 500 (vim.h), which exceeds any filesystem's NAME_MAX (typically 255); the buffer headroom therefore dominates the maximum dp->d_name length producible by readdir.

mb_ptr2len (utf_ptr2len/dbcs helpers) honors its contract of returning 1 for invalid or truncated characters, never consuming the terminating NUL; the multibyte copy loop is safe only under this contract.
vim_regfree() handles a NULL regprog (checked free), as on the EW_NOTWILD path where regexp compilation may fail.
rem_backslash and the STRNCPY/STRCPY macros are Vim's standard definitions operating on NUL-terminated strings within the allocated buffer.
limitations: No explicit bounds check on STRCPY(s, dp->d_name): safety relies entirely on BASENAMELEN exceeding the maximum directory entry name length. If BASENAMELEN were ever smaller than NAME_MAX, this would be a heap buffer overflow; hardening only.

EW_NOTWILD fallback compares fnamencmp(path + (s - buf), dp->d_name, e - s); after backslash removal between wildoff and s, the offset s - buf no longer matches the component's offset in path, producing a misaligned in-bounds comparison that can match the wrong entry. Logic defect, no security impact in this function.

The non-'**' recursion (one level per wildcard component) has no depth guard like stardepth < 100; a pattern with tens of thousands of '*/' components causes deep recursion and potential stack exhaustion. Robustness/DoS-only degradation requiring an absurd self-supplied pattern.
When the wildcard component is empty (path ending in '/') with EW_NOTWILD, fnamencmp compares zero bytes and matches every directory entry; a globbing behavior quirk, not a security bypass.

verdict.summary: createRandomCursorExecutor performs guarded arithmetic on user-influenced sampleSize and server-computed numRecords purely for plan-selection heuristics. All division sites are protected by explicit checks in this code (numRecords <= 100 early return for non-timeseries; the '!(bucketUnpacker && numRecords)' bail for time-series, which also prevents the NaN case), the optional bucketUnpacker is checked before both dereferences, the record-store random cursor is null-checked, and the executor construction result is checked with a fail-closed error path. No memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, integer-overflow, injection, or authorization sink is reachable with inputs this code permits.

assumptions: sampleSize originates from the user's $sample stage but is validated upstream (DocumentSourceSample requires a non-negative numeric size); this function is an internal planner routine, not a trust-boundary intake point.
gTimeseriesBucketMaxCount is a positive server parameter; numRecords comes from the storage engine and is non-negative.
The invariant asserting the collection lock is a documented precondition of the calling context.
limitations: numRecords includes orphaned documents on sharded collections, so the initial optimization decision can be wrong; this is a performance heuristic corrected by TrialStage, with no security impact.

Even if a negative sampleSize somehow bypassed upstream validation, the arithmetic here yields only a ratio clamped to [0.25, 1.0] (timeseries) or floored at 0.05 (sharded) used for plan choice, not any memory or authz-sensitive value.
The static_cast<MultiIteratorStage*> immediately follows construction of that exact dynamic type and is safe; noted only for completeness.
CSS/sharding metadata calls could yield stale metadata, affecting plan choice only; both candidate plans apply the same ownership filter, so there is no authz gap.

verdict.summary: reserve_sfa_size() sizes a heap buffer from the caller-supplied signed int attr_len, a length ultimately derived from untrusted netlink flow-action attributes, without validating its sign or range. NLA_ALIGN(attr_len) is stored into size_t req_size, so a negative attr_len sign-extends to a huge value; the size_t expression next_offset + req_size then wraps and is truncated into the int new_acts_size, defeating both MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE checks and causing nla_alloc_flow_actions() to return an undersized buffer while (*sfa)->actions_len += req_size corrupts the running offset. The caller subsequently writes the real action bytes at the returned pointer, producing a heap out-of-bounds write (kernel memory corruption reachable via crafted Open vSwitch netlink messages).

evidence.reason: The attacker-influenced signed length attr_len (derived from netlink action attributes crossing the genl trust boundary) is converted into a size_t with no sign or range validation. A negative attr_len sign-extends to a huge req_size, poisoning every subsequent comparison and arithmetic operation; this is the missing intake check that constitutes the root cause.

next_offset + req_size is computed in size_t and wraps when req_size is huge (e.g., attr_len = -8 with actions_len = 0 gives 16 + (2^64-8) = 8), then the result is truncated into the int new_acts_size. The truncated small value passes the outer check at line 16 and the inner check at line 17 re-evaluates the same wrapped size_t expression (8 <= MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE), so both MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE guards are bypassed and nla_alloc_flow_actions() allocates an undersized buffer into which the caller later writes the true action bytes — heap out-of-bounds write.

On the wrapped path the huge req_size (from an unvalidated negative attr_len) is added to actions_len, wrapping the running offset to a near-SIZE_MAX value; all subsequent calls compute next_offset = offsetof(actions) + actions_len with a poisoned state, so the bounds accounting used for the returned write pointer (line 37) and the allocation guard is corrupted, enabling further out-of-bounds writes.

assumptions: attr_len is supplied by the OVS generic-netlink action-copy path (net/openvswitch/ovs_nla.c callers such as copy_action/add_action) and is ultimately derived from user-supplied netlink flow-action attributes; reaching those commands requires CAP_NET_ADMIN over the flow's netns, which unprivileged users can obtain via user namespaces.
MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE is the upstream 32 KiB constant and nla_alloc_flow_actions() rejects sizes above it and allocates sizeof(struct sw_flow_actions) + size.
Callers write the action header/payload of the length they believe was reserved at the pointer returned by this function, so an undersized allocation is directly overflowed by the caller's copy.
limitations: With strictly non-negative attr_len values (e.g., lengths derived from u16 nla_len fields, per-attribute maximum ~64 KiB, and actions_len bounded by MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE), the arithmetic in this function cannot wrap and all paths are memory-safe; the overflow requires an attr_len whose sign this code never checks.

The early-fit branch uses ksize(*sfa) slack, so actions_len can modestly exceed the MAX_ACTIONS_BUFSIZE policy limit when the allocator size class is larger than requested; writes still remain within the ksize()-guaranteed allocation, so this is a policy softening, not memory corruption.
The memcpy at line 29 copies only the bounded (*sfa)->actions_len bytes and the allocation-failure path is handled via IS_ERR, so no separate findings arise there.

verdict.summary: In st21nfca_connectivity_event_received, the EVT_TRANSACTION validation uses '&&' instead of '||' (fail-open: any skb whose first byte is the AID tag 0x81 passes regardless of skb->len, and skb->data[0] is read even when skb->len == 0). The transaction buffer is allocated as skb->len - 2 bytes (also omitting sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction)), and then attacker-controlled length bytes skb->data[1] (aid_len, up to 255) and skb->data[aid_len+3] (params_len, up to 255) are used directly as memcpy lengths into that undersized allocation, and as indexes into skb->data without any check against skb->len. A malformed transaction event from the NFC controller/secure element causes kernel heap out-of-bounds writes (memcpy of aid_len/params_len bytes into an allocation smaller than the fixed struct) and out-of-bounds reads of the skb.

evidence.reason: Fail-open validation: the '&&' means the length check is bypassed whenever skb->data[0] == AID_TAG (0x81), so undersized/malformed device-supplied packets proceed; additionally skb->data[0] is read even when skb->len == 0 (OOB read). This is the missing trust-boundary check that permits all downstream overflows.

Allocation is sized skb->len - 2 without adding sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) (which contains u32 aid_len, u8 aid[32], u32 params_len), so the buffer can be far smaller than the struct fields written into it; with skb->len < 2 the unsigned subtraction also underflows (allocation then fails).

aid_len is an attacker-controlled device byte (0-255, spec says 5-16 but is never checked) used directly as a memcpy length into transaction->aid[32] within an skb->len-2 allocation, and as a read of &skb->data[2] beyond skb->len. Trigger: EVT_TRANSACTION skb {0x81, 0xFF, ...} with len 4 → 255-byte memcpy into a 2-byte heap allocation (CWE-787 heap OOB write).

Indexes skb->data[aid_len+2] (line 35), [aid_len+3], and the memcpy source at aid_len+4 are never checked against skb->len (OOB read, CWE-125), and params_len (attacker byte up to 255) is used as a memcpy length into the undersized skb->len-2 allocation (heap OOB write, CWE-787).

assumptions: skb->data and skb->len originate from the ST21NFCA NFC controller (HCI EVT_TRANSACTION, ETSI TS 102 622), i.e., device/secure-element data crossing the kernel trust boundary; a buggy or malicious chip or crafted card-emulation transaction controls every byte and the length.

struct nfc_evt_transaction contains fixed-size members (aid_len u32, aid[NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH=32], params_len u32, params[]), so writing aid_len/params_len bytes requires allocation >= sizeof(struct) + payload, which this code does not perform.
limitations: skb->len - 2 underflows for skb->len < 2, but the resulting ~4GB devm_kzalloc fails and returns -ENOMEM, so it causes no corruption (robustness only).
Error paths at lines 24, 28 and 37 return without kfree_skb(skb), leaking the skb; no exhaustion path is shown in this code, so recorded as robustness, not a vulnerability.
On the default/unknown-event path the function returns 1 without freeing skb — same leak class, not security-critical here.

verdict.summary: mobi_parse_index_entry walks a raw pointer (control_bytes) through the attacker-controlled TAGX tag list without ever comparing it against buf->data + buf->maxlen. A malicious .mobi file whose TAGX record declares many tags with control_byte == 1 advances control_bytes arbitrarily far past the end of the heap-allocated record buffer; the next non-control tag dereferences control_bytes[0], causing a heap out-of-bounds read whose value steers subsequent parsing.

evidence.reason: control_bytes (initialized at line 45 as buf->data + buf->offset) is advanced once per tag whose control_byte == 1, but tagx->tags_count and each tag's control_byte come directly from the file's TAGX record and are unvalidated here; nothing constrains the number of control-byte tags to tagx->control_byte_count or checks control_bytes against buf->data + buf->maxlen. A crafted file with more control_byte==1 tags than bytes remaining in the record buffer makes the subsequent control_bytes[0] dereference read out of bounds of the heap buffer — an OOB read (CWE-125). Trigger: TAGX with tags_count = N, first m tags flagged control_byte==1 with m past the entry/buffer end, followed by one control_byte!=1 tag.

assumptions: INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX is 255 (libmobi definition), so label_length from mobi_buffer_get8 (max 255) fits text[INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX + 1].
mobi_buffer_get8 / mobi_buffer_get_varlen / mobi_buffer_setpos / mobi_buffer_seek enforce buf->maxlen bounds and set buf->error on overflow, per the libmobi buffer layer this code uses.
limitations: entry_length (line 7) can underflow if idxt.offsets[curr+1] < idxt.offsets[curr]; the wrapped line-16 check then shrinks buf->maxlen below buf->offset, but all reads go through bounds-checked buffer helpers, so this yields misparsed data (robustness), not an OOB access in this code.

The ORDT label branch (line 29) and the code after mobi_buffer_seek (line 46) do not check buf->error, allowing garbage index values from a truncated entry; reads remain bounds-checked, no security impact.

If mobi_buffer_setpos (line 8) fails, buf->offset is stale from a previous entry, producing wrong parsing results; no out-of-bounds access results because the line-16 guard still caps buf->maxlen <= original buffer size.

verdict.summary: st21nfca_connectivity_event_received fails to validate the length of an attacker-influenced HCI skb before using it to size a heap allocation and to index it. The guard at line 22 uses '&&' instead of '||', so any frame with data[0]==0x81 passes regardless of skb->len; there is no check that skb->len covers aid_len+4; and the params_len bound at line 47 underflows ((skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) in unsigned arithmetic) whenever skb->len < 26, fail-opening the check. The result is a heap buffer overflow (write of up to ~279 attacker-controlled bytes into a devm_kzalloc'd buffer of skb->len-2 bytes) plus out-of-bounds reads of the skb, reachable by a malicious NFC controller/RF peer sending an EVT_TRANSACTION frame such as len=10, data={0x81,0x10,...,0xFF}.

evidence.reason: The intake length check uses '&&' instead of '||', so a short skb (e.g. len=10, or even len<2) is accepted whenever data[0]==0x81. This missing validation at the trust boundary lets skb->len below the struct's needs reach the allocation and indexing code, enabling the heap out-of-bounds writes.

Unsigned underflow: for skb->len < 26 (accepted due to the faulty guard), (skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) wraps to a huge value, so any params_len (up to 255) passes. The following memcpy then writes params_len attacker-controlled bytes at offset 24 of a skb->len-2-byte heap allocation — heap buffer overflow.

Sink of the confirmed overflow: with skb->len=10, data={0x81,0x10,...,data[19]=0xFF}, the guard (lines 22-23) passes, devm_kzalloc allocates 8 bytes, the underflowed check at line 47 passes, and this memcpy writes 255 bytes at offset 24 of the 8-byte allocation with fully attacker-controlled content (also reading past skb->data).

assumptions: skb (skb->len, skb->data[]) originates from the ST21NFCA connectivity gate over HCI and is attacker-influenced (malicious NFC controller, secure element, or RF peer); it crosses a trust boundary this intake function must validate.

struct nfc_evt_transaction is packed with a u32 aid_len, aid[16] (NFC_MAX_AID_LENGTH), a u32 params_len and a flexible/zero-length params array, giving sizeof = 24 bytes and offsetof(params) = 24, matching the driver's own comment at line 46.
NFC_MIN_AID_LENGTH = 5, NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_AID_TAG = 0x81, NFC_EVT_TRANSACTION_PARAMS_TAG = 0x82.
limitations: Reading skb->data[0] before proving skb->len >= 1 (len==0 frame with data[0]==0x81 slips past the guard) is a one-byte over-read; on that path devm_kzalloc(skb->len-2=~4G) fails cleanly with -ENOMEM and skb linear buffers usually have slack, so this is robustness degradation rather than a confirmed security impact.

The aid memcpy at lines 36-37 also reads skb->data[2..aid_len+1] without checking skb->len >= aid_len+2 (OOB read of the skb); it is subsumed by the same missing-intake-validation root cause as the confirmed writes.

transaction allocated via devm_kzalloc is not freed on the early -EINVAL/-EPROTO returns at lines 34, 42, 48; because it is devm-managed it is reclaimed with the device, so this is a bounded leak, not a vulnerability.
No issue found in the ST21NFCA_EVT_CONNECTIVITY branch; 'host' is passed through to nfc_se_connectivity without use as a memory bound here.

verdict.summary: The result of calloc for mountent.mnt_opts is only guarded around the option-building strlcat block; when allocation fails, mnt_opts remains NULL and is passed unconditionally to addmntent (line 86), which dereferences the NULL options field — a NULL pointer dereference (unchecked return value) in a privileged mount helper.

evidence.reason: The calloc return value is checked only to guard the strlcat option-building block; there is no bailout on failure. If calloc returns NULL (allocation failure), execution falls through to 'rc = addmntent(pmntfile, &mountent)' at line 86 with mountent.mnt_opts == NULL, and glibc's addmntent dereferences/writes the NULL options string. Trigger: any invocation of add_mtab under memory-exhaustion/ulimit conditions; path is lines 61 (NULL) -> 62 guard skipped -> 84-86 sink reached. Root cause: missing check of the allocation result before the dereferencing sink.

assumptions: MOUNTED and MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN are trusted constants; unlock_mtab/lock_mtab/getusername/toggle_dac_capability follow their conventional contracts (idempotent unlock guarded by an internal 'lock file created' flag; getusername returns a NUL-terminated string or NULL).
devname, mountpoint, and fstype are supplied by the calling mount logic after a successful mount() and are non-NULL per the caller contract; add_mtab is invoked only after the mount syscall succeeds.
glibc addmntent dereferences the mnt_opts field (fputs/strlen); a NULL field causes undefined behavior/crash.
limitations: Double mtab unlock: unlock_mtab() is called explicitly (e.g., line 53 and before return) and again via atexit(unlock_mtab) at process exit (line 42). Whether this is harmful depends on the external unlock_mtab implementation; typical implementations guard with a 'we created the lock file' flag, so this is recorded as a robustness concern, not a confirmed vulnerability in this code.

Early return at line 40 (toggle_dac_capability failure) leaves the DAC capability enabled and the signal mask unrestored; reachable only via a broken environment, and the process exits immediately after.
Return values of endmntent, the final sigprocmask, and atexit are unchecked; failures require a pathological environment and have no security impact here.

devname/mountpoint are written verbatim into the root-owned mtab without sanitization; a caller supplying strings with embedded whitespace/newlines could corrupt/inject mtab entries, but this requires a hostile caller violating the post-mount contract and a deployment permitting user-controlled values — hardening note, not confirmed in this code.

The strlcat-based option building is correctly bounds-checked (calloc zero-fill plus MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN-bounded strlcat), so no buffer overflow exists on any flag or username path; long usernames are safely truncated.

verdict.summary: http_isfiltered is a read-only predicate over internally parsed HTTP state. The attacker-influenced strings in fm->hd[u].b are only used via strchr (NULL-checked) and a read-only lookup in http_hdr_flags; the pointer f is dereferenced only after an explicit NULL check with correct operator precedence. The one genuine candidate — no bounds check on the index u before fm->hdf[u] / fm->hd[u].b — cannot be triggered from any trust-boundary crossing visible in this code: u is a caller-supplied header index constrained by the header parser to the fixed array domain, and nothing in this function derives u from external data. All trigger paths require a caller or the parse layer to violate their documented contracts, so no vulnerability is confirmed in this code.

assumptions: u is a header index whose valid domain is bounded by the fixed dimensions of fm->hd[] and fm->hdf[], as established by the header parser that produces such indices; this function performs no intake parsing of its own.
fm->hd[u].b buffers are NUL-terminated by the header parse layer that populates struct http; this code writes nothing to fm.

http_hdr_flags performs read-only table comparison of the passed name pointer and does not require preconditions beyond e pointing within fm->hd[u].b, which holds by construction (e = strchr(b, ':')).
limitations: Missing bounds validation of the index u before the array accesses fm->hdf[u] (line 6) and fm->hd[u].b (line 8) — an out-of-range u would cause an out-of-bounds read (CWE-129/CWE-125 pattern). Dismissed because no attacker-influenced path into u exists in this code; any trigger requires a caller to pass an index outside the parser-constrained domain, violating the documented contract.
No NULL check on the fm pointer itself; a NULL fm would crash. Contract-level robustness only; no trust-boundary crossing involved.
Reliance on NUL-termination of fm->hd[u].b for strchr; triggering an unterminated buffer requires the parse layer to violate its own output invariant.
Return value of the final expression is not normalized to 0/1 (returns the raw f->flag & how bitmask when nonzero); a truthiness/contract nuance with no security impact given callers test nonzero.

verdict.summary: uECC_sign_with_k (micro-ecc) validates the external scalar k (0 < k < n), fails closed on RNG failure and on s exceeding the export width, and confines all intermediate large-integer state to uECC_MAX_WORDS-sized stack arrays. All sinks reached by trust-boundary data (private-key copy, hash parsing via internal bits2int, r/s exports into the caller's signature buffer) are size-consistent for every curve/word-size configuration in which the native-little-endian raw-byte semantics of this code are coherent. The only out-of-bounds-write scenario (native LE with word size 8 on 160/224-bit curves) requires a build whose misalignment already corrupts the private-key copy this code performs, i.e., a state the code's own logic contradicts; it is recorded as a configuration assumption, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: bits2int is an internal helper (not shown) whose SEC1-defined contract is to truncate an arbitrary-length hash to the curve's scalar width before storing into tmp; this function never performs a raw, length-bounded copy of message_hash/hash_size itself.

In uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN builds, the coherent (supported) configurations are those where curve->num_bytes is a multiple of the word size; with word size 4 this holds for all bundled curves (num_bytes == num_words*4), making EccPoint_mult's 2*num_words-word write exactly 2*num_bytes bytes into the caller's signature buffer.
curve (num_words, num_n_words, num_bytes, num_n_bits, n, G) is trusted compile-time configuration, and uECC_MAX_WORDS is sized for the largest compiled curve.
limitations: Configuration-conditional OOB write (dismissed): with uECC_VLI_NATIVE_LITTLE_ENDIAN=1 and uECC_WORD_SIZE=8 on a 160- or 224-bit curve, p aliases the caller's signature buffer and EccPoint_mult writes 2*num_words words (2*32 bytes) into a 2*num_bytes-byte (56 or 40 byte) buffer, overflowing by 8 bytes. In exactly those builds, the same function's bcopy of the private key leaves stale high bytes in tmp, producing invalid signatures before any consumer would rely on the configuration — the precondition contradicts the alignment the code's own raw-byte operations require, so this was judged a broken/unsupported build rather than a vulnerability in this code. If a deployment used such a build, this would be CWE-787.

In native LE mode the caller's signature buffer receives partial point data before the function returns 0 on later error paths (RNG failure, s-overflow); since the buffer is caller-owned and discarded on failure, this is a robustness issue with no security impact.
k words above num_n_words are not range-checked against n (only num_n_words words are compared); all subsequent uses are num_n_words-wide, so this is a correctness nuance, not a memory-safety issue.
r is not reduced modulo n (SEC1/FIPS 697-style compliance deviation common to micro-ecc); this affects signature format compliance, not memory safety or authorization.
s[num_n_words - 1] = 0; is a dead store immediately overwritten by uECC_vli_set(s, p, num_words); no security effect.

verdict.summary: http_isfiltered is a pure read-only predicate over an already-validated parsed HTTP structure. All results of external calls are NULL-checked (strchr, http_hdr_flags) before use, operator precedence correctly gates the dereference of f, and attacker-influenced bytes (header names) are only passed to bounded/terminated string operations relying on invariants established at the parser trust boundary. The sole unguarded sink is indexing fm->hdf[u]/fm->hd[u] with no local bounds check, but u is a positional index whose range is constrained by the caller (u < nhd) and by the parser's cap of nhd at the array dimension; no path within this code can produce an out-of-range u, so no vulnerability exists in this code as written.

assumptions: The parameter u is a header index supplied by internal callers that iterate u in [0, fm->nhd), with fm->nhd capped at the hdf/hd array dimension by the HTTP parser; this code contains no path that derives u from message content.
Header strings in fm->hd[].b are stored NUL-terminated by the HTTP workspace allocation at parse time, making strchr safe; this function relies on that intake invariant rather than re-validating it.

http_hdr_flags performs a read-only, length-bounded lookup of the header name in [fm->hd[u].b, e) against a static flag table; its implementation is not shown and is assumed not to introduce its own memory-safety defect.
limitations: Candidate rejected in STEP 4: this function performs no bounds check on u before fm->hdf[u] and fm->hd[u], so a caller passing u >= HTTP_HDR_MAX (or an unpopulated slot with hd[u].b == NULL) would cause an out-of-bounds read or NULL dereference. This requires the caller to violate the index contract; it is a hardening/robustness concern for this function, not a reachable vulnerability in the given code.

Candidate rejected in STEP 4: strchr(fm->hd[u].b, ':') assumes NUL-termination of attacker-supplied header bytes; a parser that stored unterminated headers would create an OOB read here, but that state cannot be produced by this code.

Candidate rejected in STEP 2: 'f != NULL && f->flag & how' was checked for precedence-induced NULL dereference; C precedence (!= and & bind tighter than &&) evaluates the NULL check first, so this is correct.

verdict.summary: In mobi_parse_index_entry, the control-byte pointer is derived directly from the heap record buffer (buf->data + buf->offset) and then walked and dereferenced in the tag loop once per TAGX tag with control_byte == 1. The number of such tags comes from the attacker-controlled TAGX record of the MOBI file, and this code never verifies that the walk stays within buf->maxlen (neither the entry boundary nor the record buffer end); the only related check, mobi_buffer_seek(buf, tagx->control_byte_count), has its return value ignored and its count is not reconciled with the tags actually walked. A crafted MOBI file whose INDX entry lies near the end of the record buffer and whose TAGX declares many control-byte tags causes control_bytes[0] to be read past the end of the heap-allocated record buffer (out-of-bounds read).

evidence.reason: A raw pointer into the heap record buffer is derived here, and the only operation that could bound the subsequent control-byte walk is mobi_buffer_seek, whose return value is discarded. The code never enforces that buf->offset plus the number of control-byte tags (attacker-controlled via the TAGX record) remains within buf->maxlen; the seek's control_byte_count is not validated against the tags actually walked. This is the missing bound for the out-of-bounds read.

Out-of-bounds read sink. control_bytes was advanced once per tag with control_byte == 1 in the loop above (line 62) with no bound against the buffer end; with a crafted TAGX declaring many control-byte tags and an entry located near the end of the record buffer (buf->maxlen was narrowed to the entry end at line 20), this dereference reads past the heap-allocated record buffer. Trigger: malicious MOBI file with inconsistent TAGX control-byte tags and an INDX entry at the record tail.

assumptions: The mobi_buffer_* helpers (mobi_buffer_get8, mobi_buffer_get_varlen, mobi_buffer_setpos, mobi_buffer_seek) perform their own bounds checks against buf->maxlen and fail safely, as is standard in libmobi; the OOB finding rests on the raw-pointer walk at lines 41-42/62/66, which bypasses those helpers.
idxt.offsets, tagx->tags/tagx->control_byte_count, ordt tables, and buf record contents are all parsed from the MOBI file and therefore cross a trust boundary into this code.
INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX is assumed to be at least 256, so the get8-derived label_length (max 255) fits text[] on input.
limitations: Integer underflow at line 7: idxt.offsets[curr_number + 1] - idxt.offsets[curr_number] is not checked for monotonicity, so a non-monotonic IDXT yields a huge size_t. Analysis of the line 16 check shows the wrapped sum is either rejected or produces a narrowed maxlen below the current offset, causing the (assumed bounds-checked) buffer helpers to fail rather than read out of bounds; recorded as data-corruption robustness degradation, not a confirmed memory-safety defect in this code.

Line 38 strncpy uses label_length as REASSIGNED by the return value of mobi_getstring_ordt/mobi_indx_get_label (lines 29/31) without revalidation against entry_length or sizeof(text). If the ORDT helper can return an expanded length exceeding INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX (UTF-8 expansion), strncpy would read past the stack array text[]. The unvalidated use exists as written, but the concrete oversized return could not be proven from the visible code, so it is not counted as confirmed evidence.

Ignored return of mobi_buffer_setpos at line 8: an offsets[curr_number] beyond maxlen leaves a stale offset and parse continues (fail-open), yielding corrupt label/tag data but no demonstrated out-of-bounds access in this code.

Memory leak on the tagvalues malloc failure path: only ptagx is freed while indx->entries[entry_number].tags and previously allocated tagvalues arrays leak; requires an OOM condition with no demonstrated exhaustion path.

tagx->tags_count * sizeof(...) multiplications at lines 52 and later are unchecked for size_t overflow, but triggering would require an implausibly large tags_count not producible from a record-bounded TAGX as visible here.

verdict.summary: In expand_case_fold_string, the multibyte character length is computed as len = enclen(reg->enc, p) without bounding it to the string node's end. For an attacker-supplied pattern whose final string node ends with a truncated multibyte lead byte (data that crosses the trust boundary at regex compile and is not validated here), len exceeds end - p, and the value is used as p + len in onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len) and passed to expand_case_fold_string_alt, causing a heap buffer over-read of up to the encoding's maximum character length past sn->end. Later upstream versions fix exactly this by passing end into enclen, confirming the missing bounds check is the root cause.

evidence.reason: Missing bounds check (root cause): enclen derives the character length solely from the attacker-controlled lead byte at p, without clamping to end. When the case-insensitive string node ends in a truncated multibyte sequence (e.g., a lone 0xC3 lead byte in UTF-8 at sn->end-1), len > end - p; the unchecked p + len then drives onig_node_str_cat(snode, p, p + len) (line 51) and expand_case_fold_string_alt(n, items, p, len, end, reg, &prev_node) (line 68), reading past the end of the node's heap buffer — a heap over-read (CWE-125) reachable from a user-supplied regex pattern.

assumptions: The encoding's enclen computes length from the lead byte (true for UTF-8/EUC-JP/GB-family encodings bundled with Oniguruma), so a truncated trailing byte yields len > end - p.

String nodes can terminate mid-character: pattern bytes reaching this function are not validated for complete multibyte sequences (raw byte escapes and invalid pattern bytes cross the trust boundary at onig_new), and this function performs no intake validation of sn->s..sn->end against reg->enc.
limitations: Error paths leak prev_node/snode when top_root is NULL (e.g., an encoding callback returning n < 0 on a later iteration after a node was created): one small node leaked per failed compile; robustness issue only, no memory-safety impact in this function.
A negative return from expand_case_fold_string_alt is reclassified as ONIGERR_MEMORY via goto mem_err; error-code fidelity issue only.
alt_num (int) cannot overflow before the THRESHOLD_CASE_FOLD_ALT_FOR_EXPANSION (> 8) break, since n is bounded by ONIGENC_GET_CASE_FOLD_CODES_MAX_NUM.
swap_node(node, top_root)/onig_node_free(top_root) was traced across all goto paths and found ownership-consistent; no UAF/double-free candidate survived STEP 4.

verdict.summary: In win_redr_status, the buffer-name string is built in the fixed MAXPATHL-byte NameBuff, but the flag append at line 54 ('*(p + len++) = ' ';') is performed without any check that len leaves room for the space and a NUL terminator. A buffer whose file name is exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes (attacker-influenced file path crossing a trust boundary) plus any status flag (changed/read-only/help/preview) makes the append overwrite the terminator and sets len == MAXPATHL; the following vim_snprintf gets a size of 0 (writes nothing) and 'len += (int)STRLEN(p + len)' then reads past the end of the 1024-byte NameBuff buffer (CWE-125). If the out-of-bounds bytes are non-NUL and a second flag block runs, len exceeds MAXPATHL, so 'MAXPATHL - len' becomes a negative int passed as a huge size_t to the next vim_snprintf, producing an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). Additionally, for a changed terminal buffer the space is appended but the '[+]' block is skipped, leaving NameBuff unterminated at any name length.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unconditional one-byte append with no bounds check that len <= MAXPATHL - 2. When get_trans_bufname() has filled NameBuff with a MAXPATHL-1 byte (1023) buffer name (attacker-controlled file path), this write destroys the only NUL terminator in the MAXPATHL-byte buffer and sets len to MAXPATHL, leaving the string unterminated and all subsequent indexing one byte past the allocation.

evidence.snippet:
vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", "[+]");
	    len += (int)STRLEN(p + len);
evidence.reason: Sink reachable on the trigger path: with len == MAXPATHL the size argument MAXPATHL - len is 0, so vim_snprintf writes nothing and restores no terminator; STRLEN(p + len) then evaluates STRLEN(NameBuff + 1024), reading past the end of the 1024-byte NameBuff buffer (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125). If the bytes past the buffer are non-NUL and a second flag block executes (e.g. changed + read-only), MAXPATHL - len becomes negative and is passed as a huge size_t to the next vim_snprintf, which writes past the buffer (CWE-787). Trigger: open a ~1023-byte-path file that is modified or read-only and let the status line redraw.

assumptions: NameBuff is a MAXPATHL (1024)-byte buffer filled by get_trans_bufname()/home_replace(), which can legitimately produce a string of up to MAXPATHL-1 bytes, so len == MAXPATHL-1 at line 46 is a state this code permits.
vim_snprintf writes nothing (and adds no terminator) when its size argument is 0, so no terminator is restored after the space append.

Escalation to an out-of-bounds write (negative MAXPATHL - len passed as size_t) additionally requires non-NUL bytes immediately after the buffer and two flag blocks executing; the unconditional defect is the out-of-bounds read at STRLEN(p + len).
limitations: The mbyte truncation write '*p = '<'' at p + i - 1 (line 106) and the single-byte truncation p += len - (this_ru_col - 1) (lines 113-115) were examined and are in-bounds; dismissed because the loop bounds guarantee the index is inside the string.
this_ru_col is clamped (lines 83-85) and can never index out of range for the truncation or screen_fill logic; dismissed.
The 'busy' static re-entrancy guard, screen_puts/screen_fill clipping, and the get_keymap_str size-bounded copy with its line-123 guard were examined and raise no memory-safety issue; dismissed.

A changed terminal buffer leaves NameBuff unterminated at any name length because the '[+]' block is skipped for terminal buffers; it shares the same root-cause line (54) and is covered by the primary finding rather than listed as a separate vulnerability.
