verdict.summary: SProcXkbSelectEvents byte-swaps client-controlled SelectEvents header fields and trailing detail data in place. The historical out-of-bounds bug in this function (missing length validation before swapping detail data) is not present: every swap is preceded by 'if (dataLeft < (size * 2)) return BadLength;'. Since dataLeft = req_len*4 - 16 is always a non-negative multiple of 4 (req_len is in 4-byte units and is floor-checked by REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE) and each iteration consumes exactly 4 or 8 validated bytes, the detail pointer cannot leave the request buffer and dataLeft cannot underflow, including the size-1 classes that reset size to 2. All attacker-reachable memory accesses are bounds-checked before use; error paths fail closed. No exploitable path exists in this code as written.

assumptions: client->req_len, maintained by the request dispatcher, equals the number of 4-byte words actually received for this request, so req_len*4 never exceeds the allocated request buffer (standard dix contract).
sizeof(xkbSelectEventsReq) == 16 (per XKBproto.h), a multiple of 4, so dataLeft = req_len*4 - 16 is a non-negative multiple of 4 once REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE has rejected req_len < 4 words.
The request buffer is at least 4-byte aligned, so swaps()/swapl() on from.c16/from.c32 at offsets that are multiples of 4 past the header do not perform unaligned access.
ProcXkbSelectEvents (invoked at the end) independently re-validates value legality; only this function's own behavior was judged.
limitations: Candidate rejected (would be CWE-125/CWE-787, the historical CVE-2020-14345 bug): the in-place swaps(&from.c16[0..1])/swapl(&from.c32[0..1]) at lines 56-57/60-61 are guarded by the length check at lines 53-54 which precedes them for every size class (2 -> needs 4, 4 -> needs 8, 1 -> needs 2 while consuming 4, safe because dataLeft is always a multiple of 4). No input reaches a swap with insufficient data.

Candidate rejected (unsigned underflow of dataLeft): the size-1 detail classes validate only dataLeft >= 2 but then set size = 2 and subtract 4; this cannot underflow because dataLeft is invariantly a non-negative multiple of 4 in this code (smallest passing value is 4). Fragile by construction but not a reachable defect.

Candidate rejected (non-termination): maskLeft derives from the 16-bit affectWhich with the MapNotify bit cleared, and 'maskLeft &= ~bit' executes before both continue paths, so the loop is bounded by at most 16 iterations.

Potential parsing desync with ProcXkbSelectEvents for the size-1 classes (this function advances 4 bytes for what the XKB protocol defines as 2-byte details). All accesses remain within the bounds this code checks, so this is at most a semantic/interop robustness issue, not memory corruption.

The trailing check 'dataLeft > 2' effectively rejects any leftover >= 4 bytes (dataLeft is always a multiple of 4), which is stricter than a 2-byte tolerance but fails closed with BadLength; the ErrorF '%d' formatting of an unsigned value is cosmetic.

verdict.summary: No attacker-reachable vulnerability is demonstrable in multi_update::initialize_tables as written. The SQL text is the only trust boundary, and it is validated at parse/prepare time (>=1 SET pair, resolved Item_field left-hand sides, consistent server-assigned tablenr/shared indices and array sizing). All fallible operations in this function are checked except item->fix_fields(thd, 0) and temp_fields.append(), for which no attacker-controllable failure path exists in this code; the remaining anomalies (assert-only guard on fields->head(), unchecked downcast) are protected by invariants this code documents and the SQL layer enforces.

assumptions: Release build where DBUG_ASSERT is compiled out is assumed, which is why assert-based guards are treated as non-enforcing.

tmp_table_param/tmp_tables/fields_for_table array sizes, table_ref->shared, tablenr, and join->map2table are assumed consistent invariants established by the multi_update constructor and JOIN setup (code not shown), as they are all produced by the same server subsystem from one query.
Item_temptable_rowid::fix_fields (not shown) is assumed to have no SQL-syntax-controllable failure path, since the item is freshly constructed from a valid TABLE.
The SQL grammar guarantees at least one SET assignment and that left-hand sides resolve to Item_field before multi_update::initialize_tables can run.
limitations: Unchecked downcast '((Item_field *) fields->head())->field->table' guarded only by DBUG_ASSERT(fields->elements) (release no-op): would be a NULL dereference/type confusion if fields were empty or non-Item_field, but no SQL input accepted by the parse/prepare layer can produce that state; dismissed as caller-contract-protected.

Unchecked return of item->fix_fields(thd, 0): if fix_fields could fail, an unfixed item would flow into calc_group_buffer/create_tmp_table; no attacker-controllable failure trigger exists in this code, so recorded as robustness-only.

Unvalidated array indexing tmp_table_param+cnt, tmp_tables[cnt], fields_for_table[cnt], join->map2table[tablenr]: indices are server-assigned internal metadata (shared/tablenr) consistent with array sizing done by the same subsystem; not trust-boundary data, so no missing validation duty here.

Unchecked return of temp_fields.append(fields_for_table[cnt]): on allocation failure the list stays self-consistent because tmp_param->field_count is recomputed from temp_fields.elements afterwards; robustness only.
join->join_tab->table dereference assumes join_tab is non-NULL; unreachable with a non-empty update_tables since a multi-update implies at least one joined table.
Early DBUG_RETURN(1) paths and the dead local 'field_name' (computed, never used) are style/robustness issues with no security impact.

The 'goto loop_end' path skips unupdated_check_opt_tables collection when the view CHECK OPTION contains a subselect; this is the code's own documented alternative (setting UNCACHEABLE_CHECKOPTION to prevent premature subselect freeing), and the enforcement site is outside this code, so no fail-open path can be confirmed from this snippet alone.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced values consumed by qtm_decompress (decoded match lengths, match offsets, frame boundaries, buffered-output counts) are explicitly bounds-checked before every memory-access sink: match copies are guarded by the window_posn+match_length>window_size check and the j>window_size check, literal writes are bounded by frame_end<=frame_start+QTM_FRAME_SIZE<=window_size under the frame-alignment invariant this code enforces, and the potential out_bytes underflow / o_ptr-underflow path at window wrap is arithmetically unreachable. No reachable memory-safety, lifetime, or fail-open defect exists in this code as written.

assumptions: qtm->window_size is a multiple of QTM_FRAME_SIZE (and >= QTM_FRAME_SIZE), as guaranteed by the Quantum window-size encoding validated at init; without it the frame_end bound could exceed window_size, but this function cannot itself produce such a state.

QTM_GET_SYMBOL returns symbol indices within the model/array sizes (extra_bits[], position_base[], length_base[], length_extra[]) and QTM_READ_BITS terminates or errors on exhausted input; these macros are not shown, so their internal safety cannot be audited here.

The qtm window buffer is allocated and its size established by init code outside this function; initial o_ptr/o_end/frame_start state restored from qtm is assumed self-consistent (both pointers within window, o_ptr<=o_end, frame_start aligned).
limitations: A match with match_offset > window_posn on the first fill of the window copies bytes from window[window_size-j] that this code has never written (uninitialized-buffer read). It stays within the allocation (no OOB) and only becomes an information disclosure if the buffer is malloc'd uninitialized and the extracted output is exposed; allocation is not in this code, so this is not confirmed as a vulnerability.

The 0xFF rescan loop (do { QTM_READ_BITS(i,8); } while (i != 0xFF)) and all bit reads rely on the macro's input-exhaustion handling; an infinite loop or over-read there would be a macro defect, not visible in this code.

Robustness-only observations: with wflag==0 the window-wrap flush discards buffered bytes (data-loss semantics, no security impact), and the redundant clamp of i in the non-wrapping match branch can silently shorten a copy semantically while window_posn still advances by match_length — bounded and checked, no memory-safety impact.

verdict.summary: This is the post-fix form of SparseDenseBinaryOpShared: every attacker-influenced path to a memory-safety sink is validated in this code before use. Attacker-supplied sp_indices values are bounds-checked per dimension against the true broadcast dimension via FastBoundsCheck with an OP_REQUIRES that returns before rhs_ref.coeff(idx); the broadcast direction is restricted to dense-to-sparse by VecGreaterEq plus BCast::IsValid; rank is limited to 1..5 by the switch default; sp_shape non-emptiness and shape/indices/values length consistency are explicitly checked, so allocations, the gathering loop, and the final binaryExpr all operate on equal, validated extents. No reachable out-of-bounds access, integer-driven allocation overflow, lifetime, race, or fail-open path exists in the code as written.

assumptions: Op registration type attributes (sp_indices/sp_shape as int64, sp_values/dense as T) are enforced by the framework before this kernel runs, so the dtype-based casts (matrix<int64>, vec<int64>, flat<T>) cannot be fed mismatched types.
OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK abort the kernel with an error return on failure, so a failed check never continues into the guarded use.
BCast with fewer_dims=false guarantees y_reshape()/y_bcast() have rank ndims, as the code's own comment states, so shaped<T,NDIM> and ToIndexArray<NDIM> are rank-consistent.
FastBoundsCheck(idx, limit) enforces 0 <= idx < limit, matching the precondition of rhs_ref.coeff(idx).
limitations: Negative entries in sp_shape are not explicitly rejected here; depending on the TensorFlow version, TensorShape construction may CHECK-fail and abort the process (denial of service), or the value is subsequently rejected by VecGreaterEq/FastBoundsCheck. This is an abort-level robustness issue, not memory corruption in this code.

The gathering loop uses 'int i' against an int64_t nnz; if nnz exceeded 2^31 (requiring attacker tensors of tens of gigabytes and successful allocations) the loop counter would overflow. Practically allocation-bound and not reachable at realistic resource levels.
Division by zero is only guarded when the kernel type string contains 'Div'; for other ops it yields inf/NaN with no security impact.

The historic heap out-of-bounds read in this kernel (attacker-supplied sp_indices used to index the dense tensor without validation) is fixed in this version by the FastBoundsCheck/indices_valid gate and the VecGreaterEq broadcast restriction.

verdict.summary: This is a patched do_put(): the block-mode paste multiplication is guarded by an explicit INT_MAX overflow check (with the division-by-zero case excluded), both paste branches bound count*yanklen before allocation, all allocation sizes exactly match the subsequent memmove/memset/STRCPY lengths, textcol/delcount arithmetic cannot go negative on any reachable path, col==MAXCOL is unreachable as a copy length because the Visual 'col > oldlen' skip precedes it, and every u_save/ml_append/alloc failure exits via goto without using unallocated buffers. Integer wrap in 'totlen + oldlen + 1' can only produce a negative length, which makes alloc() fail and return NULL, which is checked before any write. No surviving memory-safety, lifetime, or fail-open candidate remains.

assumptions: Register invariants (y_array[i] non-NULL, y_size/y_array set together, y_width sane for MBLOCK) are maintained by the register and clipboard producers outside this function; this code itself checks y_size and y_array NULL before any dereference.

expr_result is only non-NULL for regname '=' per the documented call contract; the state do_put('=', NULL, ...) where the '=' register path would be taken and y_array wrongly freed is a caller contract violation that no existing caller performs.
alloc() with a negative/wrapped int length requests a huge size_t, fails, and returns NULL, so int-wrap in allocation sizes degrades to a handled allocation failure rather than an undersized buffer.
limitations: Block-mode allocation-size addition 'totlen + oldlen + 1' can wrap signed int (requires totlen near INT_MAX and a very long line), but the wrapped value is negative, alloc() then fails and the NULL check breaks out; this is robustness degradation with no memory corruption, so not reported as a vulnerability.

The 'vim_free(y_array)' at end: would double-free/incorrectly free a shared register array if a caller invoked do_put with regname '=' and expr_result NULL (get_spec_reg has no '=' case, so the yank-register path would be taken); reachable only by a caller violating the documented contract.

A crafted clipboard/selection register containing NULL y_array entries would crash STRLEN(y_array[0]) or STRLEN(y_array[i]); entry non-NULL-ness is an invariant of the register producer, not validated at this boundary, so recorded as an assumption rather than a confirmed finding in this code.

The '=' split loop mutates expr_result in place (*ptr = NUL); this is the documented purpose of passing the string and the caller retains ownership (allocated flag stays FALSE), so no lifetime defect.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced codes from the input stream are validated against the dictionary's current-entry limit before any table indexing, the dictionary-write path is bounded by the LZW_CODE_MAX table size, and the code-size cap ensures the code value 2^LZW_CODE_MAX is unreachable once the table is full. Dictionary chains strictly descend in index (new entries point only to prior smaller indices), preventing cyclic chains and bounding stack writes. No reachable memory-safety, input-validation, or fail-open defect exists in this function as written.

assumptions: LZW_CODE_MAX defines the maximum dictionary size such that ctx->table has 2^LZW_CODE_MAX entries and ctx->current_code_size cannot exceed LZW_CODE_MAX, as the code's own guards state.

The decoder context (ctx) is initialized by trusted setup code that sets a valid table, stack_base sized for maximum chain depth, clear_code, eoi_code, current_code_size, and an initial current_entry.
table indices below the initial current_entry contain valid entries established by the decoder's standard fixed-code prefix, whose entries form strictly descending chains.
limitations: Potential out-of-bounds read of table[code_new] when the dictionary is full requires code_new == current_entry == 2^LZW_CODE_MAX; the LZW_CODE_MAX code-width cap enforced by lzw__next_code makes this value unreachable, so it is not a vulnerability here.

Potential stack overflow or infinite loop via a cyclic dictionary chain is prevented because every new entry stores previous_entry = ctx->previous_code, a strictly smaller prior index, so chains always terminate.
A bad first-code path reading ctx->previous_code/previous_code_first before initialization would depend on context setup state outside this function's visible paths; not confirmed.

NULL or corrupted ctx, or an LZW_CODE_MAX value at or above 31 making (1 << LZW_CODE_MAX) undefined, requires violating the initialization contract or an unsupported configuration not evidenced in this code.

verdict.summary: After successfully initializing a libpng decode context from attacker-controlled PNG data, DecodePngV2 can return through the DecodeBmp or DecodeAndCropJpeg rejection branches without calling CommonFinishDecode or CommonFreeDecode. Repeated attacker-triggered calls can therefore leak decoder state and eventually exhaust process memory. The explicit width, height, product, and row-size checks prevent the more severe integer-overflow and heap-overflow paths.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(context, false,
                  errors::InvalidArgument(
                      "Trying to decode PNG format using DecodeBmp op. Use "
                      "`decode_png` or `decode_image` instead."));
evidence.reason: This early OP_REQUIRES return is reached after png::CommonInitDecode has succeeded and after output allocation has succeeded, but before CommonFreeDecode or CommonFinishDecode releases the initialized decoder state. A valid attacker-controlled PNG therefore leaks the decoder resources on each DecodeBmp rejection, giving a repeatable memory-exhaustion path.

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(context, false,
                  errors::InvalidArgument(
                      "DecodeAndCropJpeg operation can run on JPEG only, but "
                      "detected PNG."));
evidence.reason: This rejection path has the same missing decoder cleanup: CommonInitDecode has already allocated the libpng context, but the macro returns before CommonFreeDecode or CommonFinishDecode is called.

assumptions: png::CommonInitDecode returns true only after successfully allocating and retaining decoder state represented by decode.
png::CommonFinishDecode or png::CommonFreeDecode is required to release that state; DecodeContext is not shown as owning an RAII destructor.
The DecodeBmp or DecodeAndCropJpeg op_type path can be invoked with attacker-controlled PNG bytes, consistent with the branch and its comments in this code.
PNG channel counts after successful libpng initialization are limited to 1-4; the width and height checks are therefore sufficient for the visible arithmetic.
limitations: The width, height, and total-size checks prevent integer overflow in height * width * decode.channels for valid PNG channel counts; no heap overflow from those expressions was confirmed.

A very large but accepted image can still fail allocation through the framework allocator or std::bad_alloc; that is an environment-dependent OOM condition, not a confirmed memory-safety vulnerability.
The DT_FLOAT path assumes the Eigen thread-pool assignment is synchronous; no escaping use-after-free was found.

A 4-D DecodeGif output combined with output->tensor<float,3>() would be inconsistent, but this trigger is not reachable from the visible dtype/op registration and does not support a vulnerability verdict in this code.

verdict.summary: The demuxer copies a fixed 8-byte start-code scratch window from the current input packet without verifying that the packet contains the required number of bytes. A previous 1- or 2-byte packet can set bytes_in_header to 1 or 2; a following 5-byte packet then causes a 7- or 6-byte read from a 5-byte source, reading beyond the attacker-controlled packet buffer.

evidence.reason: This sink requires at least 8 - bytes_in_header valid bytes at start, but the loop only guarantees remain >= 5. The preceding short-packet path can set bytes_in_header to 1 or 2. With bytes_in_header = 1 and a following 5-byte packet, this copies 7 bytes from a 5-byte packet, producing an out-of-bounds read of raw trust-boundary media data.

assumptions: The packet data pointer exposes exactly pck_size valid bytes; reads beyond pck_size are out of bounds.
hdr_store is initialized elsewhere with sufficient capacity for its intended 8-byte scratch use; the confirmed defect is the unvalidated source length.
limitations: The u32 accumulation expressions can theoretically wrap, but a concrete multi-gigabyte hdr_store_size trigger was not established from the parser behavior shown.
Parser-produced frame and object sizes are assumed to remain within the assigned bitstream; no concrete out-of-range trigger was demonstrated in this function.
Unchecked realloc results and non-monotonic timestamp arithmetic are robustness or timing concerns without a demonstrated security sink here.

verdict.summary: The 'overflow' guards in string_number_format evaluate the size sums in wider/unsigned arithmetic (and only reject a wrap that lands below the original value), but the results are accumulated into 32-bit ints (integral/reslen) whose truncation is never checked. An attacker-controlled thousand_sep of ~42,108,500 bytes with a 309-digit double (e.g. 1.7e308, dec=0) makes 309 + 102*42108500 = 4,295,067,309 pass the '< integral' check yet truncate integral to ~100,013, so resstr is allocated ~100 KB while the copy loop writes ~4.29 GB of attacker-controlled separator bytes through it — a critical heap buffer overflow. The same flawed pattern at the dec_point accumulation (reslen += dec_point.size()) is reachable with multi-GB dec/dec_point inputs.

evidence.reason: Integer overflow in the result-buffer size computation (CWE-190) leading to a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The guard compares the sum in wider/unsigned arithmetic and only fires if the wrapped value is below integral, but line 67 stores the sum into the 32-bit int 'integral', truncating mod 2^32 with no check. Trigger: d = 1.7e308 (integral = 309 digits), dec = 0, thousand_sep = 42,108,500-byte string; sum = 4,295,067,309 = 2^32 + 100,013, which is neither a 2^64 wrap nor below 309, so the check passes and integral becomes 100,013. reslen = 100,013 allocates a ~100 KB resstr, but the loop at lines 123-131 then copies 309 digits plus 102 separators of 42,108,500 bytes (~4.29 GB of attacker-controlled content) into it — massive heap OOB write.

Same root-cause defect at the dec_point accumulation: the guard detects only a full 2^64 wrap of (reslen + dec_point.size()), while line 80 stores into the 32-bit int reslen, truncating mod 2^32 unchecked. Trigger (secondary, needs multi-GB inputs): dec ≈ 2.1e9 (successful 2.1 GB snprintf, reslen ≈ 2.1e9) plus dec_point.size() ≈ 2.147e9 makes the sum exceed 2^32 and truncate to a small positive reslen, so resstr is tiny while the declen memcpy / topad loop writes ~2.1e9 decimal bytes out of bounds.

assumptions: String::size() returns a type at least as wide as 32-bit unsigned (HPHP/HHVM semantics), so the guard expression is evaluated in wider unsigned arithmetic than the 32-bit int accumulation; on two's-complement targets the int store truncates mod 2^32 (the trigger also works if size() is int, since the 32-bit wrap lands above integral and still defeats the check).
Strings of tens of MB (and, for the secondary path, multi-GB) are constructible in the calling runtime, and raise_error() does not return (it throws).
ReserveString capacity includes a NUL terminator, consistent with the snprintf size arguments (64 / tmplen+1), so the temporary buffers themselves are not overflowed.
limitations: `reslen += dec` (line 73) is an unchecked int addition; reachable wraps land negative (String allocation with negative size), producing a crash/allocation failure (DoS) rather than a demonstrated OOB write.

If the second snprintf (line 37) could return a larger length than the first (e.g., a concurrent locale change between calls), s = tmpbuf+tmplen-1 could read past tmpbuf; not reachable with identical arguments in this code.
`if (thousand_sep && ...)` truthiness vs `.empty()` used for reslen is a latent mismatch, but with size()==0 the memcpy is 0 bytes, so there is no impact.
The -0.0 / inf / nan cases are rejected by the isdigit(tmpbuf[0]) early returns; the -0.0 early return is cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: In SingleComponentLSScan::ParseMCU (JPEG-LS run mode), the run length returned by DecodeRun is derived entirely from the attacker-controlled entropy bitstream and is used as the fill-loop bound without being validated or clamped against 'length' (the remaining samples in the line buffer sized from m_ulWidth[0]). A crafted scan in which the decoded run exceeds the remaining line length makes while(run) write LONGs past the end of line->m_pData (heap out-of-bounds write), drives the signed 'length' negative, and the subsequent if (length) / while(++lp,--length) logic treats the negative value as 'more samples', so the MCU sample loop continues writing out of bounds without terminating. Attacker controls both the overflow length and the written values.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing bounds check. 'run' (line 50, DecodeRun, decoded from attacker-crafted JPEG-LS entropy bits) is never clamped to 'length' (remaining samples in line->m_pData, capacity m_ulWidth[0] LONGs); the loop condition at line 53 tests only 'run', so the sink write at line 57 runs past the end of the line buffer. Trigger: a scan with width 4 whose run-mode gradients pass isRunMode and whose run bits decode to run=4096; the loop writes 4096 LONGs into the 4-entry buffer, then run--,length-- (line 61) makes length negative, if (length) (line 67) stays true and writes *lp OOB again (line 89), and while(++lp,--length) (line 137) never terminates for negative length, continuing the out-of-bounds writes.

assumptions: line->m_pData is allocated to hold m_ulWidth[0] LONG samples per line, per the decoder's standard line-allocation contract; the overflow is relative to that buffer.

DecodeRun's implementation is not shown; this function nevertheless consumes its return value without any clamp against length, and its own length-based control flow (if(length), while(--length)) assumes run <= length — an invariant this code never checks at the sink.
BeginReadMCU/GetContext/DecodeRun/GolombDecode return values are treated as attacker-influenced because they decode the JPEG file's bitstream.
limitations: line = line->m_pNext (line 140): if fewer lines are allocated than the up-to-8 MCU lines processed (notably the DNL path that sets lines=8 when HeightOf()==0), the walk could dereference an invalid/NULL pointer; the line allocation logic is outside this snippet so this is not confirmed.
assert()s at lines 11, 15, and 25 vanish in release builds and perform no validation; robustness note only.
m_ulRemaining[0] -= lines (line 23) cannot underflow in this code: lines is clamped to min(8, m_ulRemaining[0]) when HeightOf()>0, and the DNL case (HeightOf()==0) skips the decrement.

The same unvalidated attribute permits pooling_ratio_[3] != 1, letting cwiseMax read past in_mat's column extent. Minimal trigger: input shape [4,2,2,1] with pooling_ratio [2.0,1.0,1.0,1.0] yields out_mat with 8 columns while b=2,3 produce out_offset 8..15.

evidence.reason: The batch loop is bounded by the INPUT batch size, but its body writes into an OUTPUT tensor allocated with output_size[0]=floor(input_size[0]/pooling_ratio_[0]) (lines 22-23, 41-42, 60-61). This code never enforces pooling_ratio_[0]==1 or output_size[0]==input_size[0] (line 24 is a release-disabled DCHECK), so with attacker-chosen pooling_ratio_[0]=2.0 and input batch 4, iterations b=2,3 index columns past the output buffer: the missing bound check is the root cause (CWE-787/CWE-20).

assumptions: GeneratePoolingSequence returns a non-decreasing cumulative sequence of output_size+1 entries bounded by input_size; this contract is not enforced in the shown code.
DCHECK_GT(output_size[i], 0) is compiled out in release builds, and Eigen::Map block access performs no bounds checks in release.

limitations: Candidate C6 (height/width_cum_seq.size() vs output_size[1]/[2] mismatch) could not be confirmed because GeneratePoolingSequence's implementation is not shown; rejected as not constructible from this code.

A pooling_ratio value of 0 or negative also causes a division-by-zero/UB float-to-int cast at lines 22-23; same unvalidated-attribute site, folded into the primary finding.

verdict.summary: btrfs_rm_device dereferences the attacker-influenced 'device_path' parameter via strcmp() without any NULL check on the -ENOENT error path. Reachable through BTRFS_IOC_RM_DEV_V2 with the DEV_ID flag, which passes device_path=NULL, and a user-supplied devid=0 on a filesystem with no missing devices: btrfs_find_device_by_devspec then returns ERR_PTR(-ENOENT) and strcmp(NULL, "missing") causes a kernel NULL pointer dereference (oops/DoS). The upstream fix adds an explicit device_path NULL guard here, which is absent in this version.

evidence.reason: device_path is an input crossing the ioctl trust boundary (BTRFS_IOC_RM_DEV_V2 passes NULL when the DEV_ID flag is used) and is dereferenced by strcmp() with no NULL precondition check. Trigger: ioctl RM_DEV_V2 with flags=DEV_ID and devid=0 on a filesystem with no missing devices — btrfs_find_device_by_devspec returns ERR_PTR(-ENOENT), the PTR_ERR check matches, and strcmp(NULL, "missing") executes, causing a NULL pointer dereference in the kernel.

assumptions: This is Linux kernel btrfs code; the caller BTRFS_IOC_RM_DEV_V2 passes device_path=NULL when the user selects the DEV_ID flag and forwards vol_args->devid (attacker-supplied, 0 allowed) unvalidated.
btrfs_find_device_by_devspec treats devid==0 with a NULL path as a 'missing device' lookup and returns ERR_PTR(-ENOENT) when no device is missing.
Reaching the ioctl requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so impact is a local privileged DoS (kernel oops) rather than privilege escalation.
limitations: num_devices - 1 (lines 14 and 111) could underflow u64 in theory, but num_devices is a device count of a mounted filesystem (>=1), so the trigger state is contradicted by the code's own invariants.

error_undo (lines 140-146) re-adds the device to fs_devices->alloc_list instead of device->fs_devices->alloc_list; unreachable for the mismatched (seed) case because seed devices are read-only and never take this branch.

Freeing cur_devices at lines 128-131 when cur_devices == fs_devices would be a use-after-free of the live fs_devices, but the ONLY_WRITABLE check at lines 42-45 plus the open-bdev invariant of a mounted writable fs prevent open_devices from reaching 0 for the main fs_devices.
The uuid_mutex unlock window around btrfs_shrink_device is a documented TODO about stale superblock num_devices (consistency/robustness only, no memory-safety impact demonstrated).

verdict.summary: string_number_format computes the result-buffer length in 32-bit ints. The thousand-separator allowance integral += ((integral-1)/3) * thousand_sep.size() can exceed INT_MAX, and the preceding overflow check only detects wraparound to a negative value (sum < integral), not truncation to a small positive value via modulo 2^32. An attacker-controlled long thousand_sep (≈42 MB, with a 309-digit integral part) makes integral wrap to a small positive number, so reslen under-sizes resbuf while the copy loop still writes (integral_digits + separators) bytes — a massive attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write.

evidence.reason: The overflow guard only catches wraparound to a negative value (sum < integral). With integral = 309 digits and thousand_sep.size() ≈ 42,129,000, the product ((integral-1)/3)*size overflows 32-bit int and truncates to a small positive value, so the check passes and integral/reslen under-size the allocation at line 84; the copy loop at lines 119-127 then performs memcpy of thousand_sep.size() bytes (line 122-124) past the end of resbuf — attacker-controlled heap overflow. Trigger: d = 1e308, dec = 0, thousand_sep = 42 MB string.

assumptions: String::size()/String(int, ReserveString) and int arithmetic are 32-bit, per the code's own overflow checks (which compare against int-range behavior).
The caller (number_format-style builtin) forwards user-supplied dec_point/thousand_sep without length limits, so their sizes are attacker-controlled at this trust boundary.

The runtime allocates the ~42 MB thousand_sep String successfully in the reference environment; smaller integral digit counts or shorter separators are safe because the product stays within int range.
raise_error aborts before allocation on the negative-wrap path, so it never masks the truncating path.
limitations: Secondary triggers of the same CWE-190 root cause were merged, not separately evidenced: (a) line 69 reslen += dec needs dec ≈ INT_MAX, which forces a multi-GB snprintf first; (b) lines 72-76 reslen + dec_point.size() overflow similarly requires ~2^32 bytes of accumulated length; both are practically blocked by the enormous intermediate allocations.

A back-to-back overflow where line 63 itself wraps negative would make reslen negative and hit the String(reslen, ReserveString) constructor contract; unreachable because the guard at line 58 aborts that sub-case.

tmplen + 1 at line 33 cannot overflow (snprintf %.*F of a finite double is bounded well below INT_MAX); truncated first snprintf output (tmplen >= 64) is correctly repaired by reallocation at lines 29-39.

The function relies on portability of %.*F placing a leading digit (INF/NAN/exponent-free output); if a library emitted a non-digit lead, the isdigit early-returns cover it — robustness only, no memory-safety impact.

verdict.summary: php_wddx_pop_element deserializes attacker-controlled WDDX packets without validating the class named in the php_class_name variable: the packet string is lowercased and looked up directly in EG(class_table) (line 73), the chosen class is instantiated via object_init_ex (line 79), attacker-controlled struct members are merged in as object properties (lines 82-84), and __wakeup is then invoked on the object (line 45). Any application exposing wddx_deserialize (or unserialize of WDDX payloads) to untrusted input thus gets attacker-selected classes instantiated with attacker-controlled state and their __wakeup executed - an unserialize-style object injection that is RCE-equivalent when a gadget class (e.g., a __wakeup/__destruct chain) exists. Unknown class names fall back to __PHP_Incomplete_Class, so the trigger only requires an existing class, which the code itself permits.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the class-table lookup key (Z_STR(ent1->data)) is the attacker-supplied php_class_name string from the WDDX packet, and there is no allow-list or validation before object_init_ex instantiates the attacker-chosen class. Concrete trigger: a struct containing <var name="php_class_name"><string>Gadget</string></var> plus arbitrary property vars; at the closing tag of that <string>, the code merges the attacker's properties into the new object (zend_hash_merge, lines 82-84) and later calls Gadget::__wakeup (line 45) with attacker-controlled state, completing object injection (CWE-502/CWE-470). Only states this code permits are needed; the class name crosses the trust boundary in the packet.

assumptions: The function is the expat end-element callback of wddx_deserialize; the WDDX packet is untrusted input (network/file data) whose validation is this code's responsibility at intake.

Exploitation to code execution assumes the host application defines a class with a harmful __wakeup/__destruct gadget (standard object-injection assumption); the injection primitive itself is fully present in this code as written.
The push-element handler (not shown) is assumed to create a string-valued entry for <binary> and an ST_FIELD entry for <field>, which the pop logic here relies on for balanced stack operations.
limitations: Potential type confusion at the </binary> base64 decode (lines 32-34): ent1->data is not checked for IS_STRING before Z_STRVAL/Z_STRLEN are used. However, in well-formed packets the stack is push/pop balanced within this handler, so the entry on top at </binary> is the one created for <binary> (string data); no path in this code produces a non-string there. Recorded as unconfirmed, contingent on the unseen push handler.

retval (line 41) is uninitialized before call_user_function_ex; if the deserialized object's class lacks __wakeup and the engine left retval untouched on failure, zval_ptr_dtor(&retval) would act on uninitialized stack memory. This depends on zend_call_function's out-of-scope contract and could not be confirmed from this code.

Memory leaks: ent1->data is not destroyed when ent2 is not an array/object (e.g., value elements nested directly inside a <binary>/<string> entry), and the </field> branch frees the st_entry without freeing its varname. Bounded by request lifetime and memory_limit, so robustness degradation only.
Instantiation of unknown classes degrades safely to __PHP_Incomplete_Class; the object-injection impact requires an existing exploitable class in the host application.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled scan component count `m_ucCount` is used as the loop bound for fixed four-element stack arrays without a runtime bounds check. A crafted scan with more than four components makes `cx` reach 4 and causes an out-of-bounds stack write at `line[4]`, followed by further out-of-bounds use of `lp`, `a`, `b`, `c`, `d`, and gradient arrays.

evidence.reason: `m_ucCount` originates from attacker-controlled JPEG scan-header data. The only preceding validation is `assert(m_ucCount < 4)`, which is not a release-mode bounds check. With a crafted scan where `m_ucCount = 5`, the loop reaches `cx = 4` and writes beyond the fixed `struct Line *line[4]` array, producing an out-of-bounds stack write.

assumptions: `m_ucCount` is populated from JPEG scan-header data and can exceed the fixed array capacity before this method executes.
The analysis assumes a normal release build where `assert` is compiled out; with assertions enabled, the same malformed scan would instead cause an assertion abort.
limitations: If `DecodeRun` could return a run longer than `length`, the `while(run)` loop would write beyond the line buffer; the helper is not shown and receives `length`, so no concrete trigger is established here.

Zero or negative `m_ulWidth[0]` or `m_ulRemaining[0]` could make the do/while counters wrap, but reaching those values requires invalid frame geometry or invocation after row exhaustion not demonstrated in this code.
The `m_lJ[m_lRunIndex[0]]` access requires an out-of-range run index; no producer of that state is shown.
Ignored failure of `BeginReadMCU` and undefined signed/fractional shifts are robustness issues without a demonstrated security sink in this snippet.

verdict.summary: This TFLite Div Eval dispatcher validates its trust-boundary inputs before every sink it contains: tensor pointers are obtained via GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe with status propagation (invalid indices/NULL tensors fail closed), the type dispatch on the attacker-controlled output->type is filtered to exactly {FLOAT32, INT32} for EvalDiv and {UINT8} for EvalQuantized with a fail-closed else branch, and the error report uses a fixed literal format string. The only asymmetry observed is that EvalDiv's return status is discarded while EvalQuantized's is propagated, but no failing EvalDiv path is producible from the statements in this code (output->type is constrained at the call), and all speculative defects (int32 divide-by-zero SIGFPE, input/output type confusion, NULL params/data dereference) have their sinks inside callees not present in the given code.

assumptions: GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe validate tensor indices and NULL tensors and return an error status, so input1/input2/output are non-NULL whenever used (standard TFLite contract for the 'Safe' getters).
node->builtin_data (TfLiteDivParams) and node->user_data (OpData) are populated by the framework/op registration for a registered builtin Div operator.
EvalDiv and EvalQuantized internals, and the Div Prepare pass (type/shape consistency between inputs and output), are not part of the provided code; this analysis judges only the statements given.
kernel_type is a compile-time template parameter, not runtime attacker data.
limitations: Swallowed return status: the EvalDiv<kernel_type>(...) call's return value is discarded, so the function returns kTfLiteOk even if EvalDiv failed (asymmetric with the EvalQuantized branch which is wrapped in TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK). Within this code, output->type is constrained to FLOAT32/INT32 at that call, so no demonstrable failing path exists here; if EvalDiv can fail (e.g., on an input/output type mismatch or internal error), an attacker-crafted model could cause a swallowed error leaving the output tensor stale/unwritten. Not confirmable from the given code.
INT32 division-by-zero (SIGFPE denial-of-service) would occur inside EvalDiv, which is not included in the provided code; this function contains no arithmetic.

Dispatch is keyed only on output->type; input tensor types are not re-validated in this function. Any type-confused read of attacker tensor data would occur inside the callees, which are not provided; this code performs no typed data access itself.

params and data are reinterpret_cast without NULL checks, but they are never dereferenced in this function; dereference sinks live in the callees and in the framework's op setup, which are outside the given code.

verdict.summary: FurnaceGUI::patternRow renders pattern rows from loaded module data. The effects loop uses the file-supplied per-channel value e->song.pat[j].effectRows directly as its loop bound and computes index=4+(k<<1), then reads pat->data[i][index] and pat->data[i][index+1] without any check that the column index stays within the pattern row's fixed column width. Although the row index i is validated against song.patLen and the instrument index is validated against insLen, no equivalent check exists for the effect column index. A crafted module file declaring a large effectRows for a visible, non-collapsed channel makes the pattern view read heap memory past the end of the pattern buffer (for rows near patLen-1), causing a crash and leaking heap contents into the rendered effect text (CWE-125, root cause: missing validation of file-controlled loop/index data, CWE-20).

evidence.snippet:
for (int k=0; k<e->song.pat[j].effectRows; k++) {
        int index=4+(k<<1);
evidence.reason: effectRows originates from the loaded module file (trust boundary) and is used unvalidated as the loop bound; index=4+(k<<1) and index+1 are then used to read pat->data[i][index] (lines 194/198/202) with no check that the column stays within the pattern row's fixed width. Trigger: open a crafted module with a large effectRows (e.g., 255) on a visible, non-collapsed channel and scroll to the last pattern rows; the reads at index up to 512/513 go past the end of the pattern heap buffer, an out-of-bounds read whose values are sprintf'd into UI text.

assumptions: All e->song fields (patLen, ordersLen, hilightA/B, chanShow/chanCollapse, insLen, pat[j].effectRows) and pat->data cell values originate from a loaded module file and cross a trust boundary into this GUI code.

Each cached DivPattern in patCache[j] is non-NULL and has song.patLen rows of a fixed compile-time column width (rows are not dynamically widened per effectRows); this is what makes large effectRows read out of bounds rather than merely into adjacent rows.
The caller passes chans equal to the engine's total channel count, which does not exceed the channel-array bounds (DIV_MAX_CHANS), and patCache is sized accordingly.
noteName() returns short strings (about 3 characters), as in the stock tracker note naming.
limitations: sprintf into static id[32] cannot overflow for any values this code permits (2-char hex + up to three decimal fields + separators stays well under 32 bytes); negative shorts rendered with %.2X merely show 8 hex characters (cosmetic).
chans is not re-validated against e->song.chLen/DIV_MAX_CHANS inside this function (caller contract; the engine bounds channel counts), and patCache[j] NULL-ness is likewise the caller's contract.

Verified safe guards: chanVolMax clamped to >=1 (no division by zero), volColor clamped to 0..127, instrument index checked against insLen before e->song.ins[...] dereference, hilightA/B modulo guarded by >0 checks, fxColors/extFxColors indices bounded by the data<0x10 / data-0xe0 branch chain.
ImGui style-stack pushes/pops were traced and are balanced on all paths; the early visibility/order/row returns occur before any PushStyleColor, so no imbalance exists.
No integer overflow is reachable in this code: j*32, k<<1, and data*127 operate on small/short values far below int limits.

verdict.summary: btrfs_rm_device() drops uuid_mutex — the only lock serializing device selection and device lifetime — across the long-running btrfs_shrink_device() and never re-validates the target device after re-acquiring it. Two concurrent RM_DEV ioctls on the same non-WRITEABLE device (e.g. a missing or seed device) both pass every guard and operate on the same device; whichever finishes first frees the device (btrfs_free_device) and possibly its fs_devices (free_fs_devices), after which the second caller executes btrfs_rm_dev_item(), clear_bit, list_del_rcu(), btrfs_close_bdev() and btrfs_free_device() on freed memory, causing use-after-free/double-free and kernel memory corruption.

evidence.reason: uuid_mutex is the only serialization protecting device selection and lifetime (guards at lines 37-53 run under it, and the post-shrink section 68-131 dereferences and frees `device` under it). Dropping it across the unbounded btrfs_shrink_device() and re-acquiring it without re-validating that `device` is still present and not being removed lets a concurrent btrfs_rm_device() select the same non-WRITEABLE (missing/seed) device, pass every guard, and then run list_del_rcu/btrfs_close_bdev/btrfs_free_device on a device (and possibly fs_devices) already freed by the first caller: use-after-free and double free (CWE-362/CWE-415). Trigger: two concurrent RM_DEV ioctls naming the same missing or seed device.

assumptions: device_path/devid originate from BTRFS_IOC_RM_DEV(_V2), whose arguments cross the userspace trust boundary; the ioctl dispatcher gates the call on CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so the attacker is assumed to hold that capability — but the broken device-lifetime invariant is entirely within this function.
Nothing outside this function serializes concurrent btrfs_rm_device() calls; uuid_mutex is the only lock and it is explicitly dropped around btrfs_shrink_device().
btrfs_find_device_by_devspec() returns the same still-listed device to both concurrent callers while the device remains on fs_devices->devices (removal happens only at list_del_rcu after shrink).
Seed fs_devices are read-only, so their devices never have BTRFS_DEV_STATE_WRITEABLE set; this is why the error_undo alloc_list mismatch is dismissed as unreachable.
limitations: error_undo() re-adds device->dev_alloc_list to fs_devices->alloc_list while rw_devices is accounted on device->fs_devices; the two diverge only for seed devices, which are never WRITEABLE, so the guarded branch cannot execute for them — no reachable trigger in this code.

The rw_devices == 1 'only writable device' guard is checked before the unlocked shrink window; concurrent removal of two distinct writable devices can transiently drop rw_devices faster, but the end state equals a legal sequential sequence and the guard incidentally blocks duplicate removal of a writable device — no memory-safety impact.
btrfs_reada_undo_remove_dev() can run without a matching btrfs_reada_remove_dev() when shrink fails; at most reada bookkeeping imbalance on an already-failing removal.
num_devices/missing_devices/open_devices counters can underflow only via the confirmed duplicate-removal race (subsumed by the primary finding) or via on-disk corruption rejected at mount.
The in-code TODO acknowledges a num_devices/super_copy inconsistency with write_all_supers() — a known upstream robustness limitation, not a memory-safety defect.

verdict.summary: This RequantizeRangePerChannel-style kernel fully validates all attacker-controlled shape metadata before every memory sink: input_min/input_max element counts are pinned to `depth` (input_max.NumElements()), input is required to be non-empty, 4-D, and have `dim_size(3) == depth`, which bounds the `transposed_input.chip<0>(i)` indexing and the raw `input_min_data/input_max_data` reads to within the buffers for all `i < depth`. No reachable out-of-bounds, type-confusion, or fail-open path exists in this code; the remaining defects (std::abs(INT32_MIN) UB, 1L<<31 on LLP64, OpenMP race on is_non_negative/out_min_max, dim_size(0) called before rank validation) are numerical/robustness issues with no security impact.

assumptions: The kernel is registered with a TypeConstraint fixing `input` to DT_QINT32 and `input_min`/`input_max` to DT_FLOAT (standard registration for this op), so dtype-based reinterpretation is not attacker-reachable across the framework's dispatch boundary.
OP_REQUIRES macro semantics are the standard TensorFlow ones: on failure it records the error and returns from Compute, so all listed shape checks execute before data pointers are used.
`flat_inner_dims<qint32>()` on a 4-D NHWC tensor yields a [P, C] matrix with C = dim_size(3), so after `shuffle({1,0})` chip<0> row range is C.
limitations: std::abs(min_per_channel) is UB when min_per_channel == INT32_MIN (and `1L << 31` is UB where long is 32-bit, e.g. MSVC); the resulting ranges[i] value is numerically wrong but is only written to the scalar output_min/output_max calibration floats — no memory-safety impact.

Under ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPENMP builds, `is_non_negative` is written from the parallel loop without a reduction (data race, CWE-362-style), and the _MSC_VER branch omits `reduction(max:out_min_max)` so out_min_max can race; all writers of is_non_negative write the same value `false`, and the op is documented in-code as a calibration step removed before final inference, so only calibration accuracy can degrade.

`input_min.dim_size(0)` / `input_max.dim_size(0)` are read before any rank check; for rank-0 tensors this relies on TensorShape's documented precondition and may read uninitialized inline storage in release builds, but the value feeds only a redundant comparison — the subsequent NumElements == depth checks still bound every data access, so there is no security impact.

clip_value_max_ is a graph-defined op attribute treated as trusted configuration; if a threat model considers the model file itself untrusted, an extreme clip_value_max_ could only alter the output max float value.

verdict.summary: pgpPrtParams validates each packet through decodePkt (passing the exact remaining length) before any use, checks every parser return value, requires full consumption (p == pend) for success, and fails closed with -1 while freeing digp on all anomaly paths. digp ownership is correctly transferred or freed. No reachable memory-safety, input-validation, lifetime, or fail-open defect exists in this code as written.

assumptions: decodePkt (implementation not shown) enforces its contract that pkt.head through pkt.body + pkt.blen lies within the (pend - p) bytes passed to it, and that a non-zero return means invalid packet; this code correctly passes the remaining length and checks the return.
pgpPrtPkt (implementation not shown) parses the packet body only within the region described by pkt.head/pkt.body/pkt.blen; its return value is checked here.
pkts and pktlen describe a valid buffer region per the caller's contract, as is standard for (ptr,len) APIs.
limitations: Overshoot candidate: if decodePkt could succeed with a packet extending beyond the remaining length, p would advance past pend; however this function never dereferences past pend (loop condition p < pend re-checked, decodePkt not called again) and rc's p == pend check fails closed; a real trigger would additionally require a defect inside decodePkt, whose source is not given.

Zero/wrapped advance (infinite loop) candidate: requires pkt.body == pkt.head with pkt.blen == 0 (impossible, since the tag byte makes the header at least one byte) or blen near SIZE_MAX (a decodePkt-internal defect); not producible from states this code itself permits.
pkts + pktlen pointer overflow requires pktlen near SIZE_MAX, which only arises if the caller violates the documented (ptr,len) buffer contract.
pgpDigParamsNew returning NULL on allocation failure would feed NULL digp to pgpPrtPkt; this is OOM robustness only with no attacker-controlled exhaustion path.
When rc != 0 and ret is non-NULL, *ret is left unmodified (stale caller value possible); caller-side contract hygiene, not a security defect in this code.

verdict.summary: The Rabin-Williams private-key operation processes attacker-influenced input x but is fail-closed: the pre-return consistency check 'if (ApplyFunction(y) != x) throw' runs on the only return path, so out-of-range, degenerate (Jacobi==0), or computationally inconsistent inputs terminate in an exception rather than producing an incorrect or forged signature. All arithmetic uses arbitrary-precision Integers with internal modular reduction (no bounds/width violations), the blinding retry loop terminates for any valid odd modulus, and the OpenMP sections write distinct variables with a join before use. No memory-safety, integer, lifetime, input-validation, fail-open, or authorization defect is reachable.

assumptions: ApplyFunction is the matching public operation of the same key object and the final comparison is the authoritative verification of the output.
m_p, m_q, m_n, m_u constitute a valid RW private key (n=p*q, p,q odd primes), as enforced at key generation/load and partially by DoQuickSanityCheck().
Crypto++ Integer is arbitrary precision, so no overflow/width preconditions exist at any sink.
rng is a functioning RandomNumberGenerator; blinding quality affects only side-channel resistance, not correctness.
limitations: x is not range-checked at entry ([0, m_n)); out-of-range inputs cause a throw (per-operation denial/robustness only, no incorrect output returned).

A malformed key (even or degenerate m_n) could prevent the blinding retry loop from terminating; this contradicts the key contract that DoQuickSanityCheck and key generation enforce, so it is not a vulnerability in this code.
Degenerate inputs where x ≡ 0 mod p or q yield exceptions rather than signatures (fail-closed robustness, no security impact).
Unchecked historical bug class (signing producing a signature for a different message) is refuted here because the ApplyFunction(y) != x verification is present before return.

verdict.summary: The Div kernel validates the divisor tensor input2 using an element type selected from output->type instead of input2->type. No code in this Eval enforces that input2's declared type matches the type used by the TF_LITE_CHECK_DIV_NON_ZERO macro. A model whose Div node declares, e.g., a Float32 input2 and an Int32 output causes GetTensorData<int32_t>(input2) to return a NULL (or mistyped) pointer that the macro then indexes in its zero-check loop, producing a null-pointer dereference crash; under the reinterpret variant the check inspects float bit patterns instead of actual divisor values, defeating the div-by-zero guard before EvalDiv divides mistyped data. Trigger: malicious/malformed TFLite model with mismatched input/output tensor types for the Div op.

evidence.reason: The divisor non-zero check is instantiated with int32_t chosen solely from output->type; input2->type is never validated to match, so for a model with Float32 input2 and Int32 output the macro computes GetTensorData<int32_t>(input2) (NULL on type mismatch) and a nonzero element count from input2->bytes, then indexes that pointer (input2_data[i]) — null-deref crash, or a zero-check over mistyped bit patterns that fails to prevent integer division by zero.

Same defect on the UInt8 branch: the element type for reading input2 is derived from the output tensor type. A Float32 input2 with a UInt8 output makes the macro iterate input2->bytes times (4N) over a NULL/mistyped pointer with no input2->type validation performed anywhere in this Eval.

assumptions: Model/tensor metadata and runtime tensor contents are attacker-influenced (untrusted .tflite model) — the standard TFLite threat model; this Eval is where that data crosses into kernel logic.

GetTensorData<T>(tensor) returns nullptr when the tensor's declared type differs from T (or, in older TFLite versions, reinterprets the raw buffer); under either implementation the defective path exists — either an immediate NULL dereference in the zero-check loop or validation of the wrong bit representation that lets a real zero divisor reach the integer division.
Lines are numbered from 1 at 'TfLiteStatus Eval(...)' in the snippet as given.
limitations: The Float32 path intentionally skips the zero-divisor check (comment: infinities are returned, matching TF semantics); this is documented behavior, not a vulnerability.

params and data are reinterpret_cast from node->builtin_data/user_data without NULL checks, but these are framework-populated kernel-internal pointers that this function never dereferences, so no trigger is reachable from this code.
input2->bytes / sizeof(data_type) can truncate a non-multiple element count, but this only under-counts the loop; no out-of-bounds path results.
This analysis covers only Eval; Prepare-time validation (not shown) is not assumed to repair the missing input2->type check that this function's own dispatch logic requires.

verdict.summary: In the DEFI chunk handler of ReadOneMNGImage, the object-id bounds check `if (object_id > MNG_MAX_OBJECTS)` and the subsequent clamp `object_id=MNG_MAX_OBJECTS` are both off by one: the MngInfo arrays (exists, frozen, invisible, viewable, x_off, y_off, object_clip) are valid only for indices 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1, as enforced by every other loop and range check in this code (e.g., `i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS`, `i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS` -> continue). A crafted MNG file containing a DEFI chunk with object_id equal to or greater than MNG_MAX_OBJECTS therefore produces object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, causing out-of-bounds reads and writes one element past the array ends, including the attacker-controlled byte written to invisible[object_id] and attacker-controlled 32-bit values written to x_off[]/y_off[] in the heap-allocated MngInfo structure (heap memory corruption).

evidence.reason: Off-by-one validation of the attacker-controlled DEFI object id. The comparison uses `>` instead of `>=`, so object_id == MNG_MAX_OBJECTS passes unclamped, and out-of-range ids (e.g., 0xFFFF) are clamped to MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, which is itself one past the last valid index of the MngInfo arrays (valid range 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1, per this code's own loops and CLIP/MOVE range checks). Trigger: an MNG file with signature, MHDR, then a DEFI chunk (length >= 2) whose payload bytes yield object_id >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; the ThrowMagickException is non-fatal, execution continues, and the very next statements perform `mng_info->exists[object_id]` (OOB read), `mng_info->exists[object_id]=MagickTrue` (OOB write), `mng_info->invisible[object_id]=p[2]` (attacker-controlled byte OOB write), and x_off[]/y_off[]/object_clip[] OOB writes — memory corruption past the array ends in the heap-allocated MngInfo struct.

assumptions: MngInfo per-object arrays (exists, frozen, invisible, viewable, x_off, y_off, object_clip) are dimensioned MNG_MAX_OBJECTS, i.e., valid indices 0..MNG_MAX_OBJECTS-1; this is inferred from this code's own initialization loops (`for (i=0; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)`, `for (i=1; i < MNG_MAX_OBJECTS; i++)`) and the CLIP/MOVE guards that skip `i >= MNG_MAX_OBJECTS`.

MngInfoDiscardObject, called from the DISC/SEEK handler with an unchecked 0..65535 object index derived from file data, is assumed to validate the index internally (its body is not part of this code).

Preprocessor configuration (MNG_INSERT_LAYERS, MNG_OBJECT_BUFFERS, JNG_SUPPORTED, MNG_LOOSE, MAGICKCORE_QUANTUM_DEPTH) assumed to follow a typical build; MNG_LOOSE-dependent code paths (which would use an uninitialized loop variable `i` in the PLTE handler) are assumed not compiled.

In the LOOP chunk handler, loop_level=chunk[0] (0..255) indexes mng_info->loop_active/loop_jump/loop_count/loop_iteration with no bound check in this code; if any of those arrays is dimensioned smaller than 256 in the (externally defined) MngInfo struct, this is an additional out-of-bounds read/write on an attacker-influenced path. It could not be confirmed from the given code alone.
limitations: TERM chunk: when repeat==3, mng_get_long(&p[2]) and mng_get_long(&p[6]) are executed with only `length != 0` checked; a TERM chunk of length 1-9 with p[0]==3 reads up to 9 bytes past the valid payload. Because the chunk buffer is allocated as length+MagickPathExtent, these are reads of uninitialized heap padding (values flow into final_delay/mng_iterations/image->iterations), not out-of-bounds accesses of the allocation.

FRAM chunk: after skipping the frame name, the parser can read up to roughly 25 bytes past the declared chunk length (change flags, delays, 17-byte clip box) into the uninitialized MagickPathExtent padding of the chunk allocation; again an uninitialized-value issue, not a heap overflow.

Chunk payloads can be partially uninitialized when the read loop hits EOF, because the `length > GetBlobSize(image)` check compares against total file size rather than remaining bytes; decoded values remain subject to subsequent range checks (e.g., MHDR width/height <= 65535), limiting impact to garbage/uninitialized metadata.

MAGN magnification: magnified_width/magnified_height arithmetic ((columns-2)*magn_mx etc.) can overflow png_uint_32 for very wide images with large magnification factors; the observable effect in this code is at worst a failed assert or a NULL pixel-queue dereference (denial of service), not a demonstrated controlled out-of-bounds write.
Repeated allocation of images/layers per chunk is bounded by the file structure and NULL-checked allocations; no unbounded resource-exhaustion path beyond normal image-size limits was confirmed.

verdict.summary: This is the post-CVE-2015-2141 Crypto++ Rabin-Williams private-key operation. The blinding value is squared so Jacobi(r^2,n)=1 and the loop guarantees invertibility (rInv != 0), making the root selection deterministic in x and closing the principal-square-root leak. Key material entering from serialized state is validated at intake via DoQuickSanityCheck(). All Integer math is arbitrary precision (no overflow/bounds sinks), the OpenMP sections write disjoint variables under an implicit barrier, the halving statements divide exactly by 2 with no off-by-one, and every computational-error path (out-of-range x, wrong m_u, non-residue after halving, degenerate key) is fail-closed by the final ApplyFunction(y)!=x check that throws instead of returning a wrong result. No reachable sink lacks an enforced precondition, so no vulnerability exists in this code as written.

assumptions: DoQuickSanityCheck() (line 1) performs the library's level-1 key validation (p, q odd > 1, n == p*q) per the Crypto++ CryptoMaterial contract, as its implementation is outside the provided snippet.
Integer is Crypto++'s arbitrary-precision bignum; all shifts, additions, and multiplications are wide, so fixed-width overflow/truncation sinks do not apply.
The caller supplies a genuine RandomNumberGenerator per the library contract; rng is used only for blinding.
limitations: x is not explicitly range-checked to [0, n); however modn.Multiply reduces it and any resulting mismatch fails the final self-check with an exception (fail-closed), so this is robustness-only.
If the supplied rng were predictable, blinding would be weak; this requires the caller to violate the documented RNG contract, so it is not a defect in this code.

For some Jacobi patterns (e.g., J(x,p)=+1, J(x,q)=-1 with p≡3 mod 8) the halving branch can feed a non-residue to ModularSquareRoot; the garbage result is then rejected by the ApplyFunction(y)!=x check and throws, so the impact is a distinguishable error, not a wrong output or memory-safety issue.
The self-check throws Exception(OTHER_ERROR) on error, which callers must handle; unhandled-exception behavior is outside this function's control.

verdict.summary: patternRow validates the row index (i vs patLen) and order index, and bounds-checks the instrument index and color-table lookups, but it uses the file-derived song.pat[j].effectRows as the effect-loop bound with no bounds check: index=4+(k<<1) and index+1 index pat->data[i] with no verification that they lie within the pattern row's fixed column capacity. A crafted song/module file with a large effectRows value drives an out-of-bounds heap read whose bytes are formatted into sprintf/ImGui labels (crash and heap-data disclosure in the UI).
