No shared mutable state, allocation, or error path exists in this snippet, so race, leak, and fail-open candidates were not applicable.

verdict.summary: In the string iteration paths, args->from is used directly as an index into string bytes without any validation against the string length: 'p = string_prop.start + from' (byte-string path) and 'njs_string_offset(string_prop.start, end, from)' (UTF-8 path). If from exceeds the string's length (e.g. a guest-script-supplied start index such as 'str.lastIndexOf(x, N)' with N > str.length propagated as from), the loop decrements p backwards and reads a byte per iteration via njs_string_new(vm, &character, p, 1, 1) / njs_string_new(..., pos, p - pos, 1), dereferencing memory past the end and then before the start of the string buffer. This is an out-of-bounds read of guest-influenced string memory that leaks bytes into guest-visible one-character strings or crashes.

evidence.reason: from is never validated against string_prop.size/length before being added to the buffer pointer; combined with the following 'while (i-- > to)' loop that does 'p--' and passes p to njs_string_new(vm, &character, p, 1, 1), a from greater than the string length walks the pointer past the end and then before the start of the string buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Trigger: guest script calls a string iteration entry point (e.g. lastIndexOf with fromIndex > length) so that args->from exceeds the string length while args->to = 0.

UTF-8 path: from is passed unvalidated to njs_string_offset (index beyond the string yields a pointer at/past end), and each loop iteration then calls njs_utf8_prev(p), moving p backwards; when the iteration count (from - to + 1) exceeds the number of code points in the string, pos points before string_prop.start and is used as the source in njs_string_new(vm, &character, pos, p - pos, 1), an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). Trigger: guest-supplied UTF-8 string with args->from > codepoint count.

assumptions: args->from/args->to are supplied by the engine's iterator setup (e.g. String.prototype.lastIndexOf / iterate helpers) from script-supplied indices; this function performs no independent clamping, and the OOB is reachable whenever the caller passes from beyond the string length.
Line numbers are relative to the snippet as provided, counting from the function's opening 'njs_object_iterate_reverse(njs_vm_t *vm, ...)' line as line 1.
limitations: Array path is properly guarded: array indexing is checked with 'from < array->length && njs_is_valid(&array->start[from])' before the handler, and the fallback property lookup checks its return value (NJS_ERROR / NJS_DECLINED), so no array-path issue was confirmed.
The object/keys path range-checks the parsed index ('idx < to || idx > from') and bounds 'keys->start[--i]' by keys->length; dismissed as safe.

If to > from, 'from - to' is negative when passed to njs_fast_object; this only selects the slow keys path and both countdown loops then execute zero iterations — no memory-unsafe dereference, so recorded as robustness only, not a vulnerability.
The (size_t)length == string_prop.size comparison could in principle misclassify a >4GB string, but such sizes are not producible by this code's string allocation machinery; dismissed as unreachable.

Actual exploitability depends on whether every engine caller clamps from to the string length before calling this helper; the raw, unclamped pointer arithmetic 'string_prop.start + from' exists in this function as written, so the missing boundary validation is attributed here.

verdict.summary: protocol_client_msg validates VNC client message completeness only with equality tests (len == 1 / len == 4 / len == 8 / len == 2) instead of length-sufficiency checks, so a malicious client can have the handler invoked with a partially-filled buffer (e.g. len = 8 for SetEncodings). In the SetEncodings path, limit (read from attacker bytes 2-3, up to 0xFFFF) drives a loop that both reads and memcpy-writes at data+4+4*i with no check that len >= 4 + limit*4, producing a heap out-of-bounds read AND write far past the input buffer allocation (CWE-787, matching upstream QEMU CVE-2021-4206). The same under-fill pattern also yields out-of-bounds reads elsewhere: CutText passes data+8 with a dlen read out of bounds when len is 2-7 (bypassing the 1MB cap entirely), and SetPixelFormat/FramebufferUpdateRequest/KeyEvent/PointerEvent/QEMU-ExtKey/audio handlers read fixed offsets beyond len. All reachable by any client able to speak the VNC protocol after the server arms the handler with expect=1.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing bounds check. `limit` is read from attacker-controlled message bytes (offsets 2-3) and used as loop bound for read_s32/memcpy at data+4+4*i, but nothing verifies len >= 4 + limit*4; the only prior guard is the equality test `len == 4` (lines 26-31), which fails to reject buffers of 2-7 or 9..(4+4*limit-1) bytes. Concrete trigger: handler armed with expect=1 (line 145), client sends one 8-byte segment 02 00 FF FF 41 41 41 41 so the handler runs with len=8, limit=0xFFFF; iteration i=1 already reads/writes offsets 8-11 past the 8 valid bytes and i=65534 reaches offset 262143, past the heap-allocated input buffer -> heap out-of-bounds read and write (CWE-787). For len=2 or 3, `limit` itself is read out of bounds, same defect.

Root cause: missing length validation / fail-open guard. This sink is reached whenever 2 <= len <= 7 because the size checks only test len == 1 (line 61) and len == 8 (line 64); the 1MB dlen cap and the re-arm `return 8 + dlen` live only inside the len == 8 branch, so they are bypassed. Trigger: client sends the 2-byte segment 06 00 -> len=2 -> read_u32(data, 4) reads bytes 4-7 that were never received (out-of-bounds heap read) and data+8 points past all valid data; client_cut_text then consumes/copyies that unvalidated length from out-of-bounds memory -> out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

assumptions: The VNC input layer invokes protocol_client_msg with len equal to however many bytes are buffered (any value >= the 1-byte expectation), since TCP segmentation is fully client-controlled; this matches QEMU's vnc_read_when/vnc_read contract and the upstream fix for this exact code (CVE-2021-4206).
vs->input is a heap buffer whose capacity is finite and never checked here, so writes past capacity are heap corruption.
len >= 1 whenever the handler is called, guaranteed by the vnc_read_when(vs, protocol_client_msg, 1) arming; data[0] at line 7 is therefore in bounds.
client_cut_text, set_encodings and the other handlers consume the lengths/pointers passed to them; their internals are not shown.
limitations: Candidate E (integer overflow in 4 + limit*4) rejected: limit is uint16_t promoted to int, maximum 262140, no overflow.
Candidate F rejected: len==8 with dlen==0 passes a one-past-end pointer with length 0 to client_cut_text; no dereference occurs.

Candidate G (audio): vs->as.nchannels is assigned before validation and, after an invalid fmt, nchannels/freq are still updated after vnc_client_error; the error flags the connection for teardown, so this is transient state churn with no demonstrated memory-safety impact.
Candidate H rejected: all printf calls use literal format strings; %d with uint8/uint16 arguments is benign.

The under-filled-message OOB reads in SetPixelFormat (lines 13-20), FramebufferUpdateRequest (41-46), KeyEvent (49-52), PointerEvent (55-58), QEMU ExtKeyEvent (85-89) and the audio handlers (92-124) stem from the identical missing length-sufficiency check and are subsumed by the confirmed findings; their values are largely re-validated by the downstream handlers, so impact is lower than the SetEncodings write.
len==4 with limit>0 correctly re-arms for the full 4+limit*4 byte message, and len==8 with dlen>0 correctly re-arms for 8+dlen; those paths are not defective.

verdict.summary: check_passwd() compares binary password hashes with strncmp(), which stops at the first 0x00 byte. If the stored hash and the hash derived from the attacker's password guess share a prefix ending in an embedded NUL (simplest case: both first bytes are 0x00), strncmp returns 0 and the code sets ret = 1, accepting a wrong password and bypassing bootloader authentication without ever comparing the remaining hash bytes.

evidence.reason: Root cause: strncmp is a NUL-terminated string comparison applied to binary PBKDF2 key material; it stops at the first 0x00 byte, so only a prefix of keylen bytes is verified. Trigger: the stored env/default key (passwd2_sum + PBKDF2_SALT_LEN) begins with 0x00 and the attacker submits any guess whose pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1 output also begins with 0x00 (about 1/256 of guesses); strncmp returns 0 at the first byte, ret = 1, and the wrong password is accepted.

Same root cause on the plain-digest branch: digest_digest output and the stored hash are compared with strncmp, which terminates at the first 0x00 byte. If both hashes start with (or share a prefix ending in) an embedded NUL, the comparison returns equal and ret = 1, accepting an incorrect password and bypassing authentication.

assumptions: PBKDF2_SALT_LEN <= PBKDF2_LENGTH and other PBKDF2_* constants are sane build-time values, as in the barebox configuration this code comes from.
digest_free tolerates NULL (the external API contract; the PBKDF2 path reaches digest_free with d == NULL).
read_env_passwd/read_default_passwd write at most hash_len bytes into passwd2_sum, as their length parameter indicates.
limitations: digest_free(d) at line 62 is called with d == NULL on the PBKDF2 path; a NULL dereference would exist only if the external digest_free does not handle NULL, which cannot be verified from this snippet.
calloc(hash_len * 2, ...) at line 22 could overflow only if digest_length() returned a value above 2^30, which no real digest algorithm produces; hash_len is not attacker-settable here.
If PBKDF2_SALT_LEN exceeded PBKDF2_LENGTH, keylen would go negative and key would point past the buffer, but these are compile-time constants and such a build is not a runtime-reachable state.
When no password source is enabled the function returns -EINVAL (an error), not acceptance; there is no fail-open within this function.

Exploitability of the strncmp defect is bounded by probability: the stored hash must contain an early 0x00 byte (~1/256 per stored password), and the attacker must find a guess deriving a hash with the matching zero byte; the defective comparison path itself is unconditional in the code as written.

verdict.summary: Bootloader password verification. All heap accesses are sized from hash_len (digest length or PBKDF2_LENGTH) and every offset/length (PBKDF2_SALT_LEN + keylen = PBKDF2_LENGTH) stays exactly within the calloc(hash_len*2) buffer; allocation failure is checked, error paths fail closed (ret == 1 is assigned only after a full-length constant-time crypto_memneq match, all other paths return 0 or negative), and comparisons are constant-time. No attacker-triggerable memory-safety, input-validation, integer, or fail-open defect exists in this code; the only real defect is a digest-object leak on an OOM error path with no exhaustion path.

assumptions: PBKDF2_LENGTH >= PBKDF2_SALT_LEN (both compile-time constants), so keylen is non-negative and the salt/key layout fills passwd2_sum exactly to the allocation end.

pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1, digest_digest, read_env_passwd and read_default_passwd follow the 0-success / negative-error convention; ret == 1 is used exclusively as the password-match sentinel set only inside this function.
digest_free tolerates NULL (PBKDF2 builds call it with d == NULL), matching barebox digest_free semantics.
read_env_passwd and read_default_passwd are the intake validators for boundary-crossing credential data and honor the hash_len bound passed to them; their internals are outside the given snippet.
limitations: Resource leak: when digest_alloc() succeeds but calloc() fails, the early 'return -ENOMEM' skips digest_free(d). Reachable only under a pre-existing OOM condition, leaks one small struct, and has no exhaustion path — robustness degradation only, not a security vulnerability per STEP 4.
hash_len * 2 is computed in int; overflow would require a digest length above 2^30, which no registered digest algorithm produces — theoretically possible, not triggerable in this code.

'if (ret) goto err; ... return ret;' would fail open (caller sees 1 = match) only if pkcs5_pbkdf2_hmac_sha1 or digest_digest returned exactly 1 to signal an error; no evidence any callee does, and the code's own checks assume negative errno conventions.

If read_env_passwd reported success while writing fewer than hash_len bytes, passwd2_sum would retain calloc-zeroed bytes and be compared; validating env-content length is the callee's responsibility at its intake, and this code correctly passes the bound and a matching buffer size.
digest_free(d) is called with d == NULL in CONFIG_PASSWD_CRYPTO_PBKDF2 builds; safety depends on the callee's NULL handling (no dereference occurs in this code).

verdict.summary: net_bind frees the getaddrinfo result with freeaddrinfo(servinfo) at line 61 while the loop variable ptr still references the successfully bound node, then on the success path calls getsockname(fd, ptr->ai_addr, &ptr->ai_addrlen) (line 70) and net_port_get/net_address_get on the same freed buffer (lines 77-78). The kernel writes the bound address and its length into freed heap memory via ptr->ai_addr and &ptr->ai_addrlen, producing a use-after-free read/write on the routine success path of a network service bind routine (heap corruption potential in a multithreaded process).

evidence.reason: Use-after-free sink: freeaddrinfo(servinfo) at line 61 already freed the addrinfo chain, including the node ptr points to (the one that reached the successful break) and the sockaddr buffer ptr->ai_addr references. getsockname then writes the bound address into that freed buffer and writes a socklen_t through &ptr->ai_addrlen, and lines 77-78 (net_port_get/net_address_get) read the freed sockaddr. Trigger: cfgaddr=NULL (or a resolvable bind_address), *port=3689, type=SOCK_STREAM, and a single getaddrinfo result whose socket(), setsockopt(), and bind() calls succeed - i.e., the code's own normal success path. Root cause: premature freeaddrinfo before the addrinfo node is consumed.

assumptions: Line numbers assume the listing starts at line 1 with the net_bind signature.

getaddrinfo semantics assumed standard: the chain returned in servinfo (each node and its ai_addr buffer) is a single allocation lifetime owned by freeaddrinfo, so freeing it invalidates ptr and ptr->ai_addr.

The primary trigger (successful bind followed by the freed-pointer use) requires no attacker-controlled data; heap-corruption impact beyond undefined behavior additionally assumes the freed chunk can be reallocated between freeaddrinfo and the uses (plausible in a multithreaded process; at minimum this is a UAF read/write of freed memory).
limitations: Secondary, platform-conditional: the getaddrinfo failure check at line 22 uses 'ret < 0', but POSIX only guarantees a nonzero error return; on platforms where EAI_* codes are positive (FreeBSD, NetBSD, macOS) a resolution failure (e.g., unresolvable bind_address from the config file) is not detected, leaving servinfo uninitialized and then dereferenced while walking the list (CWE-457). On glibc/Linux, where EAI_* codes are negative, this path is not reachable, so it is recorded as a portability/robustness defect rather than a confirmed trigger for this code's reference platform.
close(fd) on the error path (line 85) can be called with fd == -1 when every socket() call fails; this is harmless (EBADF) with no security impact.
The 'ret < 0' checks around setsockopt, bind, and getsockname are correct (those APIs return -1 on error); only the getaddrinfo check is sign-sensitive.
The fd lifecycle (close of the prior iteration's socket at loop top, error-path close) was traced and found to close each descriptor at most once; no leak or double-close found.

verdict.summary: pjstun_parse_msg parses an attacker-controlled network STUN message but never bounds msg->attr_count against the fixed size of msg->attr[] (PJSTUN_MAX_ATTR = 16). A message containing 17 or more 4-byte zero-length attributes drives *attr = p_attr writes past the end of the attribute pointer array in the caller-supplied pjstun_msg structure (out-of-bounds write, up to ~16000 iterations). Additionally, the attribute loop only checks msg_len > 0 rather than msg_len >= sizeof(pjstun_attr_hdr), so a message whose length field is 1-3 bytes causes the 4-byte attribute header read to run past the end of the receive buffer (minor out-of-bounds read).

evidence.reason: Missing bound check on msg->attr_count before indexing the fixed-size msg->attr[] array. Trigger: an attacker sends an 88-byte STUN message (type 0x0001, header length = 68) containing 17 zero-length attributes; each iteration consumes 4 bytes and increments attr_count, so the 17th iteration stores a pointer at msg->attr[16], past the end of the array, and the write repeats for every additional 4-byte attribute (up to ~16384). The msg_len/len check bounds only the buffer walk, never the attribute count.

The loop guard is only 'while (msg_len > 0)', with no check that at least sizeof(pjstun_attr_hdr) (4) bytes remain, so the 4-byte attribute header is read from p_attr when 1-3 bytes are left. Trigger: an attacker sends a 23-byte STUN message whose header length field equals 3 (passing the msg_len == buf_len - 20 check); the read of (*attr)->length at buf+22 touches buf[23], one byte past the end of the received buffer.

assumptions: msg->attr is a fixed-size array (PJSTUN_MAX_ATTR = 16 in pjlib-util's pjstun.h) inside the caller-allocated pjstun_msg structure; the parser itself enforces no limit on attr_count, which is bounded only by message size (up to ~16384).
buf is a receive buffer of exactly buf_len bytes (typical for a UDP datagram passed by the calling receive path), so reads beyond buf_len-1 are out of bounds.
msg_type, msg->hdr->length, and all attribute fields are attacker-controlled network data; the parser is the trust boundary where they must be validated.
limitations: The function also lacks a minimum-length check (buf_len >= sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr)); a caller invoking it on a 0-3 byte datagram would over-read the header fields. This is a real missing intake validation but its trigger additionally depends on caller invocation with such short datagrams, so it is noted rather than confirmed.
buf_len - sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr) underflows when buf_len < 20, but the resulting size_t value can never equal the uint16 msg_len, so the function returns ESTUNINMSGLEN; no memory-safety effect.
Unknown attribute types are only logged, not rejected; this has no security consequence within this function since attributes are not further interpreted here.

verdict.summary: RaggedGatherOpBase::Compute validates every trust-boundary input it is responsible for before use: the splits list is required non-empty, the first splits tensor is rejected if scalar (dims()>0) before dim_size(0) is read, indices are range-validated via ValidateIndices against num_params before being passed to MakeSplits (with OP_REQUIRES_OK failure propagation), and params_dense_values is rank-checked before dim_size(0). No attacker-influenced value reaches an indexing, sizing, or copy sink within the shown code without these guards; the historically exploitable conditions for this op (scalar splits, out-of-range indices leading to OOB in split/value building) are precisely what these checks prevent, matching the upstream patched version.

assumptions: ValidateIndices enforces 0 <= index <= max_index for the indices tensor's dtype and returns a non-OK status that OP_REQUIRES_OK propagates, per its name and call-site contract.
The op registration guarantees input arity N+2 with ordering (N nested splits, then dense values, then indices), so context->input(size()) and context->input(size()+1) are structurally valid.
Helper functions MakeSplits/WriteSplits/WriteValues (not shown) perform their own value-range validation of split contents, as in the upstream TensorFlow implementation this snippet corresponds to.
limitations: Only Compute() is shown; the bodies of ValidateIndices, MakeSplits, WriteSplits, and WriteValues are unavailable, so monotonicity/range validation of split values and copy bounds inside those helpers cannot be audited from this code.

If params_nested_splits[0] has dim_size(0)==0 (e.g. shape [0]), num_params becomes -1; this is safe only because a correct validator rejects every index when max<0 (non-empty index tensors then fail; empty indices produce empty output). Recorded as a robustness edge case, not a vulnerability.
Theoretical truncation of the int64 dim_size(0)-1 result if SPLITS_TYPE is int32 and the first split dimension exceeds 2^31 elements; not reachable under normal TensorFlow allocation limits.

The known vulnerable variant of this function (missing scalar-splits check and missing ValidateIndices call, fixed upstream in 2021 for RaggedGather) is not what is shown here; this snippet contains those guards.

verdict.summary: net_bind() checks getaddrinfo()'s result with `if (ret < 0)`, but getaddrinfo reports errors with non-zero codes whose sign is platform-defined (negative on glibc/musl, positive on BSD-family systems such as FreeBSD/macOS, e.g. EAI_ADDRFAMILY=1, EAI_AGAIN=9, EAI_NONAME=8). On a positive failure code the error branch is skipped and `servinfo` — declared uninitialized and not written by getaddrinfo on failure — is iterated by `for (ptr = servinfo, ...)` and passed to freeaddrinfo(), i.e. a wild-pointer walk and free of uninitialized stack data. The failure is reachable from data crossing a trust boundary: the config-file `bind_address` (unresolvable hostname, transient DNS failure/NXDOMAIN, or an IPv4 literal combined with ipv6=true). Impact is a crash/DoS and potentially heap corruption via freeaddrinfo on garbage; on glibc/musl Linux the defect is latent because EAI codes are negative there.

evidence.reason: The error check `if (ret < 0)` does not match getaddrinfo's documented contract (returns 0 on success, non-zero error code on failure); on platforms where EAI_* codes are positive (FreeBSD/macOS), a failed resolution of the config-supplied `bind_address` (e.g. unresolvable host, DNS EAI_AGAIN, or IPv4 literal with ipv6 enabled yielding EAI_ADDRFAMILY) passes this guard, leaving `servinfo` (declared uninitialized at line 4, untouched by getaddrinfo on failure) to be dereferenced at line 30 (`for (ptr = servinfo, ...)`) and freed by freeaddrinfo() — use of an uninitialized variable / wild pointer (CWE-457) caused by an improper exceptional-condition check (CWE-703).

assumptions: On failure getaddrinfo() does not modify *res and leaves `servinfo` with its prior (uninitialized) contents, per POSIX which defines no value for res on error; glibc and FreeBSD behave this way.

getaddrinfo() error code sign is platform-dependent: glibc and musl use negative EAI_* values (defect latent), while BSD-family systems (FreeBSD ≥13 which also provides SOCK_CLOEXEC, macOS) use positive values (EAI_ADDRFAMILY=1, EAI_AGAIN=9, EAI_NONAME=8), making the fail-open path reachable there.

`bind_address` comes from a parsed configuration file and the resolution outcome depends on external DNS responses, so a resolution failure is producible by data crossing a trust boundary (misconfiguration or attacker-influenced DNS/network conditions).
limitations: Latent on Linux/glibc/musl: EAI_* codes are negative there, so `ret < 0` catches all failures; the defect requires a platform with positive EAI codes (FreeBSD/macOS), where the code is otherwise compilable (FreeBSD 13+ provides SOCK_CLOEXEC).

Reviewed and rejected: no fd leak or double-close — the loop-top `if (fd >= 0) close(fd)` plus the `error: close(fd)` path cover every exit path, and `close(-1)` is merely EBADF (unchecked return, no security impact).

Reviewed and rejected: `snprintf(strport, 8, "%hu", *port)` cannot truncate (max 5 digits + NUL); the `naddr_len > sizeof(naddr)` check is defensive/unreachable since getsockname never enlarges the passed length; `log_service_name` is used only as a %s argument (NULL would be a caller-contract robustness issue, not a memory-safety flaw in this code).

verdict.summary: In ReadMATImage, when image_info->ping is set, the code copies the attacker-controlled MAT header values SizeX/SizeY into image->columns/rows and jumps to done_reading, bypassing SetImageExtent — the only dimension sanity/resource check. Only a non-zero check is performed, so unbounded file-declared dimensions (and dimensions inconsistent with the declared data size, which is read and discarded) are returned across the trust boundary for the caller to allocate against.

evidence.reason: On the ping path, image->columns/rows (set directly from the file-supplied MATLAB_HDR.SizeX/SizeY with only a non-zero test at line 242) are swapped and the function jumps to done_reading, skipping the SetImageExtent call that follows immediately at line 264. Trigger: a MAT file with DataType=miMATRIX, DimFlag=8, valid StructureClass, CellType=miINT8, SizeX=0xFFFF0000, SizeY=1 yields a returned image whose dimensions were never validated against any limit or against the file's actual data size (the data-size field is read into `size` and ignored), so arbitrary header-declared dimensions cross the trust boundary unchecked.

assumptions: MATLAB_HDR.SizeX/SizeY are 32-bit values read from the file via ReadBlobXXXLong and are fully attacker-controlled.
Callers using ping mode (e.g., PingImage) trust the returned image->columns/rows for subsequent allocation/processing.
SetImageExtent is the coder's intended dimension/resource validation, as it is applied on every non-ping path.
limitations: ldblk = sample_bytes * SizeX is unchecked, but on 64-bit ssize_t a 32-bit SizeX cannot wrap it; oversized allocations fail with a checked NULL.
`image->colors = one << image->depth` is undefined behavior when depth==64 (shift by 64 of size_t); impact is a garbage metadata value, not memory corruption.
DecompressBlock is fed the attacker-controlled ObjectSize; a decompression-bomb resource-exhaustion path exists but no memory-safety defect was shown within this code.
On 4D multi-frame input, BImgBuff is re-allocated on each NEXT_FRAME pass after being freed, causing a per-frame leak with no proven exhaustion path.
The ping path also skips the 90-degree rotation applied on the normal path; this is a semantic/cosmetic difference only.

verdict.summary: In the MATLAB (MAT) coder, when image_info->ping is true the code jumps to done_reading, skipping the raster-buffer allocation (and RelinquishMagickMemory re-null handling is bypassed on the next iteration). On the next pass through NEXT_FRAME for a complex cell (FLAG_COMPLEX), CalcMinMax/ReadBlobDoublesXXX/ReadBlobFloatsXXX/InsertComplexDoubleRow/InsertComplexFloatRow are called with BImgBuff, which is still NULL (or the stale freed buffer), producing a NULL-pointer dereference or, when BImgBuff was freed via the ExitLoop/Relinquish path in an earlier frame, a use-after-free/heap overflow with attacker-controlled MATLAB header data. Additionally, image->colors = one << image->depth is computed without validating image->depth (attacker-controlled via CellType up to 64), causing the shift to wrap and producing an undersized/incorrect color count; combined with sample sizes and SizeX/SizeY read directly from the file, the allocation BImgBuff = AcquireQuantumMemory(ldblk,sizeof(double)) and the per-row reads of ldblk bytes can overflow the buffer when SizeX/SizeY are inconsistent.

evidence.reason: When image_info->ping is true, this branch jumps directly to done_reading, skipping BImgBuff = AcquireQuantumMemory(ldblk,sizeof(double)) and leaving BImgBuff NULL. After AcquireNextImage the loop continues to the next object/NEXT_FRAME; for a FLAG_COMPLEX miDOUBLE/miSINGLE cell, ReadBlobDoublesXXX(image2, ldblk, (double *)BImgBuff) and InsertComplexDoubleRow(image, (double *)BImgBuff, ...) then operate on the NULL/stale BImgBuff — the read/write sinks require a non-NULL allocated buffer of at least ldblk bytes and this code never guarantees it on the ping path. Trigger: a MAT file with a second miMATRIX object whose StructureFlag has FLAG_COMPLEX and CellType miDOUBLE, read with ping=1. Root cause: exceptional-condition/failure path skips required allocation and validation (leads to NULL-pointer dereference / heap buffer overflow).

image->depth is derived from the attacker-controlled CellType (8/16/32/64) without bounds validation; one is size_t (typically 64-bit) with value 1. one << 64 is undefined behavior (shift >= width of promoted type) and wraps the color count to 0 on typical builds, while image->colors is later used for palette/quantum handling. No check enforces depth < 64 before the shift. Trigger: CellType miUINT64/miINT64/miDOUBLE (depth=64) with any SizeX/SizeY. Root cause: missing validation of attacker-supplied depth feeding a shift — integer overflow/undefined shift (CWE-190).

After decompression (image2 != image), the first unknown4 read consumes 4 bytes, then the second read re-fills it, but MATLAB_HDR.StructureClass (from unknown5, read before) is only validated for the original image stream, not the re-read/reordered values from the decompressed image2 stream; downstream z2qtype[z] indexing and the StructureClass whitelist check (which happens BEFORE this re-read) do not cover the actual data path used. The sink ImportQuantumPixels(...,z2qtype[z],...) requires z < 4 (valid z2qtype index) and a StructureClass consistent with CellType; this code enforces neither on the decompressed path. Trigger: miCOMPRESSED DataType whose decompressed stream is a miMATRIX with DimFlag 12 (z up to 4) — wait, z!=3 rejected; for DimFlag 16, z may be 1 or 3, and z2qtype[z] with z==3 is used while StructureClass validation ran against values read from the compressed stream, allowing mismatched StructureClass/CellType and z2qtype[3] (RGB) with a StructureClass that ImportQuantumPixels interprets per a different quantum type. Root cause: input validation performed on the wrong stream (missing validation at the trust boundary of the decompressed data), enabling type confusion in pixel import.

assumptions: The build enables the ZLIB delegate so DecompressBlock and the image2 path are compiled; the ping/complex findings do not depend on this.
ReadBlobDoublesXXX/ReadBlobFloatsXXX return void and perform no bounds/NULL checks internally (they are thin wrappers over ReadBlob in ImageMagick's blob.c), so a NULL BImgBuff is dereferenced.
one is size_t and image->depth is a size_t field, so one << 64 is a shift by the full width — undefined behavior, wrapping to 0 on common builds.
Line numbers are 1-based over the function as given, counting each statement line in the provided snippet.
limitations: The `if (image->columns == 0 || image->rows == 0) goto MATLAB_KO;` check occurs AFTER AcquireQuantumInfo and the `one << image->depth` shift; the depth overflow still happens before any rejection, so the overflow itself is already executed — but its only downstream use is image->colors and the post-loop row/column==0 filter, limiting impact to a wrong colors value rather than a crash; recorded as a secondary, lower-severity defect rather than a primary memory-safety trigger.

RelinquishMagickMemory(BImgBuff) at the bottom of the while loop sets BImgBuff=NULL only after the AcquireNextImage branch; if AcquireNextImage fails (image->next == NULL) the function breaks out with BImgBuff still allocated (double-free risk is avoided because the final RelinquishMagickMemory(BImgBuff) at the end also runs — this is a leak/potential double-relinquish pattern, but RelinquishMagickMemory tolerates being called on an already-relinquished pointer only if it was set NULL; here it is not, giving a potential double free. I could not prove the exact free twice reachability because the loop-break path also passes through the final RelinquishMagickMemory with the same non-NULL pointer, which would be a second free; this is recorded as a candidate but the control flow of DestroyImageList in ThrowReaderException makes it uncertain, so it is not elevated to a confirmed finding.

Frames = ReadBlobXXXLong(image2) for DimFlag 16 is attacker-controlled and used as the NEXT_FRAME loop counter with no upper bound; combined with per-frame allocations this is a resource-exhaustion/DoS path, not memory corruption — noted as a robustness limitation.

The rotation/AppendImageToList/DeleteImageFromList block swaps blob pointers between images; failure of RotateImage leaves the original image returned while rotated_image is destroyed elsewhere — no memory-safety defect proven.
MATLAB_HDR fields are read as raw longs/shorts into a struct without a packed layout guarantee; this is a portability concern, not a proven vulnerability.

verdict.summary: pjstun_parse_msg dereferences the attribute header's length field ((*attr)->length at p_attr+2..p_attr+3) without first verifying that at least sizeof(pjstun_attr_hdr) (4) bytes of message body remain; the loop condition only requires msg_len > 0. Because msg_len is attacker-controlled via the STUN length field (only checked against buf_len-20, not for a 4-byte minimum or 4-byte alignment), a network packet whose body leaves 1-3 trailing bytes (e.g., buf_len=21 with length field=1, or a final attribute consuming all but 1-3 bytes) makes the parser read up to 3 bytes past the end of the buffer — an out-of-bounds read on attacker-controlled network input.

evidence.reason: This statement reads (*attr)->length, i.e., bytes p_attr+2 and p_attr+3, but the enclosing loop (line 36) admits msg_len values of 1, 2, or 3, for which p_attr+2..p_attr+3 lie past buf+buf_len (invariant: p_attr + msg_len == buf + buf_len, established at line 34 and preserved by lines 45/60/61). The msg_len < len check at line 45 executes only after this dereference and cannot protect it. Trigger: a STUN Binding Request with buf_len=21, header length field=0x0001, 16-byte transaction id and 1 trailing byte — the read touches buf[22..23], up to 3 bytes out of bounds; equally reachable with buf_len=25 and a first attribute of length field 0 leaving msg_len=1. Root cause: missing minimum-length validation before the attribute-header dereference (CWE-125).

assumptions: sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr) == 20 (type 2 + length 2 + transaction id 16) and sizeof(pjstun_attr_hdr) == 4, per RFC 3489 STUN as implemented by pjlib-util.
PJ_ARRAY_SIZE(msg->attr) >= 1, so the loop is entered when msg_len > 0.

buf_len accurately reflects the extent of valid/allocated data in buf; with exact-sized buffers the line-42 read is a true out-of-bounds heap/stack read, while with over-large fixed receive buffers it reads uninitialized bytes past the datagram end (still a spec violation of the length contract, no leak since the value only feeds the failing msg_len < len check).
limitations: Lines 11 and 26 read msg->hdr->type and msg->hdr->length before any check that buf_len >= sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr); for buf_len < 4 this reads past the data length, but it is only a memory-safety violation if the caller's allocation equals buf_len — typical callers pass a fixed-size receive buffer, so this is recorded as a robustness gap, not a confirmed vulnerability.
The unsigned subtraction buf_len - sizeof(pjstun_msg_hdr) wraps for buf_len < 20, but a 16-bit msg_len can never equal the wrapped value, so the message is rejected with no bypass.

The out-of-bounds-read value is never used beyond computing len, which then fails the msg_len < len check (len >= 4 > msg_len), so information-leak impact is nil; impact is limited to potential crashes on boundary-aligned allocations and reads of uninitialized memory.
Unknown attribute types are warned about but still counted and their lengths enforced, and the msg->attr[] array is bounded by attr_max_cnt, so no separate overflow exists there.

verdict.summary: The Compute method of LoadAndRemapMatrix validates only the sizes of the remapping inputs, never their values: old row IDs taken from the attacker-controlled row_remapping tensor are reduced to min_old_row/max_old_row (lines 20-29) and used to build TensorSlice start/length (lines 118-119) without ever being compared against the old checkpoint tensor's actual row count, tensor_shape.dim_size(0), even though that shape was just looked up (lines 74-75). An old-row ID at or beyond the tensor's row count produces an out-of-bounds slice that is passed to TensorSlice::SliceTensorShape and BundleReader::LookupSlice (lines 141-149), causing reads past the end of the stored tensor data (out-of-bounds read / crash / denial of service); the same missing bound also permits slice-length overflow and huge allocations with IDs near INT64_MAX. The output-matrix write itself is guarded, so the defect is confined to the unvalidated read-path construction.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing input validation (CWE-20) at the trust-boundary intake of row_remapping. min_old_row/max_old_row derive solely from attacker-controlled row_remapping values, which are only size-checked against num_rows_ (line 9) and never bounded by the old tensor's row count tensor_shape.dim_size(0) fetched at lines 74-75. Trigger: with a checkpoint tensor of shape [3,4] and row_remapping=[1000] (num_rows_=1), min=max_old_row=1000, so lines 118-119 build a slice starting at row 1000 of a 3-row tensor; the out-of-range slice flows to SliceTensorShape/LookupSlice (lines 141-149) and reads past the end of the stored tensor (CWE-125, crash/OOB read). Upstream TensorFlow fixed this exact defect by adding a max_old_row < tensor_shape.dim_size(0) OP_REQUIRES at this point.

assumptions: Op inputs (row_remapping, col_remapping, ckpt_path, old_tensor_name, initializing_values) are attacker-influenced under the TensorFlow raw-op threat model; the checkpoint bundle is attacker-supplied.

RemapVectorToMap (not shown) populates old→new maps and resizes the ids_present vectors to the remapping vector length, so the enforced size checks (row_remapping.size()==num_rows_, col_remapping.size()==num_cols_) bound new_row/new_col; the output write is additionally explicitly guarded.

TensorSlice::SliceTensorShape and BundleReader::LookupSlice (not shown) do not independently reject slices whose row range exceeds the stored tensor's dim 0, consistent with the upstream fix that added exactly that validation inside this op.
old_tensor_name is registered as an unconstrained-shape string tensor, so non-scalar shapes reach line 66.
limitations: Line 66 reads old_tensor_name via scalar<tstring>() with no NumElements==1 check, unlike ckpt_path (lines 57-61); if Tensor::scalar() CHECK-fails on element count, a shape-[2] string input aborts the process (DoS). Not counted as confirmed evidence because scalar()'s CHECK behavior is outside the given code.

Loop counters `int i`/`int row`/`int old_col` compare against int64 dims (lines 20, and the copy loops); they would overflow for tensors with >2^31 rows, but reaching that first requires allocating an output matrix with >2^31 rows and an equally large row_remapping, so this is treated as robustness, not a distinct vulnerability.

Very large row IDs (e.g., near INT64_MAX) also cause signed overflow in `max_old_row - row_start + 1` and oversized slice allocations/OOM; these are alternate manifestations of the same confirmed missing-bounds defect, not separate findings.

Resource usage (BundleReader scanning, per-slice logging at line 139) grows with the number of slices; bounded by max_old_row and max_rows_in_memory_, no distinct exhaustion path beyond the confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: When col_remapping is supplied, its old-column IDs are never validated against the loaded checkpoint tensor's second dimension. The copy loop only iterates the old tensor's actual columns (old_col < dim_size(1)), so any new column mapped from a nonexistent old column is flagged present in col_id_present, never written during the copy phase, and skipped by the initializing_values fill (which only fills cells where present flags are false). The op then succeeds and returns an output matrix containing uninitialized heap memory (information disclosure). Additionally, old_tensor_name is consumed via scalar<tstring>()() without the NumElements==1 check that ckpt_path receives, so a multi-element string input aborts the process (CHECK failure DoS).

evidence.reason: Root cause / sink: this loop only copies columns that physically exist in the old tensor, yet nothing in the code validates that every old-column ID in col_remapping is < tensor_shape.dim_size(1) (the analogous num_cols_ == dim_size(1) check at line 98 is skipped when remap_cols is true). Trigger: num_rows_=1, num_cols_=2, row_remapping=[0], col_remapping=[0,5], checkpoint tensor of shape [1,1] DT_FLOAT, initializing_values=[]. New column 1 (old column 5) is marked present by RemapVectorToMap, is never reached by this loop (dim_size(1)==1), and is skipped by the initializing_values fill at line 219 because both presence flags are true; the op returns successfully with an uninitialized heap cell in output_matrix (CWE-908 / CWE-20 information disclosure).

Missing input validation: the scalar<tstring>() accessor CHECK-requires the tensor to have exactly one element, but unlike ckpt_path (checked at lines 62-66) this input's NumElements is never validated here. Trigger: an old_tensor_name tensor containing 2 string elements passes the unguarded context->input() and aborts the process via CHECK failure — a reachable crash (DoS) from attacker-controlled runtime input.

assumptions: RemapVectorToMap (not shown) sets row_id_present/col_id_present[new_id]=true for entries with non-negative old IDs and sizes the vectors to the input vector length (== num_rows_/num_cols_, enforced here at lines 14 and 47-51).

TensorSlice::SliceTensorShape and BundleReader::LookupSlice enforce slice extents against tensor_shape, so out-of-range old ROW IDs fail closed with a status error rather than reading out of bounds; if they did not, the row dimension would share the same uninitialized-output defect.
Input dtypes are enforced by the op registration framework, so the dtype CHECKs inside vec<>/flat<>/scalar<> are not reachable via a wrong dtype.
limitations: Same-class missing shape validation as the evidenced CHECK-fail: col_remapping's rank is not checked before col_remapping_t->vec<int64_t>() at line 41 (row_remapping IS rank-checked at lines 8-12), so a rank-2 col_remapping also aborts via CHECK failure.

Extreme row_remapping values (e.g., INT64_MAX) make the slice-building while loop (lines 117-127) iterate an enormous number of times and can overflow the signed expression 'max_old_row - row_start + 1'; impact is resource exhaustion/hang (DoS) with no memory-safety or disclosure effect, so it is not counted as a vulnerability.
ckpt_path permits reading attacker-chosen files; this is the op's documented purpose (checkpoint loading) and no additional trust boundary is crossed.

The initializing_values handling is fully bounds-checked and fail-closed (lines 219-224 and 231), and the output write guard at lines 190-192 correctly bounds-checks new_row/new_col before output_matrix access.

verdict.summary: No reachable memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, input-validation, or authz defect exists in njs_await_fulfilled as written. The only attacker-influenced input is the promise-resolved value, which is consumed exclusively as a well-formed njs_value_t (copied into a scope slot, vm->retval, and re-entered into the interpreter), never as a raw pointer, length, format string, path, or command. Frame/level state save-restore is balanced on every exit path (the early 'goto failed' precedes all mutation; the interpreter-error path follows full restore), and ctx is freed exactly once on terminal paths and legitimately retained on NJS_AGAIN. Dismissed candidates (OOM-path ctx leak, unhandled interpreter return codes, retval aliasing in njs_function_call, and the ECMAScript-semantics deviation where a promise fulfilled with an Error is treated as a rejection) are robustness/semantics issues without security impact or are prevented by engine contracts.

assumptions: njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) returns a valid njs_value_t (undefined) when nargs < 2, per the njs helper contract; it does not read out of bounds.
njs_function_call copies 'this' and args into the callee frame before invocation, so passing &vm->retval simultaneously as args and retval (lines 49-50, 71-72) causes no use-after-overwrite.
njs_vmcode_interpreter returns only NJS_OK, NJS_AGAIN, or NJS_ERROR; therefore the fall-through at line 67 is unreachable.
ctx->capability and ctx->await are non-NULL engine-saved state established when the async context is created, before this handler can run.
limitations: Memory-error path (lines 58-59) returns without calling njs_async_context_free, leaking ctx. Bounded single allocation on a terminal VM OOM state with no exhaustion path; not security-relevant.

Fulfilled promise value that is an Error object is routed to the rejection handler (lines 13-15), deviating from ECMAScript await semantics where fulfillment with an Error does not throw. Correctness/semantics deviation only; no memory-safety or authorization impact.
If the interpreter contract ever allowed a fourth return code, the promise would never settle and ctx would leak; not reachable per the contract assumed above.

verdict.summary: ComparisonQuantized validates only input1's element type (line 3) before treating both inputs as input_dtype. input2->type and output->type are never checked, yet GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2) is a raw reinterpret_cast of the model-supplied tensor's data buffer. A model declaring input1 as INT8/UINT8 and input2 as a different type (e.g. FLOAT32, or a handle type with no data buffer) passes the only guard this code performs, so the comparison kernels read input2's bytes as input_dtype: type-confused garbage comparisons, or a null-pointer dereference crash when the buffer is absent. The root cause is missing trust-boundary validation of tensor metadata in this function.

evidence.reason: Unvalidated use: input2 comes from the serialized model (trust boundary), but its type is never inspected in this code. GetTensorData<input_dtype>() is a reinterpret_cast of tensor->data.raw, so a model with input1 INT8 and input2 FLOAT32 reaches this sink and input2's buffer is read as input_dtype — type confusion. The same unvalidated use exists on the broadcast path at line 26. If input2 is a handle/variant tensor with a null data buffer, the element-wise read dereferences null and crashes.

The missing check: the only type validation in the function inspects input1->type alone. input2->type and output->type are accepted unvalidated before the reinterpret-cast uses at lines 25-27 and 30-32, so a mismatched-type model (attacker-controlled tensor metadata crossing the trust boundary) produces the defective path entirely within inputs this code permits.

assumptions: input_dtype/opname are the template parameters of the enclosing kernel; GetTensorData<T> is TFLite's reinterpret_cast on tensor->data.raw with no release-build type check
Tensor type, quantization params, shape, and data all originate in the model file and are treated as untrusted

In the shipped TFLite file, ComparisonPrepare separately enforces input1->type == input2->type and output->type == kTfLiteBool; that guard is not part of this code as given, and per the re-examination step the intake validation cannot be deferred to it
limitations: Reading a wider-typed buffer (e.g. FLOAT32 read as INT8) stays within the buffer since every element type occupies at least one byte, so this path yields type-confused/garbage results rather than an out-of-bounds read; memory-safety impact is limited to a possible null dereference with handle-typed input2

Unchecked output->type (GetTensorData<bool> at lines 27/32) writes N bytes into a possibly larger buffer, leaving bytes uninitialized for a downstream reader; this is the same missing-validation defect recorded as a secondary consequence
The silent no-op when input1->type is neither UINT8 nor INT8 leaves output unwritten, but reaching it requires caller dispatch that this code neither parses nor controls — robustness issue only
requires_broadcast is trusted caller-derived state; a wrong value would make the non-broadcast kernel index mismatched shapes, but no boundary data can set it within this code
QuantizeMultiplier tolerates scale==0 (writes 0,0), so garbage zero_point/scale for a non-quantized input2 cause only computational garbage, not memory unsafety

verdict.summary: njs_await_fulfilled resumes a suspended async frame. The only trust-boundary input it consumes (the promise resolution value, args[1]) is validated (error values routed to reject; otherwise copied by value into an engine-managed scope slot), and all dangerous operations (scope write via ctx->index, frame/level save-restore, capability resolve/reject calls, ctx free) depend on invariants established by the VM's own await machinery that runtime attacker data cannot alter. Every candidate defect (ctx leak on the memory-error early return, discarded reject-call return, missing NULL checks on machinery-owned pointers, hypothetical re-entrancy/double-invocation UAF, shared function->context state) either requires an environment failure such as OOM or a contract violation by code outside this function, so none is an exploitable vulnerability in this code as written.

assumptions: ctx->index, ctx->pc, ctx->await and ctx->capability are created by njs_vmcode_await at suspension time from compiled bytecode and internal objects, not from runtime attacker-controlled data, so the scope write at '*njs_scope_value(vm, ctx->index) = *value' is in-bounds for the preserved async frame.
njs_arg(args, nargs, 1) returns a well-formed njs_value_t (undefined if absent); the promise machinery passes a normalized resolution value.
The promise resolve/reject functions called here do not synchronously execute attacker-authored jobs (microtasks are queued and run later), so no re-entrancy into this path while ctx is alive occurs.
njs_function_apply marshals arguments into the callee frame before writing the destination retval, so passing &vm->retval as both argument and retval output is safe.
The internal fulfilled-callback function object holding context = ctx is not exposed to scripts, so it cannot be captured and re-invoked after njs_async_context_free.
limitations: Memory-error early return (the 'if (njs_is_memory_error(...)) return NJS_ERROR;' branch) frees neither ctx nor ctx->capability — a resource leak (CWE-401-style) on OOM paths, with no exhaustion path reachable from this code; robustness only.
The failed path discards the return value of the reject call with '(void)', so an OOM failure inside reject leaves status unreported; robustness only.
No NULL validation of vm->top_frame->function->context before use; safe only because the await machinery always installs the context before invoking this callback.

function->context and function->await live on the shared function object; a re-entrant invocation of the same async function during the resumed interpreter run could in principle interleave with the save/clear sequence here, but any resulting mis-read would occur in VM code outside this function and no concrete trigger was provable from this code alone.

verdict.summary: ComparisonQuantized validates only input1->type (kTfLiteUInt8/kTfLiteInt8) and never checks input2's dtype or quantization metadata, yet it consumes input2->params.scale/zero_point (lines 5, 14) and reinterprets input2's raw buffer via GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2) (lines 28, 33), inferring input2's element type solely from input1; output is likewise assumed bool without a type check. Tensor type, shape, and quantization parameters all derive from the parsed model file (the trust boundary), so a crafted model declaring input1 as int8/uint8 and input2 as a different dtype (e.g., float32) reaches a type-confused comparison path and feeds a non-quantized/uncontrolled scale into QuantizeMultiplierSmallerThanOneExp, whose 0 < scale <= 1 precondition is enforced only by release-compiled-out DCHECKs. The one-sided type guard is the missing trust-boundary validation and the root cause of the type confusion.

evidence.reason: This guard is the function's only dtype validation and it checks only input1; input2's type is never verified anywhere in this code before input2's quantization params are consumed (lines 5 and 14) and input2's raw buffer is reinterpreted as input_dtype via GetTensorData<input_dtype>(input2) (lines 28 and 33). Trigger: a crafted model file (trust boundary) declaring input1 as kTfLiteInt8/kTfLiteUInt8 and input2 as a different dtype (e.g., kTfLiteFloat32) — the branch at this line is taken, a non-quantized input2's params.scale (typically 0.0) is passed to QuantizeMultiplierSmallerThanOneExp, violating its documented 0 < scale <= 1 precondition (DCHECK-only, absent in release builds), and input2's buffer is then read as input_dtype elements, producing a type-confused access. The missing symmetric type/quantization check at the model-data intake boundary is the root-cause defect (CWE-843).

assumptions: TfLiteTensor type, shape, quantization parameters, and buffer contents derive from a parsed .tflite model file; untrusted/crafted models are the threat model, so tensor metadata is attacker-influenced data crossing a trust boundary.

GetTensorData<T> is the era-consistent unchecked reinterpret_cast of the tensor's raw buffer; if a type-checked variant returning nullptr is used, the same defect manifests as a null-pointer dereference (crash/DoS) instead of a misread.
The snippet is analyzed in isolation; upstream kernel Prepare/dispatch code is not shown and, per the rules, cannot be assumed to supply validation.
limitations: Candidate B (template input_dtype wider than runtime input1->type, e.g., an <int32_t> instantiation reached with input1->type == kTfLiteInt8, causing ~4x out-of-bounds reads of input1/input2 buffers): dismissed because it requires the caller to instantiate the template inconsistently with its input1->type-based dispatch, violating a contract this code's own usage model fixes.

Candidate C (missing else: if input1->type is neither kTfLiteUInt8 nor kTfLiteInt8 the function silently writes nothing, leaving the output tensor uninitialized): dismissed as a confirmed vulnerability because it is reachable only if the caller routes non-quantized dtypes to this quantized helper, contradicting the intended dispatch; output allocation/initialization is the framework's responsibility. Robness concern only.

Candidate D (attacker-controlled params.scale outside (0,1] violating QuantizeMultiplierSmallerThanOneExp's precondition, which is DCHECK-only): reachable but within this code yields invalid fixed-point values, wrong comparison results, and debug-build aborts — no memory-safety failure inside this function; impact folded into the primary finding.

Candidate E (broadcast/shape compatibility never re-validated here): requires_broadcast and shape equality are computed by the caller from the same tensors; no constraint this code can itself contradict.

Output dtype is never verified to be kTfLiteBool (GetTensorData<bool>(output)); bool writes are 1 byte per element, so no buffer overflow is demonstrable for any output dtype — noted, not a separate vulnerability.

No out-of-bounds access is demonstrable for the reachable 1-byte input_dtype paths (input2 of a wider dtype is under-read), so severity is assessed medium (type-confused access, contract-violating scale, possible crash) rather than high.

verdict.summary: mobi_decode_infl consumes attacker-controlled rule bytes but every memory sink (memmove, decoded[pos] read/write) is preceded by a guard checking pos < 0, l < 0, and end-pointer against decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX. Negative pos drift from the c in 11..19 branch (pos -= c-10) is caught at the next use; the out-of-range pointer formations are followed by the same guard before any dereference.

assumptions: decoded is a buffer of at least INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX bytes and *decoded_size <= INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX on entry (caller contract in libmobi)
debug_print is compiled to a no-op unless DEBUG is enabled
limitations: Forming pointers d = decoded + pos / s = decoded + pos + 1 with pos == -1 (after pos-- in the delete branch with dir '<' when pos==0, or after negative drift) is technically UB pointer arithmetic, but the pos < 0 guard returns before any dereference, so there is no memory access on that path.

Sustained rule bytes 11..19 with no other byte could theoretically underflow pos toward INT_MIN (requiring ~238MB of rule data), making l = *decoded_size - pos signed-overflow; in practice the overflowed l would be negative and caught by the l < 0 check, and any interleaved byte triggers the pos < 0 check first.

debug_print("...%s...", decoded, pos) passes a possibly non-NUL-terminated buffer as a string; if debug output is enabled this can over-read past INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX. This is an error-path diagnostic dependent on build configuration, not the primary data-processing path, so it is recorded rather than confirmed.
debug_print format string mismatches (passing int pos for %i is correct, but decoded as %s) — diagnostics only.

verdict.summary: do_i2c_md accepts a fully attacker-controlled length from the console without any range or sign validation: a length with bit 31 set (e.g. 'i2c md 50 0.2 80000000') converts to a negative int at 'nbytes = length;' and the one-sided clamp at line 70 copies that negative value into linebytes, which is then passed as the byte count to dm_i2c_read()/i2c_read() writing into the fixed 16-byte stack array linebuf — the sink's non-negative, <=DISP_LINE_LEN precondition is never enforced (potential stack buffer overflow). Additionally, get_alen()'s -1 error sentinel bypasses the 'if (alen > 3)' intake check (which cannot reject negatives) and is passed unvalidated to legacy i2c_read() on non-DM builds, whereas the DM path guards it with 'alen != -1' — a fail-open validation gap.

evidence.reason: This clamp enforces only the upper bound of the read length. length comes from hextoul(argv[3], NULL) (line 48) with no validation; for argv[3]="80000000", length=0x80000000 and nbytes=(int)length=-2147483648 (line 65), so linebytes becomes negative and is passed as the length to dm_i2c_read(dev, addr, linebuf, linebytes) / i2c_read(chip, addr, alen, linebuf, linebytes), which fill the 16-byte stack buffer linebuf. The sink precondition (0 <= len <= DISP_LINE_LEN) is violated by a value produced purely from console input; the missing lower-bound/range validation is the root cause (CWE-20 / CWE-190 signedness).

The intake check for the attacker-influenced address-length argument only rejects alen > 3 and cannot reject get_alen()'s -1 error sentinel (whose existence is proven by the 'alen != -1' guard on line 53). For a malformed argv[2] such as "0.12345", alen = -1 passes this check and, on non-DM builds (the #else branch at line 75), is passed unvalidated to i2c_read(chip, addr, -1, linebuf, linebytes), whose alen must be in 0..3 — a fail-open input-validation gap at this code's own parsing boundary.

assumptions: Attacker is anyone able to enter U-Boot console commands; per the task, CLI arguments are attacker-influenced inputs crossing a trust boundary.
get_alen() (not shown) can return -1 as an error sentinel, as evidenced by the 'alen != -1' guard in the DM path.
DISP_LINE_LEN is 16, so linebuf is a 16-byte stack array, and dm_i2c_read()/i2c_read() write len bytes into it on success.
Two's-complement uint-to-int conversion on the platform toolchain, so hextoul("80000000") yields a negative nbytes.

The actual out-of-bounds write occurs inside the callee (bus driver) which is outside the reviewed code; some drivers skip loops for negative len (no write) while others widen/truncate the negative length and can overflow the 16-byte buffer. The defect confirmed here is this code failing to enforce the sink's length precondition.
limitations: Huge but in-range lengths (e.g. 0x7FFFFFFF) produce extremely long-running dumps — an availability/DoS concern inherent to the command's semantics, no memory-safety impact.

If a bus driver returned success without filling linebuf, the print loops would emit uninitialized stack bytes; this requires the callee to violate its own success contract and leaks only to the same console.
chip (argv[1]) is not validated as a legal 7/10-bit I2C address; downstream probe/read failure is handled — functional, not security.
The alen == -1 finding requires a non-DM_I2C build configuration; on DM builds it is mitigated by the 'alen != -1' guard.

verdict.summary: The U-Boot 'i2c md' handler validates every security-relevant precondition at its sinks: argv[1..3] access is guarded by the argc<3/argc>3 checks, alen is rejected when >3 (which also catches get_alen's -1 error return of 0xffffffff as unsigned), the per-line read length is clamped to DISP_LINE_LEN so linebuf[DISP_LINE_LEN] cannot be overflowed, nbytes-linebytes cannot underflow and the do/while always terminates, and dev is only passed to dm_i2c_read after the error-return guard following i2c_get_cur_bus_chip. The repeat path reloads globals that are only ever stored post-validation. No memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, injection, or fail-open defect is reachable. Residual issues are robustness-only: an unbounded 'length' argument can stall the console for a very long time (the operator already has privileged shell access), and unparsable hex silently maps to 0.

verdict.summary: No reachable vulnerability found in fiber_switch as written. All attacker-influenced inputs (fiber object, argument count/values, resume-vs-transfer path) flow to sinks that are guarded on every reachable path: the fiber-status gate raises before any state mutation for double-resume/dead/transferred-resume cases; the argument copy loop is preceded by mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2) executed on the already-switched context, bounding the writes; the MRB_PROC_ENV(c->cibase->proc) dereference is guarded by the proc NULL check (guard and sink fields coincide on all reachable CREATED states where ci==cibase); and the c->ci[1].stack[0] write in the vmexec resume path always lands on an allocated caller frame because suspension implies a pushed C frame whose push guaranteed callinfo capacity. The only theoretical defects (len+2 signed overflow near MRB_INT_MAX, envless-proc deref, ci at the last callinfo slot) require states this code cannot produce.

assumptions: len and the argument array a originate from guest Ruby call sites; mrb_int is 64-bit (current mruby default), so len+2 cannot overflow with any constructible argument count.
Fiber blocks are env-bearing procs (Fiber.new requires a block/proc whose constructors attach an environment), so MRB_PROC_ENV does not return NULL on reachable paths.

For a fiber with status MRB_FIBER_CREATED, c->ci == c->cibase holds (set by fiber_init; the ci-- adjustment happens later inside the same branch), so the guard on c->ci->proc covers the c->cibase->proc dereference.
Suspension of a fiber always occurs inside a pushed C-method frame (Fiber.yield/Fiber#transfer), whose ci push enforced callinfo capacity, so ci[1] is allocated.
limitations: len+2 in mrb_stack_extend(mrb, len+2) would signed-overflow only for len near MRB_INT_MAX; no constructible call (allocation limits on argument arrays) can produce such a count, so it is a theoretical hardening note, not a reachable overflow.

The NULL check reads c->ci->proc while the dereference uses c->cibase->proc and additionally assumes a non-NULL env; the textual mismatch cannot diverge on reachable paths (ci==cibase for CREATED fibers), and envless fiber procs are not constructible via Fiber.new, but the redundancy would be safer to fix.

The mrb_raise for 'double resume (current)' fires after fiber_switch_context already mutated mrb->c and the status fields; if the !c->ci->proc state were ever reachable, exception unwinding would proceed with switched context state. The state is not reachable for a CREATED fiber, so no defect exists as written.

c->ci[1].stack[0] = value writes through a frame pointer read from the adjacent callinfo entry; its safety rests on fiber_init/suspension invariants (a pushed C frame always exists as the caller) rather than a local bounds check.

fiber_result and fiber_switch_context are external helpers whose internal contracts could not be audited from this snippet; this analysis assumes they uphold their documented (upstream mruby) invariants.

verdict.summary: In the delete branch of mobi_decode_infl, pos is decremented (line 41) before any lower-bound validation. With rule byte 0x03 (mod='d', dir='<') followed by more delete characters than *decoded_size (e.g., decoded_size=0, rule={0x03,'A'}), pos becomes -1. The guards that follow are provably blind to negative pos: l = *decoded_size - pos = decoded_size+1 >= 0, and d + l = decoded + pos + (decoded_size - pos) = decoded + decoded_size is independent of pos. The code then reads decoded[-1] (line 49) — an unconditional heap out-of-bounds read — and, when that byte matches the rule byte, performs memmove(decoded-1, decoded, decoded_size+1) (line 53), a heap out-of-bounds write below the buffer, and drives *decoded_size negative. After the underflow, switching mod to 'i' via rule byte 0x02 (which leaves dir=='<' so pos is not reset) reaches the insert path with pos=-1, where decoded[pos] = c (line 37) writes an attacker-chosen byte at decoded[-1]. The trigger is entirely attacker-controlled rule data parsed from a MOBI file.

evidence.reason: Root cause: pos is decremented with no pos >= 0 check, and both subsequent guards cannot detect negative pos — with pos=-1, l = decoded_size+1 (not < 0) and d+l = decoded + decoded_size (independent of pos), so both pass. Trigger: rule bytes {0x03,'A'} with *decoded_size=0 leave pos=-1, enabling out-of-bounds access below the buffer start.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with pos=-1 (reached via rule {0x03, <delete char>} once deletes exceed *decoded_size), decoded[pos] reads decoded[-1], one byte before the heap buffer — unconditional on any heap contents. This read occurs before the mismatch check can reject the input.

Out-of-bounds write sink: with pos=-1 and decoded[pos]==c matching, memmove(decoded-1, decoded, l) writes l bytes starting at decoded-1 — a heap buffer underflow write below the buffer start — and (*decoded_size)-- drives decoded_size negative, after which rule byte 0x02 followed by any char reaches the insert path at pos=-1 where decoded[pos] = c (line 37) writes an attacker-chosen byte at decoded[-1].

assumptions: rule and the initial decoded contents/*decoded_size originate from parsed MOBI file data (attacker-controlled) and cross a trust boundary into this function
decoded points to a heap buffer of INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX bytes, per the buffer-end comparison the code itself performs
INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX > 0
limitations: debug_print calls format decoded with %s; if decoded is not NUL-terminated and debug output is compiled in, this could read past the logical string — contingent on instrumentation and caller termination, not confirmed as a vulnerability in this code
The insert path's upper bound was verified safe: d + l = decoded + decoded_size + 1 is checked against decoded + INDX_INFLBUF_SIZEMAX before any write, so no upper-edge overflow exists
The branch for rule bytes 11..19 correctly validates pos with pos < 0 || pos > *decoded_size before use; only the delete branch lacks the lower-bound check

The 1-byte write below the buffer at line 53 and the decoded[pos]=c write at pos=-1 require the heap byte at decoded[-1] to match a rule byte for the delete path to continue; the OOB read at line 49 occurs regardless of this match

verdict.summary: xfrm_migrate() uses the netlink-supplied num_migrate as the loop bound while writing found/migrated state pointers into fixed-size stack arrays x_cur[]/x_new[] of XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (6) entries, with no bound on num_migrate enforced anywhere in this code. With num_migrate > XFRM_MAX_DEPTH and that many migration entries each matching an installed xfrm state, the loop writes past the end of the stack arrays (x_cur[6] = x, then x_new), corrupting adjacent kernel stack memory (the CVE-2017-11600 pattern).

evidence.reason: Root cause: num_migrate is an attacker-controlled count from the XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE netlink message and is used directly as the loop bound, while x_cur/x_new are fixed stack arrays of XFRM_MAX_DEPTH (6) struct xfrm_state pointers. No check in this code bounds num_migrate (or nx_cur/nx_new) below XFRM_MAX_DEPTH before the write; the only sanity call, xfrm_migrate_check, is not shown to enforce this and nothing is enforced at the sink. Trigger: install 7 SAs, then send a migrate message with num_migrate = 7 entries whose old tuples each match an existing state; on the 7th found state nx_cur == 6 and line 31 executes x_cur[6] = x, an out-of-bounds write past the 6-element stack array (line 35, x_new[nx_new] = xc, overflows identically), corrupting adjacent kernel stack.

assumptions: XFRM_MAX_DEPTH is the kernel constant 6, so x_cur and x_new each hold 6 pointers on the stack.

num_migrate and the m[] entries come from a userspace XFRM_MSG_MIGRATE netlink message (reachable with CAP_NET_ADMIN in the target network namespace), i.e., they cross a trust boundary into this kernel code.

xfrm_migrate_check is not part of the shown code; its body cannot be read, and no visible guard bounds num_migrate. The historical fix for this exact defect (CVE-2017-11600) added the num_migrate > XFRM_MAX_DEPTH check, confirming this version lacks it.
limitations: The dir >= XFRM_POLICY_MAX check correctly rejects out-of-range directions; dir is u8 (unsigned), so no negative-value bypass exists. Not a vulnerability.
The restore_state error path consistently puts the old states and deletes the newly created ones, and pol is released on every exit path; no refcount/leak defect found.
xfrm_states_put/xfrm_states_delete only access elements in [0, nx_cur/nx_new), so aside from the overflow itself there is no separate uninitialized-read issue.

A successful trigger requires num_migrate entries that each resolve to an existing xfrm state (the attacker must first create >= XFRM_MAX_DEPTH+1 matching SAs), which raises the bar slightly but does not prevent the overflow.

verdict.summary: mruby's fiber context-switch routine. Every attacker-influenced input is validated at intake or bounds-enforced before its sink: the Fiber object is checked by fiber_check, the fiber state machine rejects double resume/transfer/dead-fiber re-entry via the status switch, and the resume arguments are either copied only after mrb_stack_extend(len+2) (len<15) or packed into a single array after mrb_stack_extend(3) (len>=15). The remaining hazard spots (c->ci[1].stack[0] write, c->ci-- pop, c->prev chain including the root) depend on callinfo/stack-layout invariants maintained by the not-shown VM/context layer and cannot be driven to a memory-safety failure by any input this code accepts, so no reachable vulnerability exists in this code as written.

assumptions: Helper functions used here (fiber_check, fiber_check_cfunc, fiber_switch_context, mrb_stack_extend, fiber_result, MARK_CONTEXT_MODIFY) enforce their documented invariants: fiber_check raises for a non-Fiber self, fiber_check_cfunc raises for contexts stopped in a C function, mrb_stack_extend grows the target stack to at least the requested size before returning, and fiber_switch_context sets the switched-to context's status to MRB_FIBER_RUNNING.

The argument-passing convention of this code revision treats cibase->n == 15 as packed-args (CALL_MAXARGS == 15), so the 3-slot stack extension combined with len = 15 in the len>=15 branch is correct.

A context is mrb->c only while its status is MRB_FIBER_RUNNING (set on entry by fiber_switch_context), so any attempt to resume/transfer the currently running fiber is rejected by the MRB_FIBER_RUNNING case; a residual self-resume gap would require the pre-switched root context to have non-RUNNING status, a state not producible by this code.
limitations: c->ci[1].stack[0] = value (line 57) writes through ci+1 with no bounds check in this function; it relies on the invariant that a fiber suspended under vmexec has a callinfo slot above ci. No trigger is constructible from this code's own logic; violation would be a robustness bug of the external VM layer, not an intake-validation gap here.

c->ci-- (line 36, vmexec/CREATED path) can underflow below cibase only if a created fiber's ci equals cibase; the dummy-callinfo pushed at fiber creation (outside this code) prevents that, and the preceding !c->ci->proc check fires first on that state.

c->prev = resume ? mrb->c : (c->prev ? c->prev : mrb->root_c) (line 27) can create a self-cycle (root_c->prev == root_c) when a fiber transfers back to the root; the only consumer of prev relevant here is Fiber.yield, which rejects yielding from the root fiber elsewhere, so the cycle has no memory-safety effect in this code.

mrb_raise inside the CREATED branch (line 33) fires after fiber_switch_context has already made c the current context; reachable only if a CREATED fiber has ci->proc == NULL, a state this code never produces.

The argument array a is trusted to contain len valid values (mrb_ary_new_from_values / the copy loop); len is never negative-checked here, but it originates from the internal argument-collection convention (mrb_get_args '*'), not from raw attacker bytes, and the len>=15 packing bounds all stack writes to 3 slots.

verdict.summary: ljpeg_start() parses an attacker-controlled JPEG byte stream. The 16-bit marker segment length read from the file is decremented by 2 into an int 'len' with no check that it is non-negative or within sizeof(data), then passed directly as fread's byte count into the fixed 64 KiB stack buffer 'uchar data[0x10000]'. A segment length of 0x0000 or 0x0001 yields len = -2/-1, which converts to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t in fread; if the file contains more than 65536 bytes after the marker, fread writes past the stack buffer, smashing the stack (return address overwrite). Trigger: file beginning FF D8 FF E0 00 00 followed by >64 KiB of data.
