Same u32 overflow class in the last-page end computation: for attacker-controlled size >= 0xFFFFFFE1 (spec-legal u32 total_blocks), `size + 31` wraps, producing a wrong `end` (e.g. size = 0xFFFFFFFF gives end = pptr + 0). On the found path this makes the allocation loop cross pages with a wrapped offset (writing all-ones words on the wrong, re-wrapped low pages) and underflows `*max` at line 123, which is then subtracted from free_blocks at line 124, corrupting the allocator's accounting with a huge value.

assumptions: size (bitmap bit count) derives from the on-disk HFS+ volume header total_blocks (u32) and bitmap file contents derive from the mounted image; both cross the trust boundary and this code imposes no upper bound on size.
PAGE_CACHE_BITS == 4096; u32 arithmetic wraps modulo 2^32.

Trigger values (total_blocks just above 0xFFFFF000 with a fully-set bitmap) are representable and spec-legal u32 values; the crafted image supplies them via mount-time metadata parsing outside this snippet.
limitations: The found-path `goto out` at lines 71-73 (start >= size) leaves the page kmapped: a genuine missing kunmap, but it only exhausts kmap slots on 32-bit highmem kernels; on 64-bit kmap is address-only, so it is a robustness/resource issue, not the primary security verdict.

read_mapping_page return values (lines 17, 57, 104) are not checked; kmap(ERR_PTR) would crash, but producing an error page requires a real I/O failure (broken environment), and beyond-EOF pages of the alloc file mapping are zero-filled rather than errors, so a crafted image alone cannot reach it.

The last-page end pointer rounds size up to a 32-bit word boundary, so padding bits beyond size are read as candidate free bits; the `start >= size` check rejects them before allocation and the only writes past size land in on-disk padding bits inside the last bitmap word (no host out-of-bounds access).
No host-memory out-of-bounds read/write exists inside the kmap'ed page: all writes are bounded by `curr < end` with end <= pptr + PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32, and len is clamped to size - start.

verdict.summary: In hfsplus_block_allocate, the page end pointer is computed as pptr + ((size + 31) & (PAGE_CACHE_BITS - 1)) / 32. When the volume's total block count ends within 31 bits of a bitmap page boundary (size & 32767 >= 32737, e.g. total_blocks = 32737, a perfectly legal volume-header value), the mask discards the round-up carry and end = pptr, i.e. the bound wraps behind curr. The first-partial-word scan (which never checks curr < end) can still find a free bit in that last in-range page, and the allocation loop's page advance (offset += PAGE_CACHE_BITS; read_mapping_page...) lacks the offset >= size break that the scan loop has, so with length remaining the allocator skips past size and marks whole words allocated at block numbers beyond total_blocks, inside pages of the attacker-sized allocation file. It then computes *max = offset + (curr - pptr) * 32 + i - start with offset already beyond size, overstating the allocation (the skipped gap between size and the page end is reported as allocated) and corrupting free_blocks via free_blocks -= *max. A crafted HFS+ filesystem image thus causes out-of-volume block allocation and free-space accounting corruption.

evidence.reason: Faulty end-pointer computation (root cause). When size and the page-aligned offset are in the same bitmap page and the page-relative position of size is >= PAGE_CACHE_BITS-31 (size & 32767 in [32737, 32767]), (size + 31) & 32767 wraps to [0, 30] and the division yields 0, so end = pptr instead of the word just past the last valid bit. The bound therefore sits behind curr (which the unguarded first-partial scan at lines 32-38 can still use to find a free bit < size), so the full-word loops treat the remaining words of the last in-range page as nonexistent. size comes straight from the mounted volume header (trust boundary), so a crafted image with total_blocks = 32737 (or any N*32768 + 32737..32767) triggers it.

Missing termination check on the allocation loop's page advance. Unlike the scan loop, which breaks on 'if (offset >= size)' before reading the next page, this path advances offset unconditionally. With the wrapped end = pptr from line 29 the inner write loop is skipped while len >= 32 remains, so offset jumps to a page whose base is greater than size and the loop then executes '*curr++ = cpu_to_be32(0xffffffff)' at block indices beyond total_blocks (the allocation-file size, and hence the existence of that page, is attacker-chosen via the volume header). *max is subsequently computed with the already-advanced offset, overstating the allocated length and under-decrementing free_blocks.

assumptions: Callers pass size = HFSPLUS_SB(sb).total_blocks read from the volume header and an offset derived from on-disk allocation state, as all in-tree hfsplus callers do.
PAGE_CACHE_BITS = 32768 (4 KiB pages), PAGE_CACHE_BITS/32 = 1024 words per bitmap page.

The HFS+ allocation-file size field in the volume header is attacker-controlled for a mounted crafted image, so read_mapping_page of the page just beyond size can succeed; if it fails instead, the code takes the 'start = size; goto out' path after already dirtying partially marked pages.
Exploitation requires mounting (or otherwise parsing with write access) an attacker-supplied HFS+ filesystem image.
limitations: Error-path accounting leak (lines 109-116 with goto out at 114-117): when read_mapping_page fails after earlier pages were dirtied with allocated bits, free_blocks is not decremented and the caller is told allocation failed, leaking blocks and over-counting free space; integrity/robustness issue, not the primary out-of-range allocation defect.
In the scan loop, the same wrapped end = pptr makes the allocator declare 'bitmap full' while free bits remain in the last page, causing spurious ENOSPC (availability/DoS impact only).

An exact-fill scenario (size % 32 == 0, request ending exactly at size) also crosses pages without the size check, but *max remains numerically consistent and only a zero word beyond EOF is dirtied, so it was not counted as a separate finding.

All pointer writes stay within a kmap'd bitmap page (end never exceeds pptr + 1024 words), so there is no direct kernel-heap out-of-bounds access; the out-of-bounds is relative to the allocation bitmap/volume block range and the free-block accounting.
The (size + 31) addition itself can wrap only for size >= 2^32 - 31; this is subsumed by the mask-carry wrap at line 29, which triggers at far smaller, fully legal values of total_blocks.

verdict.summary: This is the hardened variant of gzip's LZW (unlzw) decoder: every attacker-influenced sink is guarded — maxbits is validated against BITS before table sizing (free_ent < maxmaxcode bounds all table writes), codes above free_ent are rejected fail-closed via gzip_error before any table access, prefix chains strictly decrease so the de_stack walk terminates within the table bounds, and the chunked output-flush loop clamps each memcpy to OUTBUFSIZ-outpos before copying, which closes the historical outbuf overflow on over-long strings. Bit reads are bounded by inbits and buffer refills by INBUF_EXTRA. No reachable memory-safety, integer, lifetime, or fail-open defect could be triggered from data crossing the trust boundary.

assumptions: Standard gzip support definitions are assumed: tab_prefix/tab_suffix arrays sized 1<<BITS (65536 entries), de_stack sized at least the maximum prefix-chain length (free_ent-1 <= maxmaxcode), input() macro reading at most 3 bytes within inbuf plus INBUF_EXTRA slack, MAXCODE(n)=(1<<n)-1, INIT_BITS=9, FIRST=257, CLEAR=256, BIT_MASK<=mask of BITS.
gzip_error and read_error are assumed non-returning/terminating, as in the gzip library this code is part of.
get_byte() at end-of-input is assumed to be handled by the surrounding driver (read_buffer fills inbuf before unlzw is entered).
limitations: Edge-case maxbits values 0-8 are accepted (only maxbits > BITS is rejected); this can cause the code width n_bits to diverge from the declared maxbits on crafted input, but all sinks remain guarded (free_ent < maxmaxcode write guard and code > free_ent error), so the effect is limited to spurious 'corrupt input' errors or literal-only output — robustness only.

The diagnostic block reading p[-1]..p[3] around posbits on the code > free_ent error path would read out of bounds, but it is inside #ifdef DEBUG and therefore absent from this code as written; the path also terminates in gzip_error.

Unchecked write_buf return values and partial-read handling (rsize == 0 ending the loop with data still in inbuf) are robustness issues whose failure requires a broken environment (I/O error), not attacker-controlled memory corruption.

This function matches the fixed version of gzip unlzw.c; the historical output-buffer overflow (copying a decompressed string longer than OUTBUFSIZ in one memcpy) is specifically remediated by the clamped chunked flush loop present here.

parse_errors: no valid JSON verdict found in output

verdict.summary: bmexec_trans from grep's kwset.c contains the complete set of bounds guards: it returns -1 when the minimum pattern length exceeds the buffer (the historical CVE-2015-1341 class fix at 'if (len > size) return -1;'), bounds the skip loop's forward overshoot by the 11*len headroom (10 shifts of at most 255 bytes each plus one delta2 shift against 1+10+1 units of len), constrains the memchr fast-path result to tp <= text+size, and guards every final-loop advance with 'd <= ep - tp' before 'tp += d'. Every text dereference (tp[-1]) was verified to land at index <= size-1 on all reachable paths. The only latent defect found is signed int overflow of '12 * len' and '11 * len' when kwset->mind is ~3.58e8-3.9e8, which would compute 'ep' past the buffer and over-read; realizing it requires a ~360MB single pattern (a multi-gigabyte trie build that fails under realistic memory limits before this function runs) plus a >=360MB search buffer, and its impact is limited to crashing a read-only search. This is recorded as a hardening note, not a confirmed vulnerability.

assumptions: bm_delta2_search (external helper) verifies candidate matches, never dereferences beyond the passed 'ep', and advances *tpp by at least one position when returning false; the 'd == 0' paths rely on this to guarantee progress.
memchr_kwset behaves like memchr restricted to the given length: returns NULL or a pointer strictly inside the scanned range.
kwset->delta is a 256-entry unsigned char table, so every 'd' read from it lies in [0,255]; kwset->mind is a non-negative int produced by the pattern compiler.
kwset fields (mind, delta, target, gc1, gc2, trans) are precomputed by trusted library code; only their magnitudes derive from attacker-supplied patterns.
limitations: Latent signed-overflow hardening issue: 'if (size > 12 * len)' and 'ep = text + size - 11 * len' compute int products that overflow for kwset->mind >= ~357,913,942 (e.g. len=360,000,000: 12*len wraps to 25,032,704 while 11*len wraps to -334,967,296, making 'ep' point ~335MB past the buffer so the skip loop over-reads). Dismissed as a confirmed vulnerability because constructing a kwset with such a minimum pattern length requires a multi-gigabyte trie that fails allocation on realistic hosts before this code runs; impact would be a crash (DoS) of a read-only text filter. Computing the products in size_t would remove the UB.

Progress in the d == 0 paths (final loop and delta2 handoff) depends on the external bm_delta2_search advancing tp on failure; if it did not, the final loop would spin forever. Not verifiable from the given code, so not attributed to this function.
The delta1 lookups index the table by the untranslated byte in the trans (case-insensitive) variant; this affects shift quality, not memory safety, since bm_delta2_search performs exact verification.

verdict.summary: In sftp_mkdir, the error branch for the packet build/write frees 'buffer' and 'path' (lines 32-33) but does not return; execution falls through to lines 35-36 which free the same 'buffer' and 'path' again. Any failure of buffer_add_u32/buffer_add_ssh_string/buffer_add_attributes (OOM) or sftp_packet_write (a socket write failure that a remote peer can induce by tearing down the connection) triggers a double free, corrupting heap metadata, after which execution continues into the read/dispatch loop. The trigger crosses the network trust boundary and the path exists exactly as written, with no ownership or early-return guard.

evidence.reason: Double free (CWE-415): when buffer_add_u32/buffer_add_ssh_string/buffer_add_attributes fails or sftp_packet_write returns < 0 (a condition a remote SFTP peer can force by closing the connection), the failure block at lines 32-33 frees 'buffer' and 'path', then control falls through to lines 35-36 which free both pointers a second time. There is no 'return' and no ownership tracking, so the exact same path releases the same heap objects twice, corrupting allocator metadata before execution continues into the sftp_read_and_dispatch loop.

assumptions: ssh_buffer_free and ssh_string_free release heap allocations and do not NULL their arguments (typical for libssh wrappers); if they were refcounted or NULLing, the double free would be neutralized.
sftp_packet_write failure is inducible by the remote peer (connection teardown), making the trigger cross the network trust boundary; OOM alone would also reach the same path.
limitations: parse_status_msg output 'errormsg' is not NULL-validated before being passed as a %s argument to ssh_set_error; with a literal format string this is at most a robustness issue (undefined/implementation-defined behavior if NULL), not format-string injection.
The 'while (msg == NULL)' loop can stall indefinitely against a never-responding or malicious server (client-side DoS), but a blocking synchronous wait is the documented contract of this client API.

On SSH_FX_FAILURE with an existing path, the function sets SSH_FX_FILE_ALREADY_EXISTS and then overwrites it with SSH_REQUEST_DENIED before returning -1; cosmetic error-reporting quirk with no security impact since the return value still signals failure.
errno_attr from sftp_lstat is released with SAFE_FREE rather than sftp_attributes_free; no defect is demonstrable from this code alone.

verdict.summary: sftp_mkdir correctly validates the server-controlled reply: it checks the packet type before using message fields, NULL-checks parse_status_msg and the sftp_lstat result, passes the server-supplied error string only as a %s argument to a constant format string, and frees msg/status/errno_attr exactly once on every path. All error paths return -1 (fail-closed), and the SSH_FX_OK success path returns 0 explicitly. No memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, injection, or fail-open defect is reachable with inputs this code permits.

assumptions: parse_status_msg returns NULL when the server-supplied error string cannot be extracted, so status->errormsg is non-NULL whenever status is non-NULL (library parser contract).
sftp_dequeue(sftp, id) only returns messages whose id matches the request id, so no cross-request message confusion occurs in the reply-wait loop.
SAFE_FREE frees and NULLs the pointer, preventing a double-free of errno_attr.
limitations: The reply-wait loop 'while (msg == NULL)' has no iteration bound or timeout: a malicious or wedged SFTP server that never sends a reply matching the id can hang the client; however each iteration blocks in sftp_read_and_dispatch on socket I/O, so this is the standard blocking-RPC design of the SFTP layer, not a defect specific to this control flow, and has no memory-safety impact.
If directory is NULL, ssh_string_from_char would dereference it; this requires the caller to violate the documented parameter contract and is not attacker-influenced data.
The 'break;' following 'return 0;' in the SSH_FX_OK case is dead code (cosmetic).

In the SSH_FX_FAILURE + path-exists case, the later ssh_set_error call replaces the human-readable error message, though the EEXIST condition is preserved via the sftp error code set by sftp_set_error; minor functional, not security, behavior.

verdict.summary: The length passed to uni_utf8_get_char_n is computed as (size_t)(p - parser->end), which is always a negative ptrdiff inside the loop (since p < parser->end is the loop invariant) and wraps to a near-SIZE_MAX value when cast to size_t. The UTF-8 decoder therefore believes up to ~2^64 bytes are readable and will read past parser->end when the last byte(s) in the client-supplied buffer begin a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence. A sequence straddling the buffer end can also make p advance beyond parser->end (p += nch), after which i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp) and the trailing-WSP trim loop read out of bounds and state.poff is corrupted. A remote SMTP client triggers this by ending a command line with a truncated UTF-8 lead byte (e.g. 0xF0) exactly at parser->end.

evidence.reason: The length argument is sign-inverted: inside the loop p < parser->end always holds, so p - parser->end is negative and (size_t)(p - parser->end) wraps to a huge value. uni_utf8_get_char_n, which is supposed to be bounds-checked by this length, then reads up to 4 bytes starting at p without an effective limit, reading past the end of the network-supplied input buffer whenever the final byte(s) form a truncated UTF-8 lead sequence (e.g. 0xF0 at parser->end - 1). If the out-of-bounds bytes complete a valid sequence, nch up to 4 advances p past parser->end, and execution reaches i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp) with mp = p > end, a second out-of-bounds read. Trigger: attacker-controlled SMTP command parameter data ending at the buffer boundary with a partial multi-byte UTF-8 character.

assumptions: parser->cur, parser->end, parser->state.poff are consistent buffer bounds/state produced by earlier parser stages (internal trusted state); only the bytes in [cur, end) are attacker-controlled.

uni_utf8_get_char_n(buf, bufsize, chr) reads at most 4 bytes and only up to bufsize bytes; the OOB read arises because bufsize is passed as (size_t)(p - parser->end), a wrapped negative value, instead of parser->end - p.
Memory between parser->end and the allocation containing the buffer may or may not be mapped; the defect is the out-of-bounds read path itself as written.
limitations: The max_parameters_size/max_auth_size check occurs only after scanning the whole parameter region; in the unmodified (correct-length) case the scan is still bounded by the input buffer, so this is a hardening note, not a confirmed vulnerability.

smtp_char_is_textstr((unsigned char)ch) truncation was examined: on the non-auth path it is only reached when (ch & 0x80) == 0 (ch < 128), and on the auth path ch comes from *p (<= 255), so no truncation hazard.

If the bytes immediately past the buffer do not complete a valid UTF-8 sequence, the OOB read in uni_utf8_get_char_n still occurs (values are read and then rejected), but the p-past-end / i_strdup_until OOB path requires a valid completion; both stem from the same faulty length expression.

verdict.summary: The length passed to uni_utf8_get_char_n is computed as (size_t)(p - parser->end). Inside the loop p < parser->end, so the pointer difference is negative; casting it to size_t yields a huge value (~SIZE_MAX) instead of the remaining byte count (parser->end - p). This defeats the decoder's bounds check: when an attacker-supplied SMTP command line ends at parser->end with a multi-byte UTF-8 lead byte, uni_utf8_get_char_n reads up to 3 continuation bytes past the end of the network receive buffer (heap out-of-bounds read) and misclassifies truncated sequences instead of requesting more input.

evidence.reason: The size argument is (size_t)(p - parser->end), but p < parser->end holds inside the while loop, so the signed ptrdiff is negative and the cast produces an enormous size_t (~SIZE_MAX) rather than the remaining length (parser->end - p). The attacker (SMTP client) fully controls buffer contents and can place a multi-byte UTF-8 lead byte (e.g. 0xEF) as the last byte before parser->end; the decoder then reads continuation bytes beyond parser->end — a heap out-of-bounds read on a network-input path, and incomplete trailing sequences are misclassified instead of reported as needing more data.

assumptions: uni_utf8_get_char_n uses its size parameter to bound how many bytes it reads at the given pointer (standard Dovecot unicode API contract: returns 0 when fewer than the sequence length bytes remain, -1 on invalid UTF-8, 1 on success).

parser->cur/parser->end delimit the attacker-controlled SMTP line data received from the network; parser->end may coincide with the end of the allocated stream buffer, so reads past it are out of bounds.
Non-auth command parameters legitimately accept UTF-8, so a lead byte near end of data is a state this code explicitly permits.
limitations: The single-byte branch for auth_response (ch = *p) is correctly guarded by the loop condition p < parser->end.

The size-limit check (uoff_t)(p - parser->cur) > max_size, the trailing-whitespace trim loop, the *parser->cur deref, and i_strdup_until(parser->cur, mp) all have their preconditions enforced by this code and are not vulnerabilities.
Unchecked allocation in i_strdup_until is a robustness concern only (OOM environment), with no exhaustion path in this code.
The initial value nch = 1 combined with the p == parser->end check correctly handles the empty-loop case.

verdict.summary: This test-setup function only registers a fixed set of tests using compile-time constants (the element count of the 'name_fns' array and the address of 'call_run_cert'). It consumes no attacker-influenced data, performs no memory access, indexing, copying, or input validation, and contains no security-relevant sink. No vulnerability is present in this code.

assumptions: ADD_ALL_TESTS and OSSL_NELEM are the standard OpenSSL test-framework macro and array-size macro, whose behavior matches their documented contracts.
name_fns is a visible (complete-type) array declaration, so OSSL_NELEM yields its true element count at compile time.
limitations: The return value of the ADD_ALL_TESTS registration macro is not checked; if the framework failed to register (e.g., under OOM), tests would silently not run. This is a robustness concern in test scaffolding only, with no security impact.

If name_fns were declared extern with an incomplete or mismatched type in another translation unit, OSSL_NELEM could compute a wrong count; no such declaration appears in the given code, so this is not a defect in this snippet.

verdict.summary: setup_tests is a straight-line OpenSSL unit-test registration function. Its only inputs are compile-time constants: a fixed static table (name_fns), its element count via the OSSL_NELEM macro, and two locally defined test callbacks. No trust boundary is crossed: no network data, file contents, serialized state, environment variables, or any runtime attacker-influenced value is read. There are no memory operations, indexing, sizing, copy lengths, format strings, command execution, path handling, or authorization decisions in the function, hence no sink at which an unvalidated value could arrive. Registration macros consume only trusted constants, and their potential failure affects at most test-harness robustness, not any security property of the code under analysis.

assumptions: ADD_TEST / ADD_ALL_TESTS are the standard OpenSSL test-framework registration macros operating on an already-initialized test framework, per the harness's documented call order.
name_fns is a file-scope static array whose size and contents are fixed at compile time, so OSSL_NELEM(name_fns) is a compile-time constant.
limitations: The return values (or failure modes) of the ADD_TEST/ADD_ALL_TESTS registration macros are not checked; a registration failure would only cause a test to be skipped, which is test-infrastructure robustness with no security impact.

The function implicitly depends on the test framework being initialized before it is called; violating that harness contract would crash or misbehave in the test runner only, and no attacker-controlled data can influence this path.
This analysis covers only the code as given; the definitions of name_fns, call_run_cert, test_GENERAL_NAME_cmp, and the ADD_* macros (which live outside this snippet) were not audited.

verdict.summary: All memory accesses driven by the attacker-influenced inputs (text, size) are guarded by checks this function itself enforces: the len>size early return, the 12*len margin gating the skip loop (size > 12 * len), the per-iteration tp <= ep re-check covering the 10 bounded delta advances, the explicitly computed memchr length, and d <= ep - tp before every advance in the tail loop. The pointer-margin arithmetic (1 initial + 10 skip-loop + 1 delta2) is internally consistent, so no reachable out-of-bounds read, write, or integer defect exists in this code as written.

assumptions: kwset->delta (d1), target, gc1/gc2, trans, and mind are module-internal state built by the same component (kwsprep) with the documented invariant that each delta value is at most mind (and physically at most 255, since d1 is 'unsigned char const *'); this function only indexes that table with attacker bytes, it never populates it.

bm_delta2_search either finds a match or repositions *tpp before returning false, so the final loop's 'd != 0' / delta2 alternation always makes progress; this is the same module-internal contract the pointer-out parameter exists to serve.
The U macro is the usual ((unsigned char)(c)) cast, so d1 is indexed only within 0..255.
limitations: Theoretical signed overflow of '12 * len' / '11 * len' would require kwset->mind around 1.8e8 (a single keyword of ~180MB) plus a multi-GB text buffer; under two's-complement wrap semantics the negative product converts to a huge size_t, making 'size > 12 * len' false so the dependent pointer arithmetic is never executed, and under strict semantics such an overflow is not a defined reachable state. Robustness concern only, not a reachable vulnerability here.

If a delta table entry could exceed mind (impossible per the module's construction) the skip loop's 10 unchecked 'tp += d' advances could read past the buffer; this requires the sibling builder to violate its own invariant, not any input this function accepts.
If bm_delta2_search returned false without advancing *tpp while d == 0, the final loop would spin; the actual helper contract (and its pointer-out parameter) prevents this path.

verdict.summary: This three-line handler wrapper passes a server-constructed table path to the engine's file-deletion routine. The path ('name') originates from user DDL but is normalized and canonicalized by the server's identifier-handling layer — the actual trust boundary — before reaching this internal storage-engine API; this code is not an intake point for raw user strings and performs no sink of its own (no indexing, allocation, or memory writes). The discarded return values of ha_close() and maria_delete_table_files() are robustness/observability issues only: the deletion target and authorization state are unaffected by the ignored errors, and the void signature provides no status channel being suppressed. The DBUG_ASSERT on temporariness documents a caller precondition enforced by the server's dispatch. No trigger reachable with inputs this code's contract permits produces a security-relevant defect.

assumptions: The 'name' parameter is supplied by the SQL server layer through the MariaDB handler API as a normalized, canonical table file path under the data directory; the server's identifier validation (rejecting path separators and non-canonical table/database names) runs before this function is reached.
This drop_table entry point is dispatched only on the temporary-table deletion path; base-table drops use the separate delete_table path, matching the DBUG_ASSERT precondition.
DBUG_ASSERT is compiled out in release builds, per standard MySQL/MariaDB build conventions.
limitations: Return values of ha_close() and maria_delete_table_files() are discarded with (void) casts; a failed close followed by file deletion, or a silently failed deletion, can leave internal state inconsistent. This is a robustness/error-handling weakness only — the deleted path is still the caller-validated name and no authorization or memory-safety impact follows.
DBUG_ASSERT(file->s->temporary) provides no runtime enforcement in release builds, so the temporary-table precondition is a documented caller contract rather than a code-level check.
The function performs no NULL check on 'name'; a NULL path would require the server to violate the handler API contract and is not reachable with inputs this code permits.

verdict.summary: This five-line handler forwards an already-canonicalized table path to a file-deletion helper and discards two return values. No attacker-controlled value reaches a memory, length, format, command, or path-construction sink that this code itself fails to constrain: the table-name string is composed and identifier-validated by the SQL server layer before the handler API is invoked, and the code performs no parsing or transformation of it. The ignored return values of ha_close() and maria_delete_table_files() are error-swallowing robustness issues with no security-relevant data flow or fail-open authorization decision, and the DBUG_ASSERT only removes a debug diagnostic in release builds. No reachable, security-impacting trigger exists within this code as written.

assumptions: The `name` parameter is a server-composed canonical table path (e.g., './db/table') whose identifier components were validated by the SQL layer (path metacharacters rejected in identifiers); this function is a handler-API callee, not the intake point for that data.
`maria_delete_table_files` internally handles path joining and reports failures via MY_WME; this code is not responsible for its internal path handling.
limitations: Return value of ha_close() is discarded; a failed close before file deletion is silently ignored (CWE-252 style error swallowing) — robustness impact only, no tainted data flow or authz bypass reachable here.
Return value of maria_delete_table_files() is discarded, so a partially failed deletion is not surfaced to the caller — robustness impact only.

DBUG_ASSERT(!file || file->s->temporary) compiles out in release builds, removing a state sanity check — diagnostic-only, no reachable memory-safety trigger given the class's internal control of `file`.

verdict.summary: In the LOCK TABLES / pre-locked mode path, open_table() finds an already-open table (best_table), calls table->init() and jumps via 'goto reset' without ever assigning the local pointer 'share' (first assigned only at tdc_acquire_share, line 246) while 'from_share' remains false. At 'reset:', the branch 'if (!from_share && table->vcol_fix_expr(thd)) goto err_lock;' can therefore jump to 'err_lock:', where 'tdc_release_share(share)' is called on the uninitialized stack variable. An authenticated user who locks a table containing a generated column whose expression fails to re-fix in a later statement triggers a refcount/locking operation on an arbitrary garbage pointer, causing memory corruption (crash to potential UAF) in the server.

evidence.reason: The err_lock path unconditionally calls tdc_release_share(share), which requires 'share' to be a valid acquired TABLE_SHARE reference. On the locked-tables path (thd->locked_tables_mode != 0 and !(flags & MYSQL_OPEN_GET_NEW_TABLE)), when a matching pre-opened table is found, the code executes 'table= best_table; ... goto reset;' (lines 113-122) without ever assigning 'share' (declared uninitialized at line 9) and with from_share==false. If table->vcol_fix_expr(thd) then fails at line 442, control jumps to err_lock and tdc_release_share dereferences the uninitialized pointer. Trigger: LOCK TABLES on a table with a virtual/generated column whose expression fails fix_fields when re-fixed by a subsequent statement; the branch at line 442 lacks any guard distinguishing the locked-tables path, where no share was acquired.

assumptions: table->vcol_fix_expr(thd) can return nonzero when re-fixing a generated-column expression fails in the current statement context; on the locked-tables path expressions are re-fixed for every statement, so a context-dependent fix failure is sufficient to reach err_lock.

WITH_PARTITION_STORAGE_ENGINE/WITH_WSREP conditionals do not affect the reachability of the uninitialized-share path; the defect is present in all build configurations because 'share' is assigned only after the locked-mode block.

Exploit impact (crash vs. controlled memory corruption) depends on the residual stack contents at the err_lock label, which are attacker-influenced only indirectly; the defect itself (use of uninitialized pointer) is deterministic.
limitations: Under MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK, mdl_ticket is taken from table_list->mdl_request.ticket with no NULL check; this relies on the documented internal caller contract (flag means the caller already acquired the lock), not an external trust boundary.
Return values of ot_ctx->request_backoff_action() are deliberately ignored at lines 368, 400, 406; failure degrades to an error being reported to the user, no fail-open of validation.

On the normal (non-locked) path, jumping to err_lock from line 443 after tc_add_table leaves the newly created TABLE linked in thd->open_tables; its release is delegated to the caller's error cleanup (close_thread_tables), matching the surrounding design, and no dangling reference is created inside this function.
DBUG_ASSERT(table->file->pushed_cond == NULL) at the reset label is compiled out in release builds; all tables reaching reset have a non-NULL handler on every traced path.

verdict.summary: uncompressEntry builds the extraction path directly from the attacker-controlled ZIP entry filename without any traversal or canonicalization validation, allowing Zip-Slip: entries named with '../' segments or absolute paths are written (or, with shouldOverwriteFiles=true, deleted) outside targetDirectory. Additionally, the symlink branch creates a symbolic link whose target is attacker-controlled archive data, enabling second-order arbitrary-file overwrite.

evidence.reason: entryPath derives entirely from zei->entry.filename, an untrusted string parsed from the ZIP archive (the only validation is the isEmpty() check at line 11). getChildFile resolves '..' segments and absolute paths, so an entry named e.g. '../../../../etc/cron.d/pwn' escapes targetDirectory; the code then creates parent directories (line 33), deletes an existing file when overwriting (line 29), and writes attacker-controlled decompressed bytes (lines 46, 51) at the escaped path. Trigger: any crafted archive entry with a traversal/absolute filename — missing trust-boundary validation of archive-controlled paths (CWE-22).

originalFilePath is the fully attacker-controlled decompressed entry payload (line 38) and is used verbatim as the symlink target with no constraint that it be relative or benign. An entry flagged isSymbolicLink plants a symlink at an attacker-chosen location pointing to any absolute path; a later archive entry (or the overwrite delete at line 29) then writes/deletes through that link, achieving arbitrary file overwrite (CWE-59 unvalidated symlink target).

assumptions: JUCE's File::getChildFile resolves '..' segments and returns absolute paths as-is, so traversal/absolute entry names escape targetDirectory (standard JUCE behavior for this class).

entries and their filename/isSymbolicLink/fileTime fields are populated from parsing the ZIP archive, i.e., untrusted file data crossing a trust boundary that this extraction routine is responsible for validating.
This mirrors the known JUCE ZipFile Zip-Slip issue (fixed in later JUCE by validating entry names against traversal).
limitations: entries.getUnchecked(index) performs no bounds check, but index is a caller-supplied loop index into the archive's own entry array, not archive-controlled data within this function; an out-of-range index requires the caller to violate the documented contract, so it was dismissed as a vulnerability here.

Attacker-controlled entry.fileTime is applied via setCreationTime/setLastModificationTime/setLastAccessTime (lines 54-56) with no validation; impact is limited to integrity/cosmetic metadata manipulation, not a security vulnerability.
Non-constant Result::fail strings incorporating file paths are cosmetic (format-string-safe String concatenation); no impact.

verdict.summary: ZipFile::uncompressEntry validates the zip entry's filename against the target directory (isAChildOf), but never validates the target of a symbolic-link entry: the decompressed entry content is read as a path and passed verbatim to File::createSymbolicLink, letting an attacker plant a symlink pointing anywhere on the filesystem (e.g., 'dir/link -> /etc'). Because the only symlink-component defense (hasSymbolicPart) is conditional on followSymlinks == no, a caller using FollowSymlinks::yes (or any later consumer of the extracted tree) can be driven by a second archive entry whose lexical path passes isAChildOf but traverses the planted link, producing an arbitrary file write outside the extraction directory (symlink-based zip-slip).

evidence.reason: The symlink entry's decompressed content (fully attacker-controlled zip data) is converted into a filesystem path and passed directly to File::createSymbolicLink with no containment validation — no isAChildOf check, no canonicalization, no restriction to targetDirectory — unlike the entry filename which IS checked at line 16. Trigger: a zip entry flagged as a symlink whose payload is the string '/etc/passwd' creates targetDirectory/<name> -> /etc/passwd, planting a link to an arbitrary location; a subsequent entry such as '<name>-followup' or, with FollowSymlinks::yes, '<name>/cron-evil' writes outside the target directory through the planted link (CWE-22).

evidence.snippet:
if (followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::no && hasSymbolicPart (targetDirectory, targetFile.getParentDirectory()))
        return Result::fail ("Parent directory leads through symlink for target file: " + targetFile.getFullPathName());
evidence.reason: The only defense against writing through symlinked path components is gated behind followSymlinks == FollowSymlinks::no; with FollowSymlinks::yes the check never executes. Trigger: a two-entry archive — entry A: symlink 'link' -> '/etc' (created via the unvalidated sink at line 47), entry B: regular file 'link/passwd' — passes the lexical isAChildOf check at line 16, skips this guard, and the FileOutputStream at line 52 follows the attacker-planted symlink to write /etc/passwd (CWE-59 link resolution before file access enabling CWE-22).

assumptions: JUCE File::getChildFile lexically normalizes '..' and absolute components, and File::isAChildOf therefore rejects purely lexical '../' zip-slip; this was verified against the guard at line 16 and is the basis for dismissing the classic traversal-only candidate.
Exploitation of the symlink chain assumes the caller extracts multiple entries from one attacker-supplied archive (the normal uncompress workflow), which this function is the boundary for.
zei->entry.isSymbolicLink derives from the zip entry's Unix mode bits, which the attacker controls when crafting the archive.
limitations: entries.getUnchecked(index) performs no bounds check on the caller-supplied index, but index is an internal library API parameter not attacker-influenced; not counted as a vulnerability in this code.

A TOCTOU window exists between hasSymbolicPart (line 36) / exists() / deleteFile() (lines 27-33) and the FileOutputStream open (line 52); it requires an external racing local process and is redundant with the confirmed symlink path, so it is noted but not separately counted.
zei->entry.fileTime is attacker-controlled metadata passed to setCreationTime/setLastModificationTime/setLastAccessTime; impact is limited to timestamp forging with no memory-safety consequence.

When overwriteFiles == no and targetFile already exists as a pre-planted symlink, the function returns Result::ok() leaving the attacker artifact in place; minor fail-open behavior subsumed by the primary symlink finding.

verdict.summary: MariaDB/MySQL open_table(): attacker-controlled inputs (db name, table name, alias, partition names) are consumed only at guarded sinks — the db string is NULL-checked before every use, the memcmp is preceded by a length-equality check, partition-name and sequence mismatches produce explicit errors, and fixed-size allocations are checked. Reference handling (tdc_release_share / tc_release_table) is balanced on every path: err_lock is reachable only when no TABLE reference is held, the flushed-share paths release exactly one reference and reacquire before retry, and the mdl_ticket NULL case is guarded on the acquiring path while the MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK path relies on the documented caller contract. No memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, input-validation, or fail-open defect with a reachable trigger was found in this code as written.

assumptions: Callers honor the documented MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK contract (mdl_request.ticket was acquired by the caller before the call), as stated in the code's own comment.

table_list->alias.str is NUL-terminated by the SQL parser/lexer layer, per the invariant relied on identically by upstream MySQL/MariaDB where this same expression is used with my_strcasecmp and my_error.
Cross-thread table-definition-cache state is protected by the MDL/TDC locking protocol implemented outside this function.
DBUG_ASSERTs are compiled out in release builds and were not treated as guards.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: NULL dereference of mdl_ticket when MYSQL_OPEN_HAS_MDL_LOCK is set with a NULL ticket — requires a caller to violate the documented contract; not reachable from inputs this code validates.
Candidate dismissed: potential read past end of alias if it were not NUL-terminated — termination is guaranteed by the upstream parser invariant, not by this function; no trigger producible here.

Candidate dismissed: non-termination of the retry_share loop — loop progress depends on tdc_wait_for_old_version, which either succeeds after the old share is gone or times out; no unbounded loop constructible within this code.

Robustness-only observations, no security impact: some DBUG_RETURN(TRUE) paths (e.g., mdl_ticket==NULL, wait_result failure) rely on the Open_table_context backoff machinery to set/propagate errors; my_malloc failure is handled but my_error reporting is delegated to MY_WME; the ER_TABLE_NOT_LOCKED error uses the alias captured at function entry, which is safe since table_list is not reassigned.

verdict.summary: In the ASCII mesh-reading path, GmfOpenMesh reads whitespace-delimited tokens from the (attacker-controlled) mesh file with fscanf("%s", str) into the fixed-size stack buffer char str[GmfStrSiz], without any field-width limit. A token longer than GmfStrSiz bytes anywhere before the MeshVersionFormatted or Dimension keywords overflows the stack buffer with fully attacker-controlled file content, enabling stack memory corruption and potential code execution. The binary path validates cod/ver/dim, but the ASCII token-scan loops enforce no length constraint at all.

evidence.reason: Unbounded %s conversion writes an arbitrary-length token from the opened mesh file (data crossing a trust boundary) into the fixed stack buffer str[GmfStrSiz]. Trigger: an ASCII .mesh file whose first token exceeds GmfStrSiz bytes; the loop at lines 125-128 reads tokens until a match, so the oversized token overflows the buffer on its own iteration. No width limiter or length check exists anywhere on this path.

Second occurrence of the same unbounded %s read into the fixed stack buffer str[GmfStrSiz], while scanning for the Dimension keyword. Trigger: a valid MeshVersionFormatted header followed by any token longer than GmfStrSiz before the Dimension keyword; the token overflows str with attacker-controlled file bytes.

assumptions: GmfStrSiz is a small compile-time constant (in libMeshb it is 512), so a token longer than it is trivially placeable in a mesh file.
The mesh file being parsed is untrusted input in the threat model (files supplied by external sources, e.g., simulation/import pipelines).
Helper functions (ScaWrd, ScaKwdTab, RecWrd, GmfSetKwd) are not shown; no findings are claimed about their internals.
limitations: (*PtrVer)/(*PtrDim) output-pointer writes rely on the documented variadic API contract; NULL pointers require a contract-violating caller, not file data, so this is not a vulnerability in this code.
strlen(FilNam)+7 integer overflow would require a near-2^64-byte filename; unreachable.
The setjmp/longjmp error handler leaks nothing and is fail-closed (returns 0 on every parse error); no fail-open path found.
Uninitialized FilDes concern is void: calloc zero-initializes the structure, so the cleanup branch checks are safe.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced inputs (file contents: endian tag, version, keyword code, dimension; ASCII tokens; filename) are validated before use at every sink in this function: msh->cod is restricted to {1, 16777216}, msh->ver to 1..4, KwdCod to GmfDimension, msh->dim to {2,3} before the PtrDim/PtrVer writes; strcpy into the fixed FilNam buffer is preceded by an explicit length check; ASCII token reads use a bounded %100s width that fits str[GmfStrSiz]. The only defects found are a fixed-size memory/file-handle leak on the ScaKwdTab failure path and missing NULL checks on caller-supplied API parameters (FilNam, PtrVer, PtrDim), which require caller contract violations or unbounded external retry loops and cause no memory-safety violation in this code.

assumptions: GmfStrSiz is the canonical libMeshb value (1024), so the %100s fscanf width (max 101 bytes including NUL) fits str[GmfStrSiz]; if GmfStrSiz were defined smaller than 101, the ASCII token reads would overflow, but that contradicts the constant's use as the filename buffer whose length check reserves 7 extra bytes.
WrdSiz equals sizeof(int) (4), so read()/safe_fread of WrdSiz bytes into the int fields cod/ver/KwdCod/dim is in-bounds.

External helpers (ScaWrd, safe_fread, safe_fscanf, ScaKwdTab, RecWrd, GmfSetKwd) enforce their own error handling (the safe_* wrappers take the jmp_buf and longjmp on failure); their internals are not shown and are outside this analysis.
limitations: Resource leak (robustness, not confirmed as a vulnerability here): on the read path, 'if(!ScaKwdTab(msh)) return(0);' returns without freeing msh or closing msh->hdl/msh->FilDes, unlike all longjmp error paths which do clean up. Reachable with a corrupted attacker-supplied mesh file, but each occurrence leaks only one fixed-size struct and one descriptor; exhaustion would require the host application to repeatedly call GmfOpenMesh on failing files, which is outside this code's control.

Missing NULL-pointer checks on API parameters: strlen(FilNam) crashes if the caller passes NULL, and (*PtrVer)/(*PtrDim) writes crash on NULL output pointers. Both require the caller to violate the documented API contract (valid filename string, valid int* outputs), so they are not vulnerabilities in this code.
MshIdx = (int64_t)msh narrows a pointer to 64 bits; only relevant on hypothetical >64-bit pointer platforms.

fscanf token loops rescan in 100-byte chunks when tokens exceed 100 characters; a malformed but non-EOF stream longer than the keyword never terminates the scan loop, a potential read-only hang on pathological files.
